Name: ClpA/B, conserved site 2
ShortDescription:
The ClpA/B family of ATP-binding proteins includes the regulatory subunit of the ATP-dependent protease Clp, ClpA; heat shock proteins ClpB, 104 and 78; and chloroplast proteins CD4a (ClpC) and CD4b [[cite:PUB00004102], [cite:PUB00004707]]. The proteins are thought to protect cells from stress by controlling the aggregation and denaturation of vital cellular structures. They vary in size, but share two conserved regions of about 200 amino acids that each contains an ATP-binding site [[cite:PUB00004707]].

This entry represents a conserved site found in the second conserved region.

Proteins containing this site are listed below:

  • Escherichia coli clpA, which acts as the regulatory subunit of the ATP- dependent protease clp.
  • Rhodopseudomonas blastica clpA homolog.
  • Escherichia coli heat shock protein clpB and homologues in other bacteria.
  • Bacillus subtilis protein mecB.
  • Yeast heat shock protein 104 (gene HSP104), which is vital for tolerance to heat, ethanol and other stresses.
  • Neurospora heat shock protein hsp98.
  • Yeast mitochondrial heat shock protein 78 (gene HSP78) [[cite:PUB00003691]].
  • CD4A and CD4b, two highly related tomato proteins that seem to be located in the chloroplast.
  • Trypanosoma brucei protein clp.
  • Porphyra purpurea chloroplast encoded clpC.

Name: ClpA/B family
ShortDescription:
This family belongs to the AAA+ (ATPase associated with diverse cellular activities) superfamily. Most of these proteins of this family (ClpA, ClpC, ClpD, ClpE, ClpX, HslU) are involved in proteolysis and associate with a separate proteolytic subunit (ClpP, HslV) to form the active protease. ClpB is not involved in proteolysis but rather acts in collaboration with the DnaK (Hsp70) chaperone system to disassemble and refold large protein aggregates.

A group of ATP-binding proteins that includes the regulatory subunit of the ATP-dependent protease clpA; heat shock proteins clpB, 104 and 78; and chloroplast proteins CD4a (ClpC) and CD4b belong to this family [[cite:PUB00004102], [cite:PUB00004707]]. The proteins are thought to protect cells from stress by controlling the aggregation and denaturation of vital cellular structures. They vary in size, but share a domain which contains an ATP-binding site.

These signatures which span the ATP binding region also identify the bacterial DNA polymerase III subunit tau ([ec:2.7.7.7]), ATP-dependent protease La ([ec:3.4.21.53]) and the mitochondrial lon protease homologue ([ec:3.4.21]), both of which belong to MEROPS peptidase family S16.

This entry also includes Mitochondrial disaggregase from vertebrates, which despite its gene name (CLPB), this protein differs in domain structure from bacterial ClpB. Bacterial ClpB contains two AAA modules, one in the N-terminal part of the protein and one in the C-terminal part, separated by a coiled coil, while vertebrate CLPB contains a single C-terminal AAA region and an N-terminal ANK repeat region which is absent from bacterial ClpB.

;

Clp proteins are modular ATP-dependent chaperones and proteases that typically contain distinct domains essential for their function. Most Clp proteins have an N-terminal domain that often determines substrate specificity or interacts with adaptor proteins. In some Clp proteins, the N-domains are attached through flexible linkers to the corresponding AAA+ protein rings and mediate substrate specificity either directly or indirectly by serving as a binding platform for adaptor proteins that deliver their protein cargo upon binding to the AAA+ partner protein [[cite:PUB00106739]]. The central region usually comprises one or two AAA+ domains, also known as D1 and D2 domains, which provide the energy for substrate unfolding and translocation [[cite:PUB00160474], [cite:PUB00160475]]. In some Clp proteins, such as ClpV, the C-terminal region is involved in interactions with components of the type VI secretion system (T6SS) [[cite:PUB00093976]].

This entry represents a conserved site found in the first conserved region.

Name: Chaperonin ClpB
ShortDescription: Members of this protein family include bacterial and plant ATP-dependent chaperone ClpB. This protein belongs to the AAA family of ATPases associated with various cellular activities. This molecular chaperone does not act as a protease, but rather serves to disaggregate misfolded and aggregated proteins [[cite:PUB00043091], [cite:PUB00088088], [cite:PUB00103736]].

Name: ClpA/ClpB, AAA lid domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the α-helical AAA+ lid domain that is found to the C terminus of AAA domains.

;

Proteins containing this domain include ClpA/B [[cite:PUB00004102], [cite:PUB00004707]]. These proteins are thought to protect cells from stress by controlling the aggregation and denaturation of vital cellular structures. They vary in size, but share a domain which contains an ATP-binding site.

Name: Clp ATPase, C-terminal
ShortDescription: Most Clp ATPases form complexes with peptidase subunits and are involved in protein degradation, though some, such as ClpB, do not associate with peptidases and are involved in protein disaggregation [[cite:PUB00045432]]. This entry represents the C-terminal domain of Clp ATPases, often referred to as the D2-small domain, which forms a mixed α-β structure. Compared with the adjacent AAA D1-small domain ([interpro:IPR003959]) it lacks the long coiled-coil insertion, and instead of helix C4 contains a β-strand (e3) that is part of a three stranded β-pleated sheet. In Thermophilus the whole protein forms a hexamer with the D1-small and D2-small domains located on the outside of the hexamer, with the long coiled-coil being exposed on the surface. The D2-small domain is essential for oligomerisation, forming a tight interface with the D2-large domain of a neighbouring subunit, thereby providing enough binding energy to stabilise the functional assembly [[cite:PUB00030406]].

Name: ATP-dependent Clp protease/Chaperone ClpA/ClpB
ShortDescription: The ClpA/ClpB family proteins are molecular chaperones and ATP-dependent proteases that play crucial roles in stress responses, particularly in the recovery of cells from heat-induced damage. They are involved in the disaggregation, solubilization, and refolding of denatured protein aggregates, acting in cooperation with other chaperones such as DnaK, DnaJ, and GrpE. The ClpB chaperones have ATPase activity, which is stimulated by protein binding; the subsequent ATP hydrolysis unfolds the denatured protein aggregates. This unfolding exposes new hydrophobic binding sites on the surface of ClpB-bound aggregates, aiding in their solubilization and refolding by DnaK. The ClpA/ClpB family proteins contain nucleotide-binding domains responsible for ATP hydrolysis and oligomerization, and a coiled-coil domain essential for the rescue of proteins from an aggregated state. Some family members are also involved in the degradation of proteins by proteases like ClpP, regulation of genetic competence, and mitochondrial-mediated antiviral innate immunity.

Name: TIFY/JAZ family
ShortDescription: JASMONATE ZIM-domain (JAZ) proteins act as repressors of jasmonate (JA) signaling [[cite:PUB00090915]]. The ZIM domain recruits the co-repressors NINJA and TOPLESS to JAZ-bound transcription factors, and contains a highly conserved TIF[F/Y]XG motif that defines the larger family of TIFY proteins to which JAZs belong. This family consists of TIFY/JAZ proteins, and also includes JAZ13 (At3g22275), a non-TIFY JAZ protein that is a repressor of JA signaling [[cite:PUB00090916]]. Some of the members of the TIFY/JAZ family, such as TIFY8, are not involved in JA signaling. TIFY8 is found in protein complexes involved in regulation of dephosphorylation, deubiquitination and O-linked N-acetylglucosamine modification, suggesting an important role in nuclear signal transduction [[cite:PUB00090920]].

Name: RING finger E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases that are involved in the ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of various target proteins. They play roles in regulating transcription factors, particularly those with LIM domains, by mediating the degradation of their cofactors. This action allows the transcription factors to interact with other proteins and modulate gene expression. Some family members are involved in the regulation of telomere length and the random inactivation of the X chromosome during embryonic development. They also contribute to the establishment of proper protein complexes by regulating the stoichiometry of specific protein interactions. Additionally, they have roles in cellular processes such as axonal outgrowth and transcriptional regulation of hormone receptors.

Name: DHHA2 domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This domain is called DHHA2 since it is often associated with the DHH domain and is diagnostic of DHH subfamily 2 members [[cite:PUB00005478]]. The domain is about 120 residues long and contains a conserved DXK motif at its amino terminus. It is present in inorganic pyrophosphatases and in exopolyphosphatase of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Name: DDH domain
ShortDescription: This is a domain of predicted phosphoesterases, including Drosophila prune protein and bacterial RecJ exonuclease [[cite:PUB00005478]]. The RecJ protein of Escherichia coli plays an important role in a number of DNA repair and recombination pathways. RecJ catalyses processive degradation of single-stranded DNA in a 5'-to-3' direction. Sequences highly related to those encoding RecJ can be found in many of the eubacterial genomes sequenced to date [[cite:PUB00007151]].

Name: DHH phosphoesterase superfamily
ShortDescription: DHH phosphoesterase superfamily includes manganese-dependent inorganic pyrophosphatase (family II), Drosophila prune protein and bacterial RecJ exonuclease [[cite:PUB00026115]]. Typically, its members consist of two non-similar domains: domain 1 with parallel sheet of 6 strands and domain 2 with mixed sheet of 5 strands.

Name: DHHA2 domain
ShortDescription: This domain is called DHHA2 since it is often associated with the DHH domain ([interpro:IPR001667]) and is diagnostic of DHH subfamily 2 members [[cite:PUB00005478]]. The domain is about 120 residues long and contains a conserved DXK motif at its amino terminus. It is present in inorganic pyrophosphatases and in exopolyphosphatase of Saccharomyces cerevisiae.

Name: ABC1 atypical kinase-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents a domain found in Escherichia coli UbiB, known in Providencia stuartii as Aarf, which is required for ubiquinone (CoQ) biosynthesis [[cite:PUB00013772], [cite:PUB00007385], [cite:PUB00068672]]. Some proteins with this domain are described as aarF domain-containing protein kinases (ADCKs). This domain is also found in yeast ABC1 proteins ([swissprot:P27697]) required for function of the mitochondrial bc1 complex [[cite:PUB00007384]], in which CoQ functions as an essential cofactor.

Name: Mitochondrial structure and function regulator
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes members that are involved in various cellular processes, primarily associated with mitochondrial function and structure. Some proteins within this family appear to play a crucial role in maintaining mitochondrial cristae formation and overall mitochondrial health. They may act in a kinase-independent manner to regulate key mitochondrial structural proteins, although their exact enzymatic activity remains unclear. Additionally, certain members are implicated in the degradation of cell wall material during cell separation, and others are involved in lipid homeostasis within mitochondria. There are also proteins in this family with potential roles in the biosynthesis of antibiotics and in plant immunity as effectors that suppress cell death.

Name: ADCK1-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents a domain found in AarF domain containing kinase 1 (ADCK1) and related proteins. Drosophila ADCK1 plays an important role in maintaining mitochondrial morphologies and functions in the muscle [[cite:PUB00098514]]. Proteins containing this domain also include Mcp2, which is a component of MIOREX complexes, large expressome-like assemblies of ribosomes with factors involved in all the steps of post-transcriptional gene expression [[cite:PUB00076405]]. It is also involved in mitochondrial lipid homeostasis [[cite:PUB00090363]].

Name: Antigen-presenting and immune regulatory MHC class I-related
ShortDescription: The protein family includes antigen-presenting molecules that display peptides or lipid antigens to T-cell receptors, contributing to immune surveillance and response. Members are involved in presenting foreign antigens, including microbial and tumor-derived peptides, to the immune system. Some act as ligands for receptors like KLRK1/NKG2D, mediating natural killer cell cytotoxicity. Others bind self and non-self glycolipids, presenting them to natural killer T-cells. The family also includes proteins that regulate humoral immunity by recycling IgG, extending its half-life, and transferring passive immunity. Additionally, some members bind to transferrin receptor, modulating iron uptake, while others are involved in stress-induced self-antigen recognition or immune regulation at the maternal-fetal interface. Overall, the family plays a crucial role in immune system regulation, pathogen defense, and maintaining homeostasis.

Name: MHC classes I/II-like antigen recognition protein
ShortDescription:
Major Histocompatibility Complex (MHC) glycoproteins are heterodimeric cell surface receptors that function to present antigen peptide fragments to T cells responsible for cell-mediated immune responses. MHC molecules can be subdivided into two groups on the basis of structure and function: class I molecules present intracellular antigen peptide fragments (~10 amino acids) on the surface of the host cells to cytotoxic T cells; class II molecules present exogenously derived antigenic peptides (~15 amino acids) to helper T cells. MHC class I and II molecules are assembled and loaded with their peptide ligands via different mechanisms. However, both present peptide fragments rather than entire proteins to T cells, and are required to mount an immune response.

This superfamily represents MHC class I and II-like antigen-recognition domains from:

  • MHC class II, N-terminal domains of alpha and beta chains [[cite:PUB00025626]]
  • MHC class I, alpha-1 and alpha-2 domains [[cite:PUB00035588]]
  • MHC class I related proteins, such as gammadelta T-cell ligand [[cite:PUB00035589]], Ulbp3 [[cite:PUB00035590]], Fc (IgG) receptor (alpha-1 and -2 domains) [[cite:PUB00025007]], CD1 (alpha-1 and -2 domains) [[cite:PUB00035591]], zinc-alpha-2-glycoprotein ZAG (fat depleting factor) [[cite:PUB00035592]]
  • Immunomodulatory protein m144, alpha-1 and alpha-2 domains [[cite:PUB00035593]]
  • Haemochromatosis protein Hfe, alpha-1 and alpha-2 domains [[cite:PUB00035594]]
  • NK cell ligand RAE-1 beta [[cite:PUB00035595]]
  • Endothelial protein C receptor (phospholipid-binding protein) [[cite:PUB00035596]]

Name: MHC class I-like antigen recognition-like superfamily
ShortDescription:
Class I MHC glycoproteins are expressed on the surface of all somatic nucleated cells, with the exception of neurons. MHC class I receptors present peptide antigens that are synthesised in the cytoplasm, which includes self-peptides (presented for self-tolerance) as well as foreign peptides (such as viral proteins). These antigens are generated from degraded protein fragments that are transported to the endoplasmic reticulum by TAP proteins (transporter of antigenic peptides), where they can bind MHC I molecules, before being transported to the cell surface via the Golgi apparatus [[cite:PUB00007109], [cite:PUB00016272]]. MHC class I receptors display antigens for recognition by cytotoxic T cells, which have the ability to destroy viral-infected or malignant (surfeit of self-peptides) cells.

MHC class I molecules are comprised of two chains: a MHC alpha chain (heavy chain), and a beta2-microglobulin chain (light chain), where only the alpha chain spans the membrane. The alpha chain has three extracellular domains (alpha 1-3, with alpha1 being at the N terminus), a transmembrane region and a C-terminal cytoplasmic tail. The soluble extracellular beta-2 microglobulin chain associates primarily with the alpha-3 domain and is necessary for MHC stability. The alpha1 and alpha2 domains of the alpha chain are referred to as the recognition region, because the peptide antigen binds in a deep groove between these two domains.

  • MHC class I homologue gammadelta T-cell ligand [[cite:PUB00035589]]
  • MHC class I related Ulbp3 [[cite:PUB00035590]]
  • MHC class I related Fc (IgG) receptor, alpha-1 and alpha-2 domains [[cite:PUB00025007]]
  • MHC class I related CD1, alpha-1 and alpha-2 domains [[cite:PUB00035591]]
  • MHC class I related zinc-alpha-2-glycoprotein ZAG (fat depleting factor) [[cite:PUB00035592]]

Name: Cation-dependent O-methyltransferase
ShortDescription: The Cation-dependent O-methyltransferase family is involved in the methylation of various substrates using S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) as the methyl donor. Members of this family play crucial roles in the biosynthesis of phenylpropanoids, alkaloids, and flavonoids, contributing to plant cell wall reinforcement, pigmentation, and defense responses. They catalyze the O-methylation of compounds such as caffeoyl-CoA, norbelladine, and anthocyanins. Some members are implicated in the production of volatile phenylpropanoids in flowers, while others participate in the biosynthesis of bioactive compounds with potential anticancer properties. The family also includes enzymes involved in the modification of tRNA and the biosynthesis of macrolide antibiotics and polymethoxylated flavonoids.

Name: Class I-like SAM-dependent O-methyltransferase
ShortDescription: Members of this family are O-methyltransferases, including catechol O-methyltransferase [[cite:PUB00040056]], caffeoyl-CoA O-methyltransferase [[cite:PUB00031205]] and norbelladine 4'-O-methyltransferase [[cite:PUB00085191]]. The family includes also bacterial O-methyltransferases that may be involved in antibiotic production [[cite:PUB00003596], [cite:PUB00094548]].

Name: Active regulator of SIRT1
ShortDescription: Human SIRT1, an NAD+-dependent deacetylase, plays a role in cell death/ survival, senescence, and endocrine signalling [[cite:PUB00054115]]. Its substrates are well characterised, but evidence for the identity of its direct regulators has been wanting. Recently, the nuclear protein AROS (also termed 40S ribosomal protein S19-binding protein 1 [[cite:PUB00054116]]) has been implicated in the direct regulation of SIRT1 function - this protein has been dubbed 'active regulator of SIRT1. The protein has been shown to enhance SIRT1-mediated deacetylation of p53, in vitro and in vivo, and to inhibit p53-mediated transcriptional activity. It is the first direct SIRT1 regulator to have been identified that modulates p53-mediated growth regulation.

Name: Chondroitin sulfate glycosyltransferase
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in the biosynthesis of chondroitin sulfate, a key component of the extracellular matrix in cartilage. Members of this family exhibit glycosyltransferase activity, transferring glucuronic acid and N-acetylgalactosamine from their respective UDP-sugar donors to the growing chondroitin polymer. These enzymes play crucial roles in cartilage formation and endochondral ossification, a process where bone tissue is created. Some family members are also implicated in the metabolism of aggrecan, a major proteoglycan in cartilage, and in various developmental processes including cell division, cytokinesis, and neural development. Additionally, certain enzymes within this family are involved in the synthesis of N,N'-diacetyllactosediamine structures on glycoproteins, which are important for cell-cell interactions and signaling.

Name: Chondroitin N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferase
ShortDescription:
This family represents Chondroitin N-acetylgalactosaminyltransferases. Proteins have a type II transmembrane topology. The enzyme is involved in the biosynthetic initiation and elongation of chondroitin sulphate and is the key enzyme responsible for the selective chain assembly of chondroitin/dermatan sulphate on the linkage region tetrasaccharide common to various proteoglycans containing chondroitin/dermatan sulphate or heparin/heparan sulphate chains [[cite:PUB00019302], [cite:PUB00019303]].

This entry also includes non-catalytic components of CHSY1-CHPF2 and CHSY3-CHPF2 chondroitin sulfate synthase complexes such as Chondroitin polymerizing factor, non-catalytic subunit from human. CHPF associates with catalytically active chondroitin synthases (CHSY1/3) within heterodimeric complexes. It plays an essential role for the formation of a stable and functional chondroitin sulfate polymerase complexes [[cite:PUB00164805]].

Name: F-box-like domain superfamily
ShortDescription: First identified in cyclin-F as a protein-protein interaction motif, the F-box is a conserved domain that is present in numerous proteins with a bipartite structure [[cite:PUB00000938]]. Through the F-box, these proteins are linked to the Skp1 protein and the core of SCFs (Skp1-cullin-F-box protein ligase) complexes. SCFs complexes constitute a new class of E3 ligases [[cite:PUB00000952]]. They function in combination with the E2 enzyme Cdc34 to ubiquitinate G1 cyclins, Cdk inhibitors and many other proteins, to mark them for degradation. The binding of the specific substrates by SCFs complexes is mediated by divergent protein-protein interaction motifs present in F-box proteins, like WD40 repeats, leucine rich repeats [[cite:PUB00018180], [cite:PUB00018181]] or ANK repeats.

Name: Carbohydrate-binding/sugar hydrolysis domain
ShortDescription: The CASH domain is shared by many carbohydrate-binding proteins and sugar hydrolases. The CASH domain is characterised by internal repetitions of glycines and hydrophobic residues that correspond to the repetitive units of a predicted or observed right-handed β-helix structure of the pectate lyase superfamily. The basic structural unit of this family consists of three β-strands that form a single turn of the β-helix. Each turn contains ~20 amino acids, and is normally repeated between 7 and 11 times to form the elongated helix structure. The repeats show a low degree of sequence identity when compared with each other. The region of homology with the CASH domain corresponds to the core region of the β-helix, covering from the second to the sixth repeat [[cite:PUB00007977]].

Name: Parallel beta-helix repeat
ShortDescription: The tertiary structures of pectate lyases and rhamnogalacturonase A show a stack of parallel β-strands that are coiled into a large helix. Each coil of the helix represents a structural repeat that, in some homologues, can be recognised from sequence information alone. Conservation of asparagines might be connected with asparagine-ladders that contribute to the stability of the fold. Proteins containing these repeats most often are enzymes with polysaccharide substrates [[cite:PUB00009696]].

Name: SCF Complex Subunits and Alginate Epimerases
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes components of SCF (SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein) E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complexes, which are involved in the ubiquitination and proteasomal degradation of various target proteins. They play roles in cell cycle regulation, apoptosis, immune response, and differentiation. Some members mediate the degradation of specific substrates, such as BCL6, DTL, and p53, influencing processes like TGF-beta signaling, erythropoiesis, and antiviral responses. Other members are involved in the epimerization of polysaccharides during the synthesis of alginate, contributing to the protection of alginate from degradation and its transport through bacterial cells.

Name: F-box only protein 11, F-box domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the F-box domain of UBR11 and similar animal proteins. This domain has a role in mediating protein-protein interactions in a variety of contexts, such as polyubiquitination, transcription elongation, centromere binding and translational repression.

;

F-box only protein 11 (FBXO11, also called UBR6 and VIT-1) is an E3 ubiquitin ligase and a type II methyltransferase, which functions as a key regulator of tumour initiation and progression. FBXO11 is a substrate recognition component of a SCF (SKP1-CUL1-F-box protein) E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase complex which mediates the ubiquitination and subsequent proteasomal degradation of target proteins, such as DTL/CDT2, BCL6 and PRDM1/BLIMP1. FBXO11 does not bind N-terminal signals [[cite:PUB00103345], [cite:PUB00103342], [cite:PUB00103339], [cite:PUB00072405], [cite:PUB00103349], [cite:PUB00103340], [cite:PUB00103338], [cite:PUB00103343], [cite:PUB00103347], [cite:PUB00103337], [cite:PUB00103344], [cite:PUB00103346]]. In humans, the gene encoding this protein has been associated to intellectual developmental disorders [[cite:PUB00103348], [cite:PUB00103341]].

ShortDescription:
This entry represents the UBR-box of UBR11, its homologue from C.elegans dre-1 and similar proteins from animals.

Name: Right handed beta helix domain
ShortDescription: This region contains a parallel β-helix region that shares some similarity with Pectate lyases.

Name: Parallel beta-helix repeat-2
ShortDescription: This model represents a tandem pair of an approximately 22-amino acid (each) repeat homologous to the β-strand repeats that stack in a right-handed parallel β-helix in the periplasmic C-5 mannuronan epimerase, AlgA, of Pseudomonas aeruginosa. A homology domain consisting of a longer tandem array of these repeats is described in the SMART database as CASH (SM00722), and is found in many carbohydrate-binding proteins and sugar hydrolases. A single repeat is represented by SM00710. This TIGRFAMs model represents a flavor of the parallel β-helix-forming repeat based on prokaryotic sequences only in its seed alignment, although it also finds many eukaryotic sequences [[cite:PUB00007977]].

Name: Zinc finger, UBR-type
ShortDescription:
It has been observed that the identity of N-terminal residues of a protein is related to the half life of the protein. This observation yields a rule, called the N-end rule [[cite:PUB00033766]]. Similar but distinct versions of the N-end rule operate in all organisms examined, from mammals to fungi and bacteria. In eukaryotes, the N-end rule pathway is a part of the ubiquitin degradation system. Some proteins that have a very short half life contain a specific motif at their N terminus, the N-degron. It consists of a destabilising N-terminal residue and an internal Lys, which is the site of poly-Ub chain [[cite:PUB00033766], [cite:PUB00033767]].

The UBR1 protein was shown to bind specifically to proteins bearing N-terminal residues that are destabilising according to the N-end rule, but not to otherwise identical proteins bearing stabilising N-terminal residues [[cite:PUB00033768]]. UBR1 contains an N-terminal conserved region (the UBR-type zinc finger) which is also found in various proteins implicated in N-degron recognition. The UBR-type zinc finger defines a unique E3 class, most likely N-degron specific [[cite:PUB00033696]].

Name: G-protein-signaling modulator
ShortDescription: The GPSM family includes guanine nucleotide dissociation inhibitors (GDIs) that regulate G-protein signaling independently of G protein-coupled receptors. Members of the GPSM family are involved in maintaining G(i/o) alpha subunits in their GDP-bound state, thus controlling heterotrimeric G-protein signaling. These proteins play crucial roles in mitotic spindle pole organization, cortical dynein-dynactin complex recruitment, and metaphase spindle orientation. They are also essential for asymmetric cell divisions in cerebral cortical progenitors and may influence macroautophagy in intestinal cells. Additionally, GPSM family members are implicated in drug addiction pathways.

Name: GoLoco motif
ShortDescription:
In heterotrimeric G-protein signalling, cell surface receptors (GPCRs) are coupled to membrane-associated heterotrimers comprising a GTP-hydrolysing subunit G-alpha and a G-beta/G-gamma dimer. The inactive form contains the alpha subunit bound to GDP and complexes with the beta and gamma subunit. When the ligand is associated to the receptor, GDP is displaced from G-alpha and GTP is bound. GTP/G-alpha complex dissociates from the trimer and associates to an effector until the intrinsic GTPase activity of G-alpha returns the protein to GDP bound form. Reassociation of GDP bound G-alpha with G-beta/G-gamma dimer terminates the signal. Several mechanisms regulate the signal output at different stage of the G-protein cascade. Two classes of intracellular proteins act as inhibitors of G protein activation: GTPase activating proteins (GAPs), which enhance GTP hydrolysis (see [prositedoc:PDOC50132]), and guanine dissociation inhibitors (GDIs), which inhibit GDP dissociation. The GoLoco or G-protein regulatory (GPR) motif found in various G-protein regulators [[cite:PUB00011827], [cite:PUB00011828]] acts as a GDI on G-alpha(i) [[cite:PUB00011829], [cite:PUB00011830]].

The crystal structure of the GoLoco motif in complex with G-alpha(i) has been solved [[cite:PUB00011831]]. It consists of three small α helices. The highly conserved Asp-Gln-Arg triad within the GoLoco motif participates directly in GDP binding by extending the arginine side chain into the nucleotide binding pocket, highly reminiscent of the catalytic arginine finger employed in GTPase-activating protein (see [prositedoc:PDOC50238]). This addition of an arginine in the binding pocket affects the interaction of GDP with G-alpha and therefore is certainly important for the GoLoco GDI activity [[cite:PUB00011831]].

Some proteins known to contain a GoLoco motif are listed below:

  • Mammalian regulators of G-protein signalling 12 and 14 (RGS12 and RGS14), multifaceted signal transduction regulators.
  • Loco, the drosophila RGS12 homologue.
  • Mammalian Purkinje-cell protein-2 (Pcp2). It may function as a cell-type specific modulator for G protein-mediated cell signalling. It is uniquely expressed in cerebellar Purkinje cells and in retinal bipolar neurons.
  • Eukaryotic Rap1GAP. A GTPase activator for the nuclear ras-related regulatory protein RAP-1A.
  • Drosophila protein Rapsynoid (also known as Partner of Inscuteable, Pins) and its mammalian homologues AGS3 and LGN. They form a G-protein regulator family that also contains TPR repeats.

Name: DELLA, N-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription: Gibberellins are plant hormones which have great impact on growth signalling. DELLA proteins are transcriptional regulators of growth related proteins that lack a DNA binding domain and exert its negative regulation of gibberellin responses through interaction with other transcription factors [[cite:PUB00097402]]. DELLAs are downregulated when gibberellins bind to their receptor GID1 [[cite:PUB00097402], [cite:PUB00050430]], which forms a complex with DELLA proteins and signals them towards 26S proteasome. The N-terminal of DELLA proteins contains conserved DELLA and TVHYNP motifs which are important for GID1 binding and proteolysis of the DELLA proteins [[cite:PUB00050430], [cite:PUB00097403]].

Name: Transcriptional factor DELLA, N-terminal
ShortDescription: Gibberellins are plant hormones which have great impact on growth signalling. DELLA proteins are transcriptional regulators of growth related proteins that lack a DNA binding domain and exert its negative regulation of gibberellin responses through interaction with other transcription factors [[cite:PUB00097402]]. DELLAs are downregulated when gibberellins bind to their receptor GID1 [[cite:PUB00097402], [cite:PUB00050430]], which forms a complex with DELLA proteins and signals them towards 26S proteasome. The N-terminal of DELLA proteins contains conserved DELLA and TVHYNP motifs which are important for GID1 binding and proteolysis of the DELLA proteins [[cite:PUB00050430], [cite:PUB00097403]].

Name: Transcription factor GRAS
ShortDescription:
Sequence analysis of the products of the GRAS (GAI, RGA, SCR) gene family indicates that they share a variable N terminus and a highly conserved C terminus that contains five recognizable motifs [[cite:PUB00008372]]. Proteins in the GRAS family are major players in gibberellin (GA) signaling, which regulates various aspects of plant growth and development [[cite:PUB00008372]]. Mutation of the SCARECROW (SCR) gene results in a radial pattern defect, loss of a ground tissue layer, in the root. The PAT1 protein is involved in phytochrome A signal transduction [[cite:PUB00008373]].

A sequence, structure and evolutionary analysis showed that the GRAS family emerged in bacteria and belongs to the Rossmann-fold, AdoMET (SAM)-dependent methyltransferase superfamily [[cite:PUB00066769]]. All bacterial, and a subset of plant GRAS proteins, are predicted to be active and function as small-molecule methylases. Several plant GRAS proteins lack one or more AdoMet (SAM)-binding residues while preserving their substrate-binding residues. Although GRAS proteins are implicated to function as transcriptional factors, the above analysis suggests that they instead might either modify or bind small molecules [[cite:PUB00066769]].

    Some proteins known to belong to the GRAS family are listed below:
  • Arabidopsis thaliana SCARECROW (SCR) protein. It regulates asymetric cell divisions of cortex/endodermal initial cells during root development.
  • Arabidopsis thaliana SCARECROW-LIKE (SCL) protein.
  • Arabidopsis thaliana GIBBERELLIN-ACID INSENSITIVE (GAI) and REPRESSOR OF GA1 (RGA), two closely related proteins involved in gibberellin signaling.
  • Arabidopsis thaliana SHORT ROOT (SHR) protein. It is necessary for cell division and endodermis specification.
  • Arabidopsis thaliana PAT1 protein. It inhibits light signaling via the phytochrome A (phyA).
  • LATERAL SUPPRESSOR (LS), a protein from tomato that controls the formation of lateral branches during vegetative development.

Name: Receptor-like cytosolic serine/threonine-protein kinase RBK1/2/STUNTED
ShortDescription: This family includes a group of receptor-like cytosolic serine/threonine-protein kinases including RBK1/2 and the protein kinase STUNTED. RBK1 is involved in regulating Casparian strip formation and it also plays a roles in trichome branching and in the control of basal resistance to powdery mildew [[cite:PUB00101468]]. STUNTED promotes cell proliferation in the gibberellic acid (GA) signaling pathway, acting downstream of RGA, and possibly through a negative regulation of two cyclin-dependent kinase inhibitors SIM and SMR1 [[cite:PUB00101469]].

Name: RFX-like DNA-binding protein
ShortDescription:
This entry includes Rfx1 from budding yeasts, Sak1 from fission yeasts and RFX1-8 from humans [[cite:PUB00090092]]. They are transcription factors that contain a RFX DNA binding domain and a conserved C-terminal region [[cite:PUB00090091]].

Mutations in the RFX5 gene cause Bare lymphocyte syndrome 2 (BLS2), a severe combined immunodeficiency disease with early onset [[cite:PUB00069992]]. Mutations in the RFX6 gene cause Mitchell-Riley syndrome (MTCHRS), a disorder characterised by neonatal diabetes, hypoplastic or annular pancreas, duodenal and jejunal atresia, and absent gallbladder [[cite:PUB00094732], [cite:PUB00094733]].

Name: RFX1-4/6/8-like, BCD domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in site specific DNA binding proteins that are members of the RFX family of transcription factors, including human RFX (1-4/6/8) [[cite:PUB00090092]]. Members of this family are found in animals and fungi, and initially were identified as regulatory factors that bind to a conserved cis-regulatory element called the X-box motif. Members of the RFX family contain a highly conserved HTH DNA-binding domain ([interpro:IPR003150]) followed by another conserved domain (BCD) composed of the so-called B, C and D regions which are involved mainly in dimerisation. This entry represents the BCD domain which is predicted to fold into array of α-helices.

Name: DNA-binding RFX-type, winged-helix domain
ShortDescription: The RFX family of transcription factors is characterised by a unique approximately 75-residue DNA-binding domain. RFX genes have been isolated in yeasts, nematode and vertebrates. The characteristic RFX-type HTH DNA binding domain has been recruited into otherwise very divergent regulatory factors functioning in a diverse spectrum of unrelated systems, including regulation of the mitotic cell cycle in fission yeast, the control of the immune response in mammals and infection by human hepatitis B virus [[cite:PUB00057950], [cite:PUB00057951]].

Name: Glycerate kinase-like, C-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription: Two groups of glycerate kinases are known. The first group consists of glycerate kinases from bacterial species, primarily of the Firmicutes group and the gamma subdivision of Proteobacteria. The second group includes TM1585 and glycerate kinases from eukaryotes and archaea in addition to several bacterial species. This entry represents the C-terminal domain of TM1585 and related glycerate kinases [[cite:PUB00039565]].

Name: MOFRL domain-containing protein
ShortDescription:
This entry contains proteins with a C-terminal MOFRL (multi-organism fragment with rich Leucine) domain. Proteins with this domain frequently possess an N-terminal MOFRL-associated domain. The functions of these domains are not known. Proteins with these domains include:

  • Glycerate kinase (GLYCTK; EC 2.7.1.31), which phosphorylates D-glycerate to generate 3-phospho-D-glycerate. D-glyceric aciduria, which can lead to mental retardation or microcephaly, results from mutations in the GLYCTK gene [[cite:PUB00090069], [cite:PUB00066957]].
  • Glycerate 2-kinase (GCK; EC 2.7.1.165), with a similar function but generates 2-phospho-D-glycerate, is found in archaea [[cite:PUB00090070]] and the thermophilic bacteriumThermotoga maritima [[cite:PUB00066956]].
  • Uncharacterized protein C13B9.2 from the nematodeCaenorhabditis elegans.

Name: MOFRL domain
ShortDescription: The MOFRL(multi-organism fragment with rich Leucine) domain is found in bacteria and eukaryotes. The function of this domain is not clear, although it exists in some putative enzymes such as reductases and kinases.

Name: Glycerate kinase, N-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Two groups of glycerate kinases are known, which share no significant sequence similarity. One of the groups includes glycerate kinases from eukaryotes and archaea, in addition to several bacterial species [[cite:PUB00088274]]. TM1585 from Thermotoga maritima, a putative glycerate kinase, belongs to this group.

The TM1585 monomer is comprised of two dissimilar α-β domains: an N-terminal, Rossmann-like domain (residues 23-249) and a C-terminal domain that adopts a new fold. The N-terminal domain has a central, six-stranded, parallel β-sheet and an all-helical subdomain. The active site is likely to be in the cleft between the N- and C-terminal domains [[cite:PUB00039565]].

Name: MOFRL-associated domain
ShortDescription: This domain is frequently found at the N terminus of proteins that carrying the MOFRL domain ([interpro:IPR007835]), some of which are glycerate kinases [[cite:PUB00066957], [cite:PUB00066956]]. However, proteins matched by this entry do not have flavodoxin-like domain ([interpro:IPR018193]) or restriction-enzyme-like fold ([interpro:IPR018197]), which can be found in other type of glycerate kinases ([interpro:IPR004381]).

Name: Choline transporter-like
ShortDescription: This entry includes a group of choline transporter-like protein, including SLC44A1/2/3/4/5 from humans, Pns1 from budding yeasts, and Ctl1 from fission yeasts [[cite:PUB00053886]]. In humans, mutations of this family of proteins have been linked to several human diseases [[cite:PUB00095104]].

Name: COS domain
ShortDescription:
N-terminal RING finger/B-box/coiled coil (RBCC) or tripartite motif (TRIM) proteins, which are found in metazoa, are involved in a vast array of intracellular functions. They appear to function as part of large protein complexes and possess ubiquitin-protein isopeptide ligase activity. The following RBCC proteins contain an ~60-residue COS (C-terminal subgroup one signature) domain, which is also found in a distantly related non-RBCC microtubule-binding protein, GLFND:

  • Vertebrate MID1 and MID2, which associate with microtubules through homo- and heterodimerization
  • Animal TRIM9, which plays a regulatory role in synaptic vesicle exocytosis
  • Mammalian TRIM nine-like (TNL)
  • Mammalian TRIM36, which could play a regulatory role in exocytosis of the sperm vesicle
  • Mammalian tripartite, fibronectin type III and C-terminal B30.2/SPRY (TRIFIC)
  • Mammalian muscle-specific RING finger (MURF) family. MURF proteins have an ability to form both homo- and heterodimers with each other and to associate with the microtubule cytoskeleton

In addition to RBCC, the COS domain is also found in association with B30.2/SPRY or fibronectin type-III (FN3) domains.

The COS domain is predicted to consist of two α-helical coils [[cite:PUB00042940]].

Name: TRIM42, RING-HC finger
ShortDescription: Tripartite motif-containing protein 42 (TRIM42) belongs to the C-III subclass of TRIM (tripartite motif) family of proteins that are defined by their N-terminal RBCC (RING, Bbox, and coiled coil) domains, including three consecutive zinc-binding domains, a C3HC4-type RING-HC finger, Bbox1 and Bbox2, and a coiled coil domain. It also has a novel cysteine-rich motif N-terminal to the RBCC domain, as well as a COS (carboxyl-terminal subgroup one signature) box and a fibronectin type-III (FN3) domain positioned C-terminal to the RBCC domain. TRIM42 can interact with TRIM27, a known cancer-associated protein. Its precise biological function remains unclear [[cite:PUB00042940], [cite:PUB00093298]].

Name: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase TRIM/RNF
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases with a role in innate immune defense, particularly against viral infections [[cite:PUB00155145], [cite:PUB00100805], [cite:PUB00143666], [cite:PUB00151464]]. They mediate ubiquitination of key signalling molecules such as RIG-I and IFIH1/MDA5, which are crucial for the production of interferons in response to viral RNA [[cite:PUB00155146], [cite:PUB00155147]]. Some family members also regulate autophagy, inflammation, and cell survival pathways [[cite:PUB00155144], [cite:PUB00149599], [cite:PUB00151462]]. They can ubiquitinate various substrates, influencing processes like mRNA stability, stress granule formation, and protein degradation. The family is characterised by the presence of a RING-type zinc finger domain, which is essential for their ligase activity, and some members have a B30.2/SPRY domain for substrate interaction. They are involved in modulating signal transduction pathways by ubiquitinating different proteins, thus affecting their stability and function.

Name: TMEM192 family
ShortDescription: The function of this family of transmembrane proteins is unknown. In vertebrates, proteins in this family are located in the lysosomal membrane and late endosome [[cite:PUB00070055], [cite:PUB00070056]]. In Arabidopsis, a member of this family (protein FIP1) has been found to weakly interact with FRIGIDA, a determinant of flowering time [[cite:PUB00070054]].

Name: Palmitoyltransferase PFA4/ZDHHC16/ZDHHC20/ERF2-like
ShortDescription:
This entry includes palmitoyltransferases such as PFA4, ZDHHC16, ZDHHC20, ERF2 from fungi and its homologues.

PFA4 from S. cerevisiae mediates the reversible addition of palmitate to target proteins, thereby regulating their membrane association and biological function. It palmitoylates several amino acid permeases [[cite:PUB00080267]] and chitin synthase CHS3, which is required for its proper export from the ER [[cite:PUB00079982], [cite:PUB00100513]]. ZDHHC16 is a palmitoyl acyltransferase that mediates palmitoylation of proteins such as PLN and ZDHHC6 [[cite:PUB00090229]]. In zebrafish, there are two ZDHHC16 homologues, ZDHHC16A and ZDHHC16B. They are involved in the proliferation of neural stem cells by regulating the FGF/ERK pathway [[cite:PUB00090230]].

Palmitoyltransferase ZDHHC20 can catalyse the addition of palmitate onto various protein substrates [[cite:PUB00155123], [cite:PUB00155124], [cite:PUB00155027]]. It catalyses the palmitoylation of Cys residues in the cytoplasmic C-terminal of EGFR, and modulates the duration of EGFR signalling by modulating palmitoylation-dependent EGFR internalisation and degradation [[cite:PUB00155123]]. ZDHHC20 can also utilise acyl-CoA with C14 and C18 fatty acid chains [[cite:PUB00155124]].

ERF2 from S. cerevisiae forms a complex with SHR5, palmitoyltransferase specific for Ras proteins. It palmitoylates RAS2, which is required for its proper plasma membrane localisation [[cite:PUB00020585]]. In S. pombe it forms a complex with erf4 complex, a palmitoyltransferase with a major role in driving sexual development [[cite:PUB00044889], [cite:PUB00155125]]. It palmitoylates ras1, isp3 and rho3 [[cite:PUB00155125]].

Name: Palmitoyltransferase, DHHC domain
ShortDescription:
This entry refers to the DHHC domain, found in DHHC proteins which are palmitoyltransferases [[cite:PUB00053955]].

Palmitoylation or, more specifically S-acylation, plays important roles in the regulation of protein localization, stability, and activity. It is a post-translational protein modification that involves the attachment of palmitic acid to Cys residues through a thioester linkage. Protein acyltransferases (PATs), also known as palmitoyltransferases, catalyse this reaction by transferring the palmitoyl group from palmitoyl-CoA to the thiol group of Cys residues. They are characterised by the presence of 50-residue-long domain called the DHHC domain, which in most but not all cases is also cysteine-rich and gets its name from a highly conserved DHHC signature tetrapeptide (Asp-His-His-Cys). The Cys residue within the DHHC domain forms a stable acyl intermediate and transfers the acyl chain to the Cys residues of a target protein [[cite:PUB00082711], [cite:PUB00082712]].

Some of the proteins containing a DHHC domain are listed below:

  • Drosophila DNZ1 protein [[cite:PUB00001882]]
  • Mouse Abl-philin 2 (Aph2) protein. Interacts with c-Abl. May play a role in apoptosis [[cite:PUB00082716]]
  • Mammalian ZDHHC9, an integral membrane protein [[cite:PUB00072195]]
  • Yeast ankyrin repeat-containing protein AKR1 [[cite:PUB00033761]]
  • Yeast Erf2 protein. This protein localizes to the endoplasmic reticulum and seems to be important for Ras function [[cite:PUB00005678]]
  • Arabidopsis thaliana tip growth defective 1 [[cite:PUB00033762]]

Name: Peptidase M20
ShortDescription:
This group of proteins contains the metallopeptidases and non-peptidase homologues (amidohydrolases) that belong to the MEROPS peptidase family M20 (clan MH) [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The peptidases of this clan have two catalytic zinc ions at the active site, bound by His/Asp, Asp, Glu, Asp/Glu and His. The catalysed reaction involves the release of an N-terminal amino acid, usually neutral or hydrophobic, from a polypeptide [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The peptidase M20 family has four subfamilies:

  • M20A -type example, glutamate carboxypeptidase from Pseudomonas sp. RS16 ([swissprot:P06621])
  • M20B -type example, peptidase T from Escherichia coli ([swissprot:P29745])
  • M20C -type example, X-His dipeptidase from E. coli ([swissprot:P15288])
  • M20D -type example, carboxypeptidase Ss1 from Sulfolobus solfataricus ([swissprot:P80092])

Homologues from the family that are not peptidases include:

  • Acetylornithine deacetylase, which releases an acetyl group and L-ornithine from N(2)-acetyl-L-ornithine [[cite:PUB00014890]]
  • N-acetyldiaminopimelate deacetylase, which catalyses the conversion of N-acetyl-diaminopimelate to diaminopimelate and acetate [[cite:PUB00085192]]
  • N-carbamoyl-L-amino-acid hydrolase, which converts D,L-5-monosubstituted hydantoins into D-or L-amino acids [[cite:PUB00019732]]
  • Aminoacylase-1, which hydrolyses N-acylated or N-acetylated amino acids [[cite:PUB00030157]]
  • Succinyl-diaminopimelate desuccinylase ([ec:3.5.1.18]), which catalyses the hydrolysis of N-succinyl-L,L-diaminopimelic acid, forming succinate and LL-2,6-diaminoheptanedioate (DAP, a component of bacterial cell walls) [[cite:PUB00079915]]

Name: Peptidase M20/M20A family hydrolases
ShortDescription: The peptidase M20 family is composed of enzymes that catalyze the hydrolysis of various substrates, including dipeptides and specific amino acid derivatives. Members of the peptidase M20A subfamily, such as Xaa-Arg dipeptidases, are involved in metabolite repair mechanisms, specifically by hydrolyzing dipeptides with basic amino acids at the C-terminus, which may be by-products of carnosine synthesis. Other members of the peptidase M20 family, like p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate hydrolases, participate in the cleavage of p-aminobenzoyl-glutamate to p-aminobenzoate and glutamate, a process important in folate metabolism. Additionally, some enzymes, such as indole-3-acetyl-aspartic acid hydrolase, exhibit high substrate specificity, hydrolyzing compounds like indole-3-acetyl-aspartate to indole-3-acetic acid. The diverse functions of the peptidase M20 family reflect its role in various biological processes, including amino acid metabolism, peptide degradation, and plant hormone metabolism.

Name: Xaa-Arg dipeptidase
ShortDescription:
Over 70 metallopeptidase families have been identified to date. In these enzymes a divalent cation, which is usually zinc but may be cobalt, manganese or copper, activates the water molecule. The metal ion is held in place by amino acid ligands, usually three in number. In some families of co-catalytic metallopeptidases, two metal ions are observed in crystal structures ligated by five amino acids, with one amino acid ligating both metal ions. The known metal ligands are His, Glu, Asp or Lys. At least one other residue is required for catalysis, which may play an electrophilic role. Many metalloproteases contain an HEXXH motif, which has been shown in crystallographic studies to form part of the metal-binding site [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The HEXXH motif is relatively common but can be more stringently defined for metalloproteases as 'abXHEbbHbc', where 'a' is most often valine or threonine and forms part of the S1' subsite in thermolysin and neprilysin, 'b' is an uncharged residue, and 'c' a hydrophobic residue. Proline is never found in this site, possibly because it would break the helical structure adopted by this motif in metalloproteases [[cite:PUB00003579]].

;

This family includes Xaa-Arg dipeptidases ([ec:3.4.13.4] also known as beta-Ala-Lys dipeptidases), metallopeptidases that belong to the M20A peptidase family, subfamily D (MEROPS M20.021). These proteins catalyse the peptide bond hydrolysis in dipeptides having basic amino acids lysine, ornithine or arginine at C-terminal. They may function in a metabolite repair mechanism by eliminating alternate dipeptide by-products formed during carnosine synthesis [[cite:PUB00099558]].

Name: Peptidase M20, dimerisation domain
ShortDescription: This domain consists of 4 β-strands and two α-helices which make up the dimerisation surface of members of the MEROPS peptidase family M20 [[cite:PUB00015203]]. This family includes a range of zinc exopeptidases: carboxypeptidases, dipeptidases and specialised aminopeptidases [[cite:PUB00003579]].

Name: Bacterial exopeptidase dimerisation domain
ShortDescription: This superfamily consists of a protein domain with four β strands and two α helices which make up the dimerisation surface of members of the MEROPS peptidase family M20 [[cite:PUB00015203]]. This entry includes a range of zinc exopeptidases: carboxypeptidases, dipeptidases and specialised aminopeptidases [[cite:PUB00003579]].

Name: Ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 13
ShortDescription: This entry represents ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 13 (ANKRD13). At least 4 subtypes are known to exist, termed A-D. ANKRD13C has been experimentally characterised and acts as a chaperone for biogenesis and folding of the DP receptor for prostaglandin D2 [[cite:PUB00057233]]. ANKRD13A/B/D are ubiquitin-binding proteins that specifically recognise and bind Lys-63-linked ubiquitin. They positively regulate the internalisation of ligand-activated EGFR by binding to the Ub moiety of ubiquitinated EGFR at the cell membrane [[cite:PUB00155297]].

Name: Ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 13, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of ankyrin repeat domain-containing protein 13 (ANKRD13). At least 4 subtypes are known to exist, termed A-D. ANKRD13C has been experimentally characterised and acts as a chaperone for biogenesis and folding of the DP receptor for prostaglandin D2 [[cite:PUB00057233]]. ANKRD13A/B/D are ubiquitin-binding proteins that specifically recognise and bind Lys-63-linked ubiquitin. They positively regulate the internalisation of ligand-activated EGFR by binding to the Ub moiety of ubiquitinated EGFR at the cell membrane [[cite:PUB00155297]]. This domain belongs to the LolA/B superfamily of lipoprotein sorting proteins.

Name: Abnormal Spindle-like Microcephaly-associated
ShortDescription: The Abnormal Spindle-like Microcephaly-associated (ASPM) protein family is involved in the regulation and coordination of mitotic spindle dynamics during cell division. Members of this family play a crucial role in maintaining the structure of the centrosomal microtubule organizing center (MTOC) and are essential for proper neurogenesis, germ cell mitosis, and oocyte differentiation. They interact with the katanin complex, enhancing microtubule severing activity and influencing microtubule dynamics at spindle poles, including spindle orientation, astral microtubule density, and poleward microtubule flux. The family's ability to block microtubule minus-end growth is also modulated by its association with the katanin complex.

Name: Abnormal spindle-like microcephaly-associated protein, ASH domain
ShortDescription: The ASH (ASPM-SPD-2-Hydin) domain or N-terminal domain of abnormal spindle-like microcephaly-associated protein (ASPM) is found in proteins associated with cilia, flagella, the centrosome and the Golgi complex [[cite:PUB00075914], [cite:PUB00075915]]. The domain is also found in Hydin and OCRL whose deficiencies are associated with hydrocephalus and Lowe oculocerebrorenal syndrome (OCRL), respectively. The presence of ASH in centrosomal and ciliary proteins indicates that ASPM may possess roles not only in mitotic spindle regulation, but also in ciliary and flagellar function [[cite:PUB00075913]].

Name: E2F Family
ShortDescription: The E2F family of transcription factors plays a crucial role in the control of cell cycle [[cite:PUB00096666], [cite:PUB00096667]] and action of tumour suppressor proteins. This family consists of eight members and is divided into activators (E2F1-3) and repressors (E2F4-8) depending on cellular context, target gene and cofactors [[cite:PUB00096666]]. The E2F proteins contain several evolutionarily conserved domains found in most members of the family. These domains include a DNA-binding domain, a dimerisation domain which determines interaction with the differentiation regulated transcription factor proteins (DP), a transactivation domain enriched in acidic amino acids, and a tumour suppressor protein association domain which is embedded within the transactivation domain [[cite:PUB00008097]]. Classical E2Fs (E2F1-6) contain one DNA-binding domain which form heterodimers with DP proteins; atypical family members, E2F7 and E2F8, possess two DNA-binding domains, form homodimers or heterodimers, thus regulating transcription in a DP-independent manner [[cite:PUB00096666]].

Name: E2F/DP family, winged-helix DNA-binding domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the DNA-binding domain of the E2F and DP proteins, which have a fold related to the winged-helix DNA-binding motif [[cite:PUB00019485]]. The mammalian transcription factor E2F plays an important role in regulating the expression of genes that are required for passage through the cell cycle. Multiple E2F family members have been identified that bind to DNA as heterodimers, interacting with proteins known as DP - the dimerisation partners [[cite:PUB00008097]].

Name: Actin-binding Rho-activating protein
ShortDescription: Actin-binding Rho-activating protein is also known as striated muscle activator of Rho-dependent signaling (STARS) in mouse and myocyte stress 1 (MS1) in rat. STARS acts as an activator of serum response factor (SRF)-dependent transcription, possibly by inducing nuclear translocation of MKL1 or MKL2 and through a mechanism requiring Rho-actin signaling [[cite:PUB00060030], [cite:PUB00060031]].

Name: Costars domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the Costars domain superfamily.

;

This domain is found both alone (in the costars family of proteins) and at the C terminus of actin-binding Rho-activating protein (ABRA). It binds to actin, and in muscle regulates the actin cytoskeleton and cell motility [[cite:PUB00060030], [cite:PUB00067376]]. It has a winged helix-like fold consisting of three α-helices and four antiparallel β strands. Unlike typical winged helix proteins it does not bind to DNA, but contains a hydrophobic groove which may be responsible for interaction with other proteins [[cite:PUB00067375]].

Name: Costars domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found both alone (in the costars family of proteins) and at the C terminus of actin-binding Rho-activating protein (ABRA). It binds to actin, and in muscle regulates the actin cytoskeleton and cell motility [[cite:PUB00060030], [cite:PUB00067376]]. It has a winged helix-like fold consisting of three α-helices and four antiparallel β strands. Unlike typical winged helix proteins it does not bind to DNA, but contains a hydrophobic groove which may be responsible for interaction with other proteins [[cite:PUB00067375]].

Name: Pseudouridine synthase I, TruA
ShortDescription:
This entry represents pseudouridine synthase I (TruA) from prokaryotes and tRNA pseudouridine synthase 1 (Pus1) from eukaryotes, which belongs to the TruA family. TruA from Escherichia coli modifies positions uracil-38, U-39 and/or U-40 in tRNA [[cite:PUB00015686], [cite:PUB00042017]]. TruA contains one atom of zinc essential for its native conformation and tRNA recognition and has a strictly conserved aspartic acid that is likely to be involved in catalysis [[cite:PUB00000455]]. This protein adopts a dimeric assembly and shows two positively charged, RNA-binding clefts along their surface. Each cleft contains a highly conserved aspartic acid located at its centre. The structural domains have a topological similarity to those of other RNA-binding proteins, though the mode of interaction with tRNA appears to be unique. Pus1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae acts at positions 27 and 28 of tRNAs, at positions 34 and 36 of intron-containing precursor tRNA(Ile), at position 35 in the intron-containing tRNA(Tyr) and at position 44 in U2 snRNA [[cite:PUB00091708], [cite:PUB00100729], [cite:PUB00100731]]. This enzyme also catalyses pseudouridylation of mRNAs [[cite:PUB00100730]].

;

Pseudouridine synthases catalyse the isomerisation of uridine to pseudouridine (Psi) in a variety of RNA molecules, and may function as RNA chaperones. Pseudouridine is the most abundant modified nucleotide found in all cellular RNAs. There are four distinct families of pseudouridine synthases that share no global sequence similarity, but which do share the same fold of their catalytic domain(s) and uracil-binding site and are descended from a common molecular ancestor. The catalytic domain consists of two subdomains, each of which has an α+β structure that has some similarity to the ferredoxin-like fold (note: some pseudouridine synthases contain additional domains). The active site is the most conserved structural region of the superfamily and is located between the two homologous domains. These families are [[cite:PUB00045922], [cite:PUB00092579]]:

  • Pseudouridine synthase I, TruA.
  • Pseudouridine synthase II, TruB, which contains and additional C-terminal PUA domain.
  • Pseudouridine synthase RsuA. RluB, RluE and RluF are also part of this family.
  • Pseudouridine synthase RluA. TruC, RluC and RluD belong to this family.
  • Pseudouridine synthase TruD, which has a natural circular permutation in the catalytic domain, as well as an insertion of a family-specific α+β subdomain.
