This entry also includes the N-terminal domain of several different pseudouridine synthases from family 3, including: RsuA (acts on small ribosomal subunit), RluB, RluE and RluF (act on large ribosomal subunit).

RsuA from Escherichia coli catalyses formation of pseudouridine at position 516 in 16S rRNA during assembly of the 30S ribosomal subunit [[cite:PUB00018355], [cite:PUB00037953]]. RsuA consists of an N-terminal domain connected by an extended linker to the central and C-terminal domains. Uracil and UMP bind in a cleft between the central and C-terminal domains near the catalytic residue Asp 102. The N-terminal domain shows structural similarity to the ribosomal protein S4. Despite only 15% amino acid identity, the other two domains are structurally similar to those of the tRNA-specific psi-synthase TruA, including the position of the catalytic Asp. All four families of pseudouridine synthases share the same fold of their catalytic domain(s) and uracil-binding site.

RluB, RluE and RluF are homologous enzymes which each convert specific uridine bases in E. coli ribosomal 23S RNA to pseudouridine:

  • RluB modifies uracil-2605.
  • RluE modifies uracil-3457.
  • RluF modifies uracil-2604 and to a lesser extent U-2605.

Name: ORMDL family
ShortDescription: ORMDL family members include ORMDL1/2/3 from humans and their homologues, such as protein Orm1 and Orm2 from budding yeasts. ORMDLs may be involved in protein folding in the endoplasmic reticulum [[cite:PUB00019967]]. In budding yeast, Orm1 and Orm2 proteins mediate sphingolipid homeostasis [[cite:PUB00071216]].

Name: Sex comb on midleg-like, SAM domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the SAM (sterile alpha motif) domain of Polycomb-group proteins from the Scm (Sex comb on midleg) subfamily, including Scm from Drosophila melanogaster and human SCML1/2/4. It is a protein-protein interaction domain. Members of this group are found mainly in vertebrates and arthropods.

;

The Scm (Sex comb on midleg) subfamily of Polycomb group includes transcriptional repressors associated with PRC1 complex. Originally the Scm protein was described in Drosophila as a regulator required for proper spatial expression of homeotic genes [[cite:PUB00018531]]. It plays a major role during early embryogenesis. SAM domains of Scm proteins can interact with each other, forming homooligomers, as well as with SAM domains of other proteins, in particular with SAM domains of Ph (polyhomeotic) proteins, forming heterooligomers. Homooligomers are similar to the ones formed by SAM Pointed domains of the TEL proteins. Such SAM/SAM oligomers apparently play a role in transcriptional repression through polymerization along the chromosome. Mammalian Scmh1 protein is known be indispensable member of PRC1 complex; it plays a regulatory role for the complex during meiotic prophase of male sperm cells, and is particularly involved in regulation of chromatin modification at the XY chromatin domain of the pachytene spermatocytes [[cite:PUB00037381], [cite:PUB00006191], [cite:PUB00103485], [cite:PUB00102442], [cite:PUB00102446]].

Name: SLED domain
ShortDescription: The SLED (Scm-Like Embedded Domain) domain is a double-stranded DNA binding domain found in Scml2 which is a member of the Polycomb group of proteins involved in epigenetic gene silencing [[cite:PUB00081213]].

Name: Polycomb group protein, RNA binding region
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the RNA-binding region of human SCML2/4, also found in other Polycomb-group proteins from the Scm (Sex comb on midleg) subfamily. Members of this group are found in vertebrates.

;

Sex comb on midleg-like protein 2 (SCML2) is a mammalian Polycomb-group protein, which associates with the Polycomb repressive complex-1 (PRC1) that is essential for the epigenetic regulation of gene expression. Isoform SCML2A has been shown to bind to PRC1 via its SPM domain and to interact with ncRNAs through a novel RNA-binding region (RBR). The RBR is necessary for targeting of SCML2A to chromatin and PRC1 recruitment, suggesting a role for ncRNAs in regulating SCML2 function [[cite:PUB00081244]].

;

Sex comb on midleg-like protein 4 (SCML4), which is thought to have a similar function, has been associated with coronary artery disease [[cite:PUB00103484]].

Name: SLED domain superfamily
ShortDescription: The SLED (Scm-Like Embedded Domain) domain is a double-stranded DNA binding domain found in Scml2 which is a member of the Polycomb group of proteins involved in epigenetic gene silencing [[cite:PUB00081213]].

Name: Polycomb group and chromatin remodeling factors
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes Polycomb group (PcG) components and related factors that are involved in chromatin remodeling and transcriptional repression. They play a crucial role in maintaining the repressive state of genes, including homeotic genes, throughout development. Members of this family are characterized by their ability to recognize and bind specific methylated lysine residues on histone proteins, acting as 'readers' of post-translational modifications. This binding can lead to chromatin compaction and gene silencing. Some members also participate in DNA damage repair by promoting homologous recombination. Additionally, they may be involved in cell proliferation, differentiation, and the regulation of ubiquitin-dependent protein degradation. The family includes proteins with MBT repeats, SAM domains, and other domains that contribute to their function in gene regulation and chromatin structure.

Name: OCRE domain
ShortDescription: The OCtamer REpeat (OCRE) has been annotated as a 42-residue sequence motif with 12 tyrosine residues in the spliceosome trans-regulatory elements RBM5 and RBM10 (RBM [RNA-binding motif]), which are known to regulate alternative splicing of Fas and Bcl-x pre-mRNA transcripts [[cite:PUB00091636]]. The structure of the domain consists of an anti-parallel arrangement of six β strands.

Name: AGGF1, OCRE domain
ShortDescription:
Angiogenic factor with G patch and FHA domains 1 (AGGF1, also known as VG5Q) functions as a potent angiogenic factor in promoting angiogenesis through interacting with TWEAK (also known as TNFSF12), which is a member of the tumour necrosis factor (TNF) superfamily that induces angiogenesis in vivo. VG5Q can bind to the surface of endothelial cells and promote cell proliferation, suggesting that it may act in an autocrine fashion. The chromosomal translocation t(5;11) and the E133K variant in VG5Q are associated with Klippel-Trenaunay syndrome (KTS), a disorder characterised by diverse effects in the vascular system. In addition to a forkhead-associated (FHA) domain and a G-patch motif, VG5Q contains an N-terminal OCtamer REpeat (OCRE) domain that is characterised by a 5-fold, imperfectly repeated octameric sequence [[cite:PUB00085726], [cite:PUB00085727]].

;

The OCRE (OCtamer REpeat) domain contains five repeats of an 8-residue motif, which were shown to form β-strands. Based on the architectures of proteins containing OCRE domains, a role in RNA metabolism and/or signalling has been proposed [[cite:PUB00085724]].

Name: Angiogenic factor with G patch and FHA domains 1
ShortDescription: The AGGF1 family is characterized by its role in promoting angiogenesis and endothelial cell proliferation. Members of the family have the ability to bind to endothelial cells, which may suggest an autocrine mechanism of action. The angiogenic factor with G patch and FHA domains, which defines this family, is involved in the physiological process of new blood vessel formation, a critical aspect of various developmental and repair processes in the body. The family's function in angiogenesis highlights its potential significance in both normal vascular development and pathological conditions where angiogenesis is a factor.

Name: Yaf2/RYBP C-terminal binding motif
ShortDescription:
This motif is found in the C-terminal region of the Yaf2 and RYBP proteins, which are homologous parts of the PRC1 complex [[cite:PUB00058599]].

RYBP is a zinc finger protein with an essential role during embryonic development, which binds transcriptional factors, Polycomb products, and mediators of apoptosisis [[cite:PUB00081263]]. RYBP also binds ubiquitin and Cbx proteins via the C-terminal docking module [[cite:PUB00081261], [cite:PUB00057727]]. RYBP is natively unstructured until it binds to the C-terminal region of the Polycomb protein Ring1B or to DNA [[cite:PUB00081263]]. Yaf2 binds to MYC and inhibits MYC-mediated transactivation [[cite:PUB00081262]].

Name: RING1 and YY1-binding protein/YY1-associated factor 2
ShortDescription:
Proteins included in this entry have an N-terminal RanBP2-type zinc finger and a Yaf2/RYBP C-terminal binding motif. Proteins with these regions include Yaf2 and RYBP proteins, which are homologous parts of the PRC1 complex [[cite:PUB00058599]].

RYBP is a zinc finger protein with an essential role during embryonic development, which binds transcriptional factors, Polycomb products, and mediators of apoptosisis [[cite:PUB00081263]]. RYBP also binds ubiquitin and Cbx proteins via the C-terminal docking module [[cite:PUB00081261], [cite:PUB00057727]]. RYBP is natively unstructured until it binds to the C-terminal region of the Polycomb protein Ring1B or to DNA [[cite:PUB00081263]]. Yaf2 binds to MYC and inhibits MYC-mediated transactivation [[cite:PUB00081262]].

Name: Hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase, MBL domain
ShortDescription:
Hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase is also known as glyoxalase II, S-2-hydroxylacylglutathione hydrolase, hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase, or acetoacetylglutathione hydrolase. In the second step of the glyoxalase system this enzyme hydrolyzes S-d-lactoylglutathione to d-lactate and regenerates glutathione in the process. It has broad substrate specificity for glutathione thiol esters, hydrolyzing a number of these species to their corresponding carboxylic acids and reduced glutathione [[cite:PUB00085866], [cite:PUB00030264]].

Glyoxalase II belongs to the metallo-beta-lactamase (MBL)-fold metallo-hydrolase superfamily which is comprised mainly of hydrolytic enzymes which carry out a variety of biological functions [[cite:PUB00085867]]. The enzyme consists of two domains. The first domain folds into a four-layered β sandwich, similar to that seen in the metallo-beta-lactamases. The second domain is predominantly α-helical. The active site contains a binuclear zinc-binding site and a substrate-binding site extending over the domain interface [[cite:PUB00030264]].

Name: Hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase
ShortDescription: This entry represents hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase, a detoxification enzyme also known as glyoxalase II. It follows lactoylglutathione lyase, also known as glyoxalase I, and acts to remove the toxic metabolite methylglyoxal and related compounds. This protein belongs to the broader metallo-beta-lactamase family [[cite:PUB00043111], [cite:PUB00043112]].

Name: Ribonuclease Z/Hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase-like
ShortDescription: Proteins in this superfamily contains a fold consisted of duplication of β(4)-α-β-α motif. Apart from the beta-lactamases and metallo-beta-lactamases, a number of other proteins also contain this fold [[cite:PUB00001273]]. These proteins include thiolesterases, members of the glyoxalase II family, that catalyse the hydrolysis of S-D-lactoyl-glutathione to form glutathione and D-lactic acid and a competence protein that is essential for natural transformation in Neisseria gonorrhoeae and could be a transporter involved in DNA uptake. Except for the competence protein, these proteins bind two zinc ions per molecule as cofactor.

Name: Metallo-beta-lactamase
ShortDescription: Metallo beta lactamases exhibit low sequence identity between enzymes but they are structurally similar. They have a characteristic α-β/β-α sandwich fold in which the active site is at the interface between domains. Apart from the beta-lactamases and metallo-beta-lactamases, a number of other proteins contain this domain and share the same fold type [[cite:PUB00001273], [cite:PUB00095151]]. These proteins include thiolesterases, members of the glyoxalase II family, that catalyse the hydrolysis of S-D-lactoyl-glutathione to form glutathione and D-lactic acid and a competence protein that is essential for natural transformation in Neisseria gonorrhoeae and could be a transporter involved in DNA uptake. Except for the competence protein these proteins bind two zinc ions per molecule as cofactor.

Name: Hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found at the C terminus of hydroxyacylglutathione hydrolase enzymes. Substrate binding occurs at the interface between this domain and the catalytic domain ([interpro:IPR001279]) [[cite:PUB00030264], [cite:PUB00076253], [cite:PUB00048973]].

Name: Ras guanine-nucleotide exchange factors catalytic domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the catalytic domain of the Ras guanine-nucleotide exchange factors.

;

Ras proteins are membrane-associated molecular switches that bind GTP and GDP and slowly hydrolyze GTP to GDP [[cite:PUB00004087]] in fundamental events such as signal transduction, cytoskeleton dynamics and intracellular trafficking. The balance between the GTP bound (active) and GDP bound (inactive) states is regulated by the opposite action of proteins activating the GTPase activity and that of proteins which promote the loss of bound GDP and the uptake of fresh GTP [[cite:PUB00004162], [cite:PUB00001017]]. The latter proteins are known as guanine-nucleotide exchange (or releasing) factors (GEFs or GRFs) (or also as guanine-nucleotide dissociation stimulators (GDSs)). GEFs catalyze the dissociation of GDP from the inactive GTP-binding proteins. GTP can then bind and induce structural changes that allow interaction with effectors [[cite:PUB00081668], [cite:PUB00000728]].

The crystal structure of the GEF region of human Sos1 complexes with Ras has been solved [[cite:PUB00001237]]. The structure consists of two distinct α helical structural domains: the N-terminal domain which seems to have a purely structural role and the C-terminal domain which is sufficient for catalytic activity and contains all residues that interact with Ras. A main feature of the catalytic domain is the protrusion of a helical hairpin important for the nucleotide-exchange mechanism. The N-terminal domain is likely to be important for the stability and correct placement of the hairpin structure.

Some proteins known to contain a Ras-GEF domain are listed below:

  • Cdc25 from yeast.
  • Scd25 from yeast.
  • Ste6 from fission yeast.
  • Son of sevenless (gene sos) from Drosophila and mammals.
  • p140-RAS GRF (cdc25Mm) from mammals. This protein possesses both a domain belonging to the CDC25 family and one belonging to the CDC24 family.
  • Bud5 from yeast, that may interact with the ras-like protein RSR1/BUD1.
  • Lte1 from yeast, whose target protein is not yet known.
  • ralGDS from mammals, which interacts with the ras-like proteins ralA and ralB [[cite:PUB00001237]].

Name: Adapter protein with SH2 and Ras-GEF domains
ShortDescription: This family of proteins functions as adapter molecules in various signaling pathways, particularly those involving growth factor receptors. They are involved in promoting cellular processes such as proliferation, migration, and actin cytoskeleton reorganization. These proteins mediate the activation of MAPK signaling and DNA synthesis in response to insulin and other stimuli. They also play roles in cell adhesion by interacting with phosphorylated proteins and influencing integrin-mediated signaling. Additionally, they are implicated in the regulation of the cell cycle and may have a role in maintaining the structural integrity of the ocular lens. Some family members possess a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) activity for small GTPases, although this function is disputed in some studies. They also appear to be involved in the regulation of the immune response and the development of specific cell types.

Name: Ras guanine-nucleotide exchange factor, catalytic domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Ras proteins are membrane-associated molecular switches that bind GTP and GDP and slowly hydrolyze GTP to GDP [[cite:PUB00004087]] in fundamental events such as signal transduction, cytoskeleton dynamics and intracellular trafficking. The balance between the GTP bound (active) and GDP bound (inactive) states is regulated by the opposite action of proteins activating the GTPase activity and that of proteins which promote the loss of bound GDP and the uptake of fresh GTP [[cite:PUB00004162], [cite:PUB00001017]]. The latter proteins are known as guanine-nucleotide exchange (or releasing) factors (GEFs or GRFs) (or also as guanine-nucleotide dissociation stimulators (GDSs)). GEFs catalyze the dissociation of GDP from the inactive GTP-binding proteins. GTP can then bind and induce structural changes that allow interaction with effectors [[cite:PUB00081668], [cite:PUB00000728]].

The crystal structure of the GEF region of human Sos1 complexes with Ras has been solved [[cite:PUB00001237]]. The structure consists of two distinct α helical structural domains: the N-terminal domain which seems to have a purely structural role and the C-terminal domain which is sufficient for catalytic activity and contains all residues that interact with Ras. A main feature of the catalytic domain is the protrusion of a helical hairpin important for the nucleotide-exchange mechanism. The N-terminal domain is likely to be important for the stability and correct placement of the hairpin structure.

Some proteins known to contain a Ras-GEF domain are listed below:

  • Cdc25 from yeast.
  • Scd25 from yeast.
  • Ste6 from fission yeast.
  • Son of sevenless (gene sos) from Drosophila and mammals.
  • p140-RAS GRF (cdc25Mm) from mammals. This protein possesses both a domain belonging to the CDC25 family and one belonging to the CDC24 family.
  • Bud5 from yeast, that may interact with the ras-like protein RSR1/BUD1.
  • Lte1 from yeast, whose target protein is not yet known.
  • ralGDS from mammals, which interacts with the ras-like proteins ralA and ralB [[cite:PUB00001237]].
;

This entry represents the C-terminal catalytic domain of the Ras guanine-nucleotide exchange factors.

Name: Ras guanine nucleotide exchange factor domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Small GTPases of the Ras family alternate between 2 conformations induced by the binding of either GTP or GDP. Guanine nucleotide exchange factors (GEFs) induce the dissociation of GDP to allow association of the more abundant GTP. The Ras-like family of small GTPases includes, among others, Ras, Rap1, R-ras, and Ral. The family is characterised by similarities in the effector domain. The Ras GTPase Rap1 is activated rapidly in response to activation of a variety of receptors. Rap1 activation is mediated by several second messengers, including calcium, diacylglycerol, and cAMP. GEFs have been identified that mediate these effects. One such GEF is Epac, an exchange protein directly activated by cAMP, which represents a novel cAMP-induced, protein kinase A-independent pathway [[cite:PUB00010624]].

;

This superfamily represents a multihelical domain found in Ras GEFs. It can be subdivided in two domains: Ras GEF catalytic domain ([interpro:IPR001895]) and Ras GEF N-terminal domain ([interpro:IPR000651]). In the nucleotide exchange factor Son of sevenless (SOS), both of these domains are required for the Ras specific nucleotide exchange activity, and both of them together are referred to as SOS-cat [[cite:PUB00032394]].

Name: SHEP1/BCAR3/NSP1, SH2 domain
ShortDescription:
Breast cancer anti-estrogen resistance protein 3 (BCAR3) is an SH2-containing signal transducer that regulates the proliferation in breast cancer cells [[cite:PUB00069471]]. BCAR3 binds to the adaptor molecule p130Cas (also known as BCAR1), which function as key signalling nodes with important regulatory roles in normal and pathological cells [[cite:PUB00069469]]. BCAR3 promotes cell motility by regulating actin cytoskeletal and adhesion remodeling in invasive breast cancer cells [[cite:PUB00069472]]. It also promotes interactions between p130Cas and the protein tyrosine kinase c-Src, leading to increased c-Src kinase activity and p130Cas phosphorylation [[cite:PUB00069472]].

;

This entry represents the SH2 domain found in SHEP1 (also known as SH2D3C), BCAR3 and NSP1 (also known as SH2D3A). SHEP1, BCAR3 and NSP1 are cytoplasmic proteins involved in cell adhesion/migration and antiestrogen resistance. All three proteins contain an SH2 domain and an exchange factor-like domain that binds both Ras GTPases and the scaffolding protein Cas [[cite:PUB00094964]]. In general, SH2 domains are involved in signal transduction. They typically bind pTyr-containing ligands via two surface pockets, a pTyr and hydrophobic binding pocket, allowing proteins with SH2 domains to localize to tyrosine phosphorylated sites [[cite:PUB00094965]].

Name: MINDY deubiquitinase domain
ShortDescription: This domain represents the catalytic domain of a group of deubiquitinating (DUB) enzymes known as the MINDY family (MIU-containing novel DUB). Ubiquitin (Ub) is released one molecule at a time from the distal end of proteins with Lys48-linked polyubiquitin chains. Long polyubiquitin chains are preferred. The catalytic Cys and His residues have been identified by site-directed mutagenesis, as has the Gln that participates in formation of the oxyanion hole during catalysis. Despite the structural similarity to papain-like cysteine peptidases, a residue corresponding to the Asn that orientates the imidazolium ring of the catalytic His has not been identified. Members of the MINDY family of DUBs contain an MIU (motif interacting with Ub) motif, which is a helical motif that binds mono-Ub [[cite:PUB00081935]].

Name: MINDY deubiquitinase
ShortDescription: This entry represents a group of deubiquitinating (DUB) enzymes known as the MINDY family (MIU-containing novel DUB). Ubiquitin (Ub) is released one molecule at a time from the distal end of proteins with Lys48-linked polyubiquitin chains. Long polyubiquitin chains are preferred. The catalytic Cys and His residues have been identified by site-directed mutagenesis, as has the Gln that participates in formation of the oxyanion hole during catalysis. Despite the structural similarity to papain-like cysteine peptidases, a residue corresponding to the Asn that orientates the imidazolium ring of the catalytic His has not been identified. Members of the MINDY family of DUBs contain an MIU (motif interacting with Ub) motif, which is a helical motif that binds mono-Ub [[cite:PUB00081935]].

Name: Testis-expressed sequence 29 protein
ShortDescription: TEX29, testis-expressed sequence 29 protein, is a family of proteins found in eukaryotes. Proteins in this family are typically between 39 and 150 amino acids in length.

Name: Sialic acid-binding Ig-like lectin
ShortDescription: The SIGLEC family proteins are sialic acid-binding Ig-like lectins involved in cell-cell adhesion, immune regulation, and maintenance of immune cells in a resting state. They recognize and bind to sialic acid-bearing glycans, mediating interactions with a preference for alpha-2,3- or alpha-2,6-linked sialic acid. SIGLEC family members contain immunoreceptor tyrosine-based inhibitor motifs (ITIMs) in their cytoplasmic domains, which upon phosphorylation, recruit SH2-containing phosphatases to modulate cellular responses. They play roles in inhibiting signal transduction, regulating B-cell antigen receptor signaling, controlling autoimmunity, and protecting neurons against apoptosis. Some SIGLEC proteins are involved in the negative regulation of neurite outgrowth and may act as inhibitory receptors in the immune response.

Name: Sperm-associated microtubule inner protein 4
ShortDescription:
This family (previously DUF4555) includes the homologs of human sperm-associated microtubule inner protein 4 (SPMIP4, also known as C7orf31) that is found predominantly in testis [[cite:PUB00151495]]. SPMIP4 is a microtubule inner protein (MIP) part of the axonemal dynein-decorated doublet microtubules (DMTs).

Members of this family adopt rather extended conformation and contain a single or multiple Mn motifs. Each Mn motif consists of a 5- to 6-residue helix flanked by a Tyr/Phe residue on one end and by a Ser/Thr on the other that binds the shoulder of the α-tubulin S9/S10 loop [[cite:PUB00151502]]. It was reported that a single Mn motif is sufficient for microtubule binding in vitro [[cite:PUB00151501]]. Members of this family are likely to stabilise the microtubule structure in the sperm flagella [[cite:PUB00151496]].

Name: Protein FAM133
ShortDescription: This family consists of functionally uncharacterised proteins.

Name: GOLM1/CASC4 family
ShortDescription: This entry represents proteins from the Golgi membrane protein 1 (GOLM1) and cancer susceptibility candidate 4 (CASC4), also known as GOLM2, family. GOLM1 is a Golgi-localised protein that is upregulated by viral infection [[cite:PUB00060103]], but whose precise function is unknown. CASC4, like GOLM1, appears to be a single pass membrane protein.

Name: UDP-glucuronic acid decarboxylase-like
ShortDescription:
This family represents UDP-glucuronic acid decarboxylases (UXS, also known as UDP-glucuronate decarboxylase or UDP-XYL synthase) which catalyse the NAD-dependent decarboxylation of UDP-glucuronic acid to form UDP-xylose, a sugar donor required for the synthesis of glycoproteins, polysaccharides, various metabolites, and oligosaccharides in plants, animals, fungi and bacteria [[cite:PUB00057839], [cite:PUB00096336]]. They are members of the short-chain dehydrogenase/reductase (SDR) superfamily that also include epimerases, dehydratases, and reductases that use nucleotide-activated monosaccharides as substrates and share a Rossmann-fold NAD(P)H/NAD(P)(+) binding domain [[cite:PUB00096336]].

This entry also includes UDP-N-acetyl-alpha-D-glucosaminuronate decarboxylase, a bacterial homologue that catalyses the NAD-dependent decarboxylation of UDP-N-acetylglucosaminuronic acid to UDP-N-acetylxylosamine and cannot utilise as substrates UDP-uronates, such as UDP-glucuronic acid and UDP-galacturonic acid [[cite:PUB00158922]].

Name: UDP-glucuronate decarboxylase N-terminal
ShortDescription: The N terminus of the UDP-glucuronate decarboxylases may be involved in localisation to the perinuclear Golgi membrane [[cite:PUB00057839], [cite:PUB00057840]].

Name: NAD(P)-binding domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents NAD- and NADP-binding domains with a core Rossmann-type fold, which consists of 3-layers α/β/α, where the six β-strands are parallel in the order 321456. Many different enzymes contain an NAD/NADP-binding domain, including:

  • C-terminal domain of alcohol dehydrogenases [[cite:PUB00031657]]
  • Tyrosine-dependent oxidoreductases (also known as short-chain dehydrogenases) [[cite:PUB00000446]]
  • N-terminal domain of glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase [[cite:PUB00023536]]
  • NAD-binding domain of formate/glycerate dehydrogenases [[cite:PUB00032846]]
  • N-terminal domain of sirohaem synthase [[cite:PUB00029889]]
  • N-terminal domain of lactate dehydrogenase [[cite:PUB00025866]]
  • N-terminal domain of 6-phosphogluconate dehydrogenase (the β-sheet is extended to 8 strands) [[cite:PUB00041823]]
  • C-terminal domain of amino acid dehydrogenases (an extra N-terminal helix displaces the C-terminal helix [[cite:PUB00025375]]
  • NAD-binding domain of certain potassium channels [[cite:PUB00025981]]
  • C-terminal domain of the transcriptional repressor Rex [[cite:PUB00032388]]
  • Ornithine cyclodeaminase [[cite:PUB00031693]]
  • CoA-binding N-terminal domain of the alpha chain of succinyl-CoA synthetase [[cite:PUB00015984]]

Name: Sperm microtubule inner protein 6
ShortDescription: This entry represents the homologues of Sperm microtubule inner protein 6 (SPMIP6, formerly Spermatid-specific manchette-related protein 1 -SMRP1). SPMIP6 is a sperm-specific microtubule inner protein (MIP) that is found in mammmals. SPMIP6 interacts with alpha-tubulin and associates with protofilament B01 [[cite:PUB00151496]]. It may be involved in differentiation or function of ciliated cells [[cite:PUB00067671]].

Name: SLAIN motif-containing protein
ShortDescription: This family consists of SLAIN motif-containing proteins, including SLAIN1 and SLAIN2. SLAIN1 was named after the SLAIN amino acid stretch in its C terminus. It is expressed at the stem cell and epiblast stages of ESC differentiation and in the epiblast, nervous system, tailbud and somites of the developing embryo in mice [[cite:PUB00060165]]. SLAIN2 has been shown to bind to the plus end of microtubules and to regulate microtubule dynamics and organisation. It promotes cytoplasmic microtubule nucleation and elongation. It is required for normal structure of the microtubule cytoskeleton during interphase [[cite:PUB00060166]].

Name: RNA-recognition motif (RRM) Nup35-type domain
ShortDescription:
The nuclear pore complex (NPC) mediates the transport of macromolecules across the nuclear envelope (NE). The NPC is composed of a relatively small number of proteins (~30), termed nucleoporins or Nups. The vertebrate nuclear pore protein Nup35, the ortholog of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Nup53p, is suggested to interact with the NE membrane and to be required for nuclear morphology. The highly conserved region between vertebrate Nup35 and yeast Nup53p is predicted to contain an RNA-recognition motif (RRM) domain.

The sequences of the RRM Nup-35-type domain are highly conserved in all eucaryotes. The RRM Nup35-type domain adopts the characteristic BetaAlphaBeta BetaAlphaBeta topology of the secondary structure elements, with a four- stranded antiparallel β-sheet packed against two α helices. The RRM Nup35-type domain forms a homodimer and contains atypical rinonucleoprotein (RNP) motifs, which lack the conserved residues that typically bind RNA in canonical RRM domains. The dimer interface involves the β-sheet surface, with its atypical RNP motifs, which is generally used to bind RNA in typical RRM domains [[cite:PUB00038167]].

This entry represents the RRM Nup35-type domain.

Name: Nucleoporin, NUP53
ShortDescription:
The nuclear pore complex (NPC) mediates the transport of macromolecules across the nuclear envelope (NE). The NPC is composed of a relatively small number of proteins (~30), termed nucleoporins or Nups. The vertebrate nuclear pore protein Nup35, the orthologue of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Nup53p, is suggested to interact with the NE membrane and to be required for nuclear morphology [[cite:PUB00057985]].

This entry also includes Asm4 (a paralogue of Saccharomyces cerevisiae Nup53p) from Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Nup40 from Schizosaccharomyces pombe.

Name: WDR36/Utp21, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the first β-propeller domain, found at the N-terminal in WDR36 and Utp21.

;

Utp21 from yeast and WDR36 its orthologue in animals are part of the small subunit (SSU) processome, the first precursor of the small eukaryotic ribosomal subunit. They are involved in the nucleolar processing of SSU 18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00090524], [cite:PUB00151110]].

Name: WDR36/Utp21, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
Utp21 is a component of the SSU processome, which is required for pre-18S rRNA processing. It interacts with Utp18 [[cite:PUB00035836]].

;

Utp21 from yeast and WDR36 its orthologue in animals are part of the small subunit (SSU) processome, the first precursor of the small eukaryotic ribosomal subunit. They are involved in the nucleolar processing of SSU 18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00090524], [cite:PUB00151110]].

Name: WDR36/Utp21, second beta-propeller domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the second β-propeller domain, found in the middle region of WDR36 and Utp21.

;

Utp21 from yeast and WDR36 its orthologue in animals are part of the small subunit (SSU) processome, the first precursor of the small eukaryotic ribosomal subunit. They are involved in the nucleolar processing of SSU 18S rRNA [[cite:PUB00090524], [cite:PUB00151110]].

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein mL64 domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents a domain found in the large ribosomal subunit protein mL64, also known as Growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible proteins-interacting protein 1 and CRIF1 [[cite:PUB00151135]]. These proteins act as negative regulators of G1 to S cell cycle phase progression by inhibiting cyclin-dependent kinases. Inhibitory effects are additive with GADD45 proteins but occur also in the absence of GADD45 proteins. Furthermore, they act as a repressor of the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A1 by inhibiting AB domain-mediated transcriptional activity [[cite:PUB00044211]]. They may be involved in the hormone-mediated regulation of NR4A1 transcriptional activity.

Structurally, this domain consists of 4 α helices.

Name: Large ribosomal subunit protein mL64
ShortDescription: This entry represents the large ribosomal subunit protein mL64, also known as Growth arrest and DNA damage-inducible proteins-interacting protein 1. Members of this family of proteins act as negative regulators of G1 to S cell cycle phase progression by inhibiting cyclin-dependent kinases. Inhibitory effects are additive with GADD45 proteins but occur also in the absence of GADD45 proteins. Furthermore, they act as a repressor of the orphan nuclear receptor NR4A1 by inhibiting AB domain-mediated transcriptional activity [[cite:PUB00044211]]. They may be involved in the hormone-mediated regulation of NR4A1 transcriptional activity.

Name: CEP76, C2 domain
ShortDescription: A C2 domain is usually involved in targeting proteins to cell membranes. This entry represents a C2 domain found in the CEP76 proteins [[cite:PUB00069718]]. CEP76 is a centrosomal protein involved in regulation of centriole duplication [[cite:PUB00069719]].

Name: Centrosomal protein of 76 kDa, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain found at the C-terminal of centrosomal protein of 76 kDa, a protein involved in regulation of centriole duplication to limit centriole duplication to once per cell cycle by preventing centriole reduplication [[cite:PUB00069719]]. This domain may adopt a fold similar to the CAP domain. This entry also includes CC2D2A/B from human. CC2D2A is a component of the tectonic-like complex, a complex localised at the transition zone of primary cilia and acting as a barrier that prevents diffusion of transmembrane proteins between the cilia and plasma membranes. It is required for ciliogenesis and sonic hedgehog/SHH signalling [[cite:PUB00069721]].

This domain is also found in C2 domain-containing proteins TgDOC22 and PfDOC21 from T. gondii and P. falciparum, respectively, which regulate the microneme secretion [[cite:PUB00159961], [cite:PUB00159962]].

Name: CEP76/DRC7, peptidase-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents a domain found in the middle of centrosomal protein of 76 kDa, a protein involved in regulation of centriole duplication to limit centriole duplication to once per cell cycle by preventing centriole reduplication [[cite:PUB00069719]]. This domain is also found towards the C-terminal of C2D2A/B, and in dynein regulatory complex subunit 7 (DRC7). C2D2A is a component of the tectonic-like complex, a complex localised at the transition zone of primary cilia and acting as a barrier that prevents diffusion of transmembrane proteins between the cilia and plasma membranes. It is required for ciliogenesis and sonic hedgehog/SHH signalling [[cite:PUB00069721]]. DRC7 is a component of the nexin-dynein regulatory complex (N-DRC) a key regulator of ciliary/flagellar motility which maintains the alignment and integrity of the distal axoneme and regulates microtubule sliding in motile axonemes [[cite:PUB00156015]]. In DRC7, this model covers the C-terminal part of the domain as it has an insertion not present in the other members of the entry. This domain is may adopt a fold related to peptidases.

Name: Centrosomal protein of 76 kDa
ShortDescription: The CEP76 family comprises centrosomal proteins that play a crucial role in ensuring proper centriole duplication. Members of the CEP76 family are essential for maintaining the fidelity of cell division by restricting centriole duplication to a single event per cell cycle, thereby preventing centriole reduplication. This regulatory function is vital for cell cycle progression and genomic stability.

Name: CEP76, N-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents a domain found at the N-terminal of centrosomal protein of 76 kDa, a protein involved in regulation of centriole duplication to limit centriole duplication to once per cell cycle by preventing centriole reduplication [[cite:PUB00069719]].

Name: Nuclear protein localization protein 4
ShortDescription: Npl4 forms the Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 complex, which is a segregase complex that is involved in several ubiquitin-related processes. By coupling the ubiquitin-binding properties of Ufd1-Npl4 with the ATPase activity of Cdc48 (p97 in mammals), Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 is believed to aid in the extraction of ubiquitylated proteins from higher order complexes [[cite:PUB00077106]]. It also plays a role in the regulated destruction of resident ER membrane proteins [[cite:PUB00077110]].

Name: Nuclear pore localisation protein NPL4, C-terminal
ShortDescription: The HRD4 gene is identical to NPL4, a gene previously implicated in nuclear transport. Using a diverse set of substrates and direct ubiquitination assays, analysis revealed that HRD4/NPL4 is required for a poorly characterised step in ER-associated degradation following ubiquitination of target proteins but preceding their recognition by the 26S proteasome [[cite:PUB00010193]]. Npl4p physically associates with Cdc48p via Ufd1p to form a Cdc48p-Ufd1p-Npl4p complex. The Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 complex functions in the recognition of several polyubiquitin-tagged proteins and facilitates their presentation to the 26S proteasome for processive degradation or even more specific processing [[cite:PUB00019939]].

Name: Nuclear pore localisation protein Npl4, ubiquitin-like domain
ShortDescription:
Npl4, along with Ufd1, forms the heterodimer adaptor complex UN, which is involved in the recruitment of p97, an AAA ATPase, for tasks involving the ubiquitin pathway.

Npl4 has a N-terminal ubiquitin-like domain which has within its structure a β-grasp fold with a helical insert [[cite:PUB00048694]]. This entry represents the ubiquitin-like domain.

Name: NPL4, zinc-binding putative
ShortDescription: The HRD4 gene is identical to NPL4, a gene previously implicated in nuclear transport. Using a diverse set of substrates and direct ubiquitination assays, analysis revealed that HRD4/NPL4 is required for a poorly characterised step in ER-associated degradation after ubiquitination of target proteins but before their recognition by the 26S proteasome [[cite:PUB00010193]]. This region of the protein contains possibly two zinc binding motifs. Npl4p physically associates with Cdc48p via Ufd1p to form a Cdc48p-Ufd1p-Npl4p complex. The Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 complex functions in the recognition of several polyubiquitin-tagged proteins and facilitates their presentation to the 26S proteasome for processive degradation or even more specific processing.

Name: PDZ domain-containing scaffold protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes scaffolding proteins that play key roles in cellular signaling, localization, and structural integrity. They are involved in the formation and maintenance of tight junctions and epithelial cell polarity. Some family members act as E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases, mediating ubiquitination and degradation of specific substrates. Others are implicated in synaptic plasticity, participating in NMDAR signaling complexes that may control AMPAR potentiation. These proteins often contain PDZ domains that mediate interactions with various partners, influencing processes such as vesicle transport, cell migration, and the organization of multiprotein complexes. The family also includes proteins that regulate the feedback of phototransduction in photoreceptors and proteins that may affect the surface expression and function of ion channels in sensory neurons.

Name: Ubiquitin-activating enzyme E1, Cys active site
ShortDescription:
Ubiquitin-activating enzyme (E1 enzyme) [[cite:PUB00000623], [cite:PUB00005373]] activates ubiquitin by first adenylating with ATP its C-terminal glycine residue and thereafter linking this residue to the side chain of a cysteine residue in E1, yielding an ubiquitin-E1 thiolester and free AMP. Later the ubiquitin moiety is transferred to a cysteine residue on one of the many forms of ubiquitin- conjugating enzymes (E2).

E1 is a large monomeric protein of about 110 to 115 Kd (about 1000 residues). In yeast there are two forms (UBA1 and UBA2) [[cite:PUB00002915]], while in plants and mammals multiple forms exist including a form which is Y-linked in mouse and some other mammals and which may be involved in spermatogenesis.

It has been shown that the last of the five cysteines that are conserved in the sequence of E1 from various species is the one that binds ubiquitin [[cite:PUB00002725]]. This entry represents a conserved region containing the active site cysteine.

Name: Ubiquitin activating enzyme, alpha domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
Ubiquitin-activating enzyme (E1 enzyme) activates ubiquitin by first adenylating with ATP its C-terminal glycine residue and thereafter linking this residue to the side chain of a cysteine residue in E1, yielding an ubiquitin-E1 thiolester and free AMP. Later the ubiquitin moiety is transferred to a cysteine residue on one of the many forms of ubiquitin-conjugating enzymes (E2) [[cite:PUB00044523]]. This domain carries the last of five conserved cysteines that is part of the active site of the enzyme, responsible for ubiquitin thiolester complex formation, the active site being represented by the sequence motif PICTLKNFP [[cite:PUB00044524]]. Not all proteins in this entry contain a functional active site.

;

This superfamily represents an α orthogonal bundle domain found in ubiquitin-activating enzyme and ubiquitin-like NEDD8-activating enzyme.

Name: NEDD8-activating enzyme E1 catalytic subunit, N-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This group of proteins includes NEDD8-activating enzyme E1 catalytic subunit (Uba3) from fungi, plants and invertebrates. In budding yeasts, it is a catalytic subunit of the dimeric Uba3-Ula1 E1 enzyme that activates NEDD8/Rub1 before neddylation, the process by which the ubiquitin-like protein NEDD8 is conjugated to its target proteins [[cite:PUB00034991]]. In C.elegans, Uba3 (also known as rfl-1) is required for cytokinesis and mitotic spindle orientation [[cite:PUB00072977]]. In mammals, it down-regulates steroid receptor activity and is necessary for cell cycle progression [[cite:PUB00101598], [cite:PUB00073565], [cite:PUB00101596], [cite:PUB00101597]].

;

This entry represents the N-terminal domain of Uba3.

Name: E2 binding
ShortDescription: E1 and E2 enzymes play a central role in ubiquitin and ubiquitin-like protein transfer cascades. This is an E2 binding domain that is found on NEDD8 activating E1 enzyme. The protein resembles ubiquitin, and recruits the catalytic core of the E2 enzyme Ubc12 in a similar manner to that in which ubiquitin interacts with ubiquitin binding domains [[cite:PUB00032601]].

Name: Membrane protein FAM174-like
ShortDescription: This entry represents a group of animal membrane proteins, including human Membrane protein FAM174B, which is essential for Golgi structural integrity [[cite:PUB00151893]].

Name: Type II phosphatidylinositol 4-kinase Lsb6/PI4K2
ShortDescription: This entry represents a group of type II phosphatidylinositol 4-kinases, including Lsb6 from yeasts and PI4K2alpha/beta from animals [[cite:PUB00090059], [cite:PUB00090060], [cite:PUB00090061]]. PI4K2alpha catalyzes the phosphorylation of phosphatidylinositol (PI) to phosphatidylinositol 4-phosphate (PI4P), a lipid that plays important roles in endocytosis, Golgi function, protein sorting and membrane trafficking and is required for prolonged survival of neurons. The structure of PI4K2alpha has been revealed [[cite:PUB00090062], [cite:PUB00090063]].

Name: DmX-like/RAVE complex component
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes members that are involved in various cellular processes. Some proteins in this family may function as scaffold proteins, interacting with other proteins such as MADD and RAB3GA on synaptic vesicles, and are implicated in the regulation of neuronal and endocrine homeostatic processes. Other family members are components of the RAVE complex, which is essential for the stable assembly of the V-ATPase complex, a critical component for vacuolar acidification and membrane transport. These proteins play roles in the brain and are key controllers of homeostasis, as well as being involved in the transport between endosomal compartments and the assembly of vacuolar ATPase.

Name: RAVE complex protein Rav1 C-terminal
ShortDescription: This domain family is found in the C-terminal region of the protein Rav1 [[cite:PUB00057224]], a component of the RAVE (regulator of the ATPase of vacuolar and endosomal membranes) complex. Rav1p is involved in regulating the glucose dependent assembly and disassembly of vacuolar ATPase V1 and V0 subunits [[cite:PUB00057225]].

Name: TCP10L/CENPJ
ShortDescription:
Proteins in this family include T-complex protein 10 homolog 1 (TCP10L) and its paralogue centromere protein J (CENPJ, also known as Centrosomal P4.1-associated protein, CPAP). TCP10L is expressed specifically in the nucleus of spermatogenic cells during spermatogenesis and it interacts with DAPK-3 which implies that TCP10L might play crucially important roles in spermatogenesis through its interaction with DAPK-3 [[cite:PUB00132810]]. It may be involved in transcriptional regulation [[cite:PUB00076436]]. It acts as a tumour suppressor in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) cells [[cite:PUB00076437]].

;

CENPJ is involved in centriole-length regulation. It allows persistent slow growth of the centriolar microtubule plus end and its overexpression leads to abnormally long microtubules [[cite:PUB00160710]]. CENPJ not only inhibits microtubule nucleation from the centrosome, but acts as a microtubule plus-end tracking protein that stabilises centriolar microtubules and inhibits microtubule polymerisation and extension from the distal ends of centrioles [[cite:PUB00158960], [cite:PUB00101595], [cite:PUB00033370], [cite:PUB00052372], [cite:PUB00060686]].

Name: Serine/threonine-protein kinase haspin, C-terminal
ShortDescription: This domain may be a potential Haspin-related leucine-zipper. A leucine zipper was proposed to be present towards the C-terminal of human Haspin, (upstream of the current family) [[cite:PUB00056073]]; however, as this domain would appear to span several helices and be largely within a loop structure [[cite:PUB00056074]], the actual zipper might be further downstream, and be represented by this entry, which is the very C-terminal part of the Schizosaccharomyces pombe sequence.

Name: Vesicle transport protein SFT2
ShortDescription: Sft2 is a non-essential membrane protein that localizes to a late-Golgi compartment and is involved in vesicle fusion with the Golgi complex [[cite:PUB00009891], [cite:PUB00087251]]. It is thought to interact with Sed5, a yeast t-SNARE protein that plays a role in ER-Golgi and intra-Golgi vesicular transport [[cite:PUB00015208], [cite:PUB00087253]]. Sft2 and related proteins are found in eukaryotes and show four putative transmembrane regions.

Name: Vesicle transport protein, Got1/SFT2-like
ShortDescription: Traffic through the yeast Golgi complex depends on a member of the syntaxin family of SNARE proteins, Sed5, present in early Golgi cisternae. Got1 is thought to facilitate Sed5-dependent fusion events [[cite:PUB00009891]]. This is a family of sequences derived from eukaryotic proteins. They are similar to a region of a SNARE-like protein required for traffic through the Golgi complex, SFT2 protein ([swissprot:P38166]) [[cite:PUB00015208]]. This is a conserved protein with four putative transmembrane helices, thought to be involved in vesicular transport in later Golgi compartments [[cite:PUB00009891]].

Name: Coiled-coil domain-containing protein 107
ShortDescription: Proteins in this family are found in mammals. Their function is not known.

Name: Protein POF1B
ShortDescription: Proteins in this family may be involved in ovary development. Defects in POF1B are the cause of premature ovarian failure type 2B (POF2B), an ovarian disorder defined as the cessation of ovarian function under the age of 40 years. It is characterised by oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, in the presence of elevated levels of serum gonadotropins and low estradiol [[cite:PUB00060175]].

Name: POF1B, helix-loop-helix domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in human protein POF1B and its homologues. Human POF1B plays a key role in the organization of epithelial monolayers by regulating the actin cytoskeleton [[cite:PUB00155803], [cite:PUB00060175]]. This domain is predicted to adopt a structure consisting of two helices connected by a loop region. The function of this domain is unknown but mutation of a conserved arginine 329 in human is associated with premature ovarian failure. This point mutation reduces the capacity of the mutant protein to bind non-muscle actin filaments [[cite:PUB00060175]].

Name: ZNRF4 /RNF13/RNF167, PA domain
ShortDescription:
This PA domain is found in ZNRF4 /RNF13/RNF167 from animals and RMR1-6 from Arabidopsis. These proteins contain a C3H2C3 RING finger and some of them are predicted to be membrane-anchored RING finger ubiquitin ligases [[cite:PUB00096989], [cite:PUB00097293]]. ZNRF4 is an ER-localized RING finger ubiquitin ligase and a regulator of calnexin stability and ER homeostasis [[cite:PUB00097293]]. RNF13 is highly enriched in ER and serves as a critical mediator for facilitating ER stress-induced apoptosis through the activation of the IRE1alpha-TRAF2-JNK signaling pathway [[cite:PUB00097292]]. RMR1 (also known as ReMembR-H2) is a sorting receptor involved in transport of storage proteins to protein storage vacuoles [[cite:PUB00096988]].

The significance of the PA domain to these proteins has not been ascertained. It may be a protein-protein interaction domain. At peptidase active sites, the PA domain may participate in substrate binding and/or promoting conformational changes, which influence the stability and accessibility of the site to substrate. It has been suggested that this domain forms a lid-like structure that covers the active site in active proteases, and is involved in protein recognition in vacuolar sorting receptors [[cite:PUB00019976]].

Name: PA domain
ShortDescription: The PA (Protease associated) domain is found as an insert domain in diverse proteases, which include the MEROPS peptidase families A22B, M28, and S8A [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The PA domain is also found in a plant vacuolar sorting receptor [swissprot:O22925] and members of the RZF family, e.g. [swissprot:O43567]. It has been suggested that this domain forms a lid-like structure that covers the active site in active proteases, and is involved in protein recognition in vacuolar sorting receptors [[cite:PUB00019976]].

Name: PA domain superfamily
ShortDescription: The PA (Protease associated) domain is found as an insert domain in diverse proteases, which include the MEROPS peptidase families A22B, M28, and S8A [[cite:PUB00003579]]. The PA domain is also found in some plant vacuolar sorting receptors and members of the RZF family, including [swissprot:O43567]. It has been suggested that this domain forms a lid-like structure that covers the active site in active proteases, and is involved in protein recognition in vacuolar sorting receptors [[cite:PUB00019976]].

Name: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase and sorting receptor
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in various cellular processes including protein ubiquitination, signaling pathway regulation, protein trafficking, and cellular growth control. Members of this family function as E3 ubiquitin-protein ligases, catalyzing the attachment of ubiquitin to substrate proteins, thereby targeting them for degradation or altering their cellular location and function. They play roles in the regulation of the TORC1 signaling pathway through polyubiquitination of specific proteins, influencing nutrient response and growth regulation. Some members are also implicated in the sorting and trafficking of proteins to vacuoles, acting as sorting receptors. Additionally, they are involved in synaptic transmission regulation and endosomal trafficking by mediating ubiquitination of receptors and vesicular proteins. The family includes proteins that regulate lysosome positioning and are involved in the G1/S transition of the cell cycle.

Name: Methyl-CpG-binding domain protein 2/3, p55-binding region
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a second MBD domain of methyl-CpG-binding domain proteins 2 and 3. This region has been implicated in binding the RbAp46/48 (retinoblastoma protein-associated protein) homologue p55, which is one of the components of the MBD2-NuRD complex. The MBD2-NuRD complex is a nucleosome remodelling and deacetylation complex [[cite:PUB00059692]].

;

Methylation at CpG dinucleotide, the most common DNA modification in eukaryotes, has been correlated with gene silencing associated with various phenomena such as genomic imprinting, transposon and chromosome X inactivation, differentiation, and cancer. Effects of DNA methylation are mediated through proteins which bind to symmetrically methylated CpGs. Such proteins contain a specific domain of ~70 residues, the methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD), which is linked to additional domains associated with chromatin, such as the bromodomain, the AT hook motif, the SET domain, or the PHD finger. MBD-containing proteins appear to act as structural proteins, which recruit a variety of histone deacetylase (HDAC) complexes and chromatin remodelling factors, leading to chromatin compaction and, consequently, to transcriptional repression. The MBD of MeCP2, MBD1, MBD2, MBD4 and BAZ2 mediates binding to DNA, in case of MeCP2, MBD1 and MBD2 preferentially to methylated CpG. In case of human MBD3 and SETDB1 the MBD has been shown to mediate protein-protein interactions [[cite:PUB00015393], [cite:PUB00015391]].

Name: Methyl-CpG binding protein 2/3, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found at the C-terminal of the methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD) containing proteins MBD2 [[cite:PUB00058179]] and MBD3 [[cite:PUB00058180]]. The latter was shown to not bind directly to methyl-CpG DNA but rather interact with components of the NuRD/Mi2 complex [[cite:PUB00058181]], an abundant deacetylase complex.

Effects of DNA methylation are mediated through proteins which bind to symmetrically methylated CpGs. Such proteins contain a specific domain of ~70 residues, the methyl-CpG-binding domain (MBD), which is linked to additional domains associated with chromatin, such as the bromodomain, the AT hook motif, the SET domain, or the PHD finger. MBD-containing proteins appear to act as structural proteins, which recruit a variety of histone deacetylase (HDAC) complexes and chromatin remodelling factors, leading to chromatin compaction and, consequently, to transcriptional repression. The MBD of MeCP2, MBD1, MBD2, MBD4 and BAZ2 mediates binding to DNA, in case of MeCP2, MBD1 and MBD2 preferentially to methylated CpG. In case of human MBD3 and SETDB1 the MBD has been shown to mediate protein-protein interactions [[cite:PUB00015393], [cite:PUB00015391]].

Name: Microprocessor complex subunit DGCR8
ShortDescription: Primary microRNA transcripts (pri-miRs) are cleaved by Microprocessor, a complex containing RNase III DROSHA and its cofactor DGCR8 [[cite:PUB00090871]]. DGCR8 functions as a molecular anchor necessary for the recognition of pri-miRNA at dsRNA-ssRNA junction and directs DROSHA to cleave 11 bp away form the junction to release hairpin-shaped pre-miRNAs that are subsequently cut by the cytoplasmic DICER to generate mature miRNAs [[cite:PUB00090871], [cite:PUB00090873]]. DGCR8 binds heme, and this binding activates DGCR8 to recognize pri-miRs by specifically binding the terminal loop near the 3' single-stranded segment [[cite:PUB00090872]].

Name: Titin, Z repeat
ShortDescription: This entry represents the Z-repeat (approximately 45 amino acid sequences) found in the N terminus of titin [[cite:PUB00046420]]. The Z-repeat recognises and binds to the C-terminal calmodulin-like domain of alpha-actinin-2 (Act-EF34). It adopts a helical structure, and binds in a groove formed by the two planes between the helix pairs of Act-EF34. This interaction is essential for sarcomere assembly [[cite:PUB00025570]].

Name: PPAK motif
ShortDescription: PPAK is a repeated protein motif found in the PEVK (Pro-Glu-Val-Lys) domain of the titin protein and in a number of other proteins. Titin ([ec:2.7.11.1]) is a giant elastic protein found in striated muscle that is a key component in the assembly and functioning of sarcomeres [[cite:PUB00044085]]. PPAK motifs (PPAK refers to the four amino acids found at the beginning of the motif) occur 60 times in human soleus titin [[cite:PUB00020167]]. PPAK motifs occur in groups of 2-12 that are separated by regions rich in glutamic acid (approximately 45%) and termed polyE segments. The charge fluctuation between the PPAK and polyE regions suggests ionic interactions between these segments and their involvement in the elastic function of titin.

Name: MyBP-C, tri-helix bundle domain
ShortDescription: This domain can be found in the myosin-binding motif (m-domain) region present in myosin-binding protein C (MyBP-C). MyBP-C is a sarcomeric assembly protein necessary for the regulation of sarcomere structure and function [[cite:PUB00091296]]. The MyBP-C family of proteins consists mainly of modules with immunoglobulin (Ig) or fibronectin folds [[cite:PUB00091297]]. This domain exhibits a three-helix bundle fold and there is a known actin-binding motif, LK(R/K)XK positioned in the third helix (alpha3), similar to that found in villin and related proteins [[cite:PUB00091296]].

Name: Ribonuclease II/R
ShortDescription: This entry represents the catalytic domain of ribonuclease II [[cite:PUB00045119]]. It includes characterised and related sequences to exoribonuclease II (RNase II) and ribonuclease R, a bacterial 3' --> 5' exoribonuclease homologous to RNase II [[cite:PUB00015537], [cite:PUB00017190], [cite:PUB00017191]].

Name: RNR Ribonuclease
ShortDescription: The RNR ribonuclease family is characterized by its involvement in RNA processing and degradation. Members of this family exhibit 3'-5' exoribonuclease activity, releasing 5'-nucleoside monophosphates and participating in the maturation of structured RNAs such as rRNA, snRNA, snoRNA, and mRNAs. Some family members are implicated in mRNA degradation by hydrolyzing single-stranded polyribonucleotides processively from the 3' to 5' direction. Others are part of the RNA exosome complex, contributing to cellular RNA processing and degradation events, including the turnover of unstable mRNAs and surveillance pathways to prevent translation of aberrant mRNAs. Certain subfamilies, such as DIS3L2, specialize in recognizing and degrading polyuridylated RNAs, playing roles in cell proliferation and mitosis. The family's function is essential for maintaining RNA stability and integrity, ensuring proper gene expression and cellular homeostasis.

Name: Ribonuclease B, N-terminal OB domain
ShortDescription: This domain includes the N-terminal OB domain found in ribonuclease B proteins in one or two copies.

Name: Ribonuclease II
ShortDescription: This family consists of exoribonuclease II (RNase II), the product of the rnb gene, as found in a number of gamma proteobacteria. In Escherichia coli, it is one of eight different exoribonucleases. It is involved in mRNA degradation [[cite:PUB00015537]] and tRNA precursor end processing [[cite:PUB00056786]].

Name: Ribonuclease II/ribonuclease R
ShortDescription: This family is defined to identify a pair of paralogous 3'->5' exoribonucleases in Escherichia coli, plus the set of proteins apparently orthologous to one or the other in other eubacteria. VacB was characterised originally as required for the expression of virulence genes, but is now recognised as the exoribonuclease RNase R (Rnr). Its paralog in Escherichia coli and Haemophilus influenzae is designated exoribonuclease II (Rnb) [[cite:PUB00015537]]. Both are involved in the degradation of mRNA, and consequently have strong pleiotropic effects that may be difficult to disentangle. Both these proteins share domain-level similarity (RNB, S1) with a considerable number of other proteins, and full-length similarity scoring below the trusted cut-off to proteins associated with various phenotypes but uncertain biochemistry; it may be that these latter proteins are also 3' exoribonucleases.

Name: Ribonuclease II/R, conserved site
ShortDescription: This entry represents a conserved site for the ribonuclease II family. Proteins with this signature include characterised and related sequences to exoribonuclease II (RNase II) [[cite:PUB00045119]] and ribonuclease R, a bacterial 3' --> 5' exoribonuclease homologous to RNase II [[cite:PUB00015537], [cite:PUB00017190], [cite:PUB00017191]].

Name: Natural killer cell receptor-like, C-type lectin-like domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a C-type lectin-like domain (CTLD) of the type found in natural killer cell receptors (NKRs), including proteins similar to oxidized low density lipoprotein (OxLDL) receptor (LOX-1), CD94, CD69, NKG2-A and -D, osteoclast inhibitory lectin (OCIL), dendritic cell-associated C-type lectin-1 (dectin-1), human myeloid inhibitory C-type lectin-like receptor (MICL), mast cell-associated functional antigen (MAFA), killer cell lectin-like receptors: subfamily F, member 1 (KLRF1) and subfamily B, member 1 (KLRB1), and lys49 receptors. CTLD refers to a domain homologous to the carbohydrate-recognition domains (CRDs) of the C-type lectins [[cite:PUB00081335]].

NKRs are variously associated with activation or inhibition of natural killer (NK) cells. Activating NKRs stimulate cytolysis by NK cells of virally infected or transformed cells; inhibitory NKRs block cytolysis upon recognition of markers of healthy self cells. Most Lys49 receptors are inhibitory; some are stimulatory. OCIL inhibits NK cell function via binding to the receptor NKRP1D. Murine OCIL in addition to inhibiting NK cell function inhibits osteoclast differentiation [[cite:PUB00082014]]. MAFA clusters with the type I Fc epsilon receptor (FcepsilonRI) and inhibits the mast cells secretory response to FcepsilonRI stimulus [[cite:PUB00082019], [cite:PUB00082024]]. CD72 is a regulator of B cell receptor signaling [[cite:PUB00082027]]. NKG2D is an activating receptor for stress-induced antigens; human NKG2D ligands include the stress induced MHC-I homologs, MICA, MICB, and ULBP family of glycoproteins. Several NKRs have a carbohydrate-binding capacity which is not mediated through calcium ions (e.g. OCIL binds a range of high molecular weight sulfated glycosaminoglycans including dextran sulfate, fucoidan, and gamma-carrageenan sugars) [[cite:PUB00025835]]. Dectin-1 binds fungal beta-glucans and is involved in the innate immune responses to fungal pathogens [[cite:PUB00082018], [cite:PUB00082023]]. MAFA binds saccharides having terminal alpha-D mannose residues in a calcium-dependent manner. LOX-1 is the major receptor for OxLDL in endothelial cells and thought to play a role in the pathology of atherosclerosis [[cite:PUB00032684]]. Some NKRs exist as homodimers (e.g.Lys49, NKG2D, CD69, LOX-1) and some as heterodimers (e.g. CD94/NKG2A). Dectin-1 can function as a monomer in vitro.

Name: C-type lectin and matrix domain-containing protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes various C-type lectin domain-containing proteins, which are primarily involved in immune system processes. Members of this family function as cell surface receptors that can bind to specific carbohydrate structures. They are involved in a range of biological processes including lymphocyte proliferation, signal transduction, modulation of T-cell expansion, immune recognition, and inhibition of osteoclast formation. Some members have a role in antigen capture and presentation, potentially influencing dendritic cell function and interferon expression. Additionally, this family includes matrix proteins from sea urchin embryos that direct and inhibit crystal growth during spicule formation. There are also viral proteins that down-regulate MHC-I expression, participate in viral hemadsorption, and inhibit apoptosis. Collectively, these proteins contribute to immune defense, bone homeostasis, and developmental processes.

Name: T-complex protein 1, zeta subunit
ShortDescription:
Members of this eukaryotic family are part of the group II chaperonin complex called CCT (chaperonin containing TCP-1 or Tailless Complex Polypeptide 1) or TRiC [[cite:PUB00004127], [cite:PUB00001019]]. Chaperonins are involved in productive folding of proteins [[cite:PUB00080867]]. They share a common general morphology, a double toroid of 2 stacked rings. The archaeal equivalent group II chaperonin is often called the thermosome [[cite:PUB00080871]]. Both the thermosome and the TCP-1 family of proteins are weakly, but significantly [[cite:PUB00004124]], related to the cpn60/groEL chaperonin family (see [interpro:IPR001844]).

The TCP-1 protein was first identified in mice where it is especially abundant in testis but present in all cell types. It has since been found and characterised in many other animal species, as well as in yeast, plants and protists. The TCP1 complex has a double-ring structure with central cavities where protein folding takes place [[cite:PUB00074264]]. TCP-1 is a highly conserved protein of about 60kDa (556 to 560 residues) which participates in a hetero-oligomeric 900kDa double-torus shaped particle [[cite:PUB00004129]] with 6 to 8 other different, but homologous, subunits [[cite:PUB00064264]]. These subunits, the chaperonin containing TCP-1 (CCT) subunit beta, gamma, delta, epsilon, zeta and eta are evolutionary related to TCP-1 itself [[cite:PUB00001034], [cite:PUB00005432]]. Non-native proteins are sequestered inside the central cavity and folding is promoted by using energy derived from ATP hydrolysis [[cite:PUB00080868], [cite:PUB00080869], [cite:PUB00080873]]. The CCT is known to act as a molecular chaperone for tubulin, actin and probably some other proteins [[cite:PUB00074265], [cite:PUB00074266]].

ShortDescription: The FAM168 family consists of FAM168A and FAM168B. The function of FAM168A is unknown, but FAM168B has been renamed as myelin-associated neurite-outgrowth inhibitor (MANI), as it is an inhibitor of neuronal axonal outgrowth [[cite:PUB00069931]]. MANI interacts with cell division cycle protein 27 (Cdc27) [[cite:PUB00069932]].

Name: AP-3 complex subunit sigma
ShortDescription: APS3 is part of the AP-3 complex, an adaptor-related complex which is essential for the compartmentalization of the endocytic pathway [[cite:PUB00063067]]. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, the AP-3 complex is associated with the Golgi region as well as more peripheral structures [[cite:PUB00063067]]. It facilitates the budding of vesicles from the Golgi membrane and may be directly involved in trafficking to the vacuole [[cite:PUB00061731]]. It is required for the transport via the ALP pathway, which directs the transport of the cargo proteins Pho8 and Vam3 to the vacuole [[cite:PUB00063068]].

Name: Adaptor protein complex, sigma subunit
ShortDescription:
The adaptor protein complexes mediate both the recruitment of clathrin to membranes and the recognition of sorting signals within the cytosolic tails of transmembrane cargo molecules [[cite:PUB00096960]]. Adaptor protein complex 1 (AP-1) is a heterotetramer composed of two large adaptins (gamma-type subunit AP1G1 and beta-type subunit AP1B1), a medium adaptin (mu-type subunit AP1M1 or AP1M2) and a small adaptin (sigma-type subunit AP1S1 or AP1S2 or AP1S3). Subunits of clathrin-associated adaptor protein complex 1 play a role in protein sorting in the late-Golgi/trans-Golgi network (TGN) and/or in endosomes.

Name: Clathrin adaptor complex, small chain
ShortDescription:
Proteins synthesized on the ribosome and processed in the endoplasmic reticulum are transported from the Golgi apparatus to the trans-Golgi network (TGN), and from there via small carrier vesicles to their final destination compartment. This traffic is bidirectional, to ensure that proteins required to form vesicles are recycled. Vesicles have specific coat proteins (such as clathrin or coatomer) that are important for cargo selection and direction of transfer [[cite:PUB00035769]].

The small sigma subunit of AP proteins have been characterised in several species [[cite:PUB00001249], [cite:PUB00000652], [cite:PUB00001249], [cite:PUB00035771]]. The sigma subunit plays a role in protein sorting in the late-Golgi/trans-Golgi network (TGN) and/or endosomes. The zeta subunit of coatomers (zeta-COP) is required for coatomer binding to Golgi membranes and for coat-vesicle assembly [[cite:PUB00003074], [cite:PUB00035772]].

Name: Symplekin/Pta1
ShortDescription:

Name: Glycogen synthase kinase-3 binding protein
ShortDescription: Glycogen synthase kinase-3 (GSK-3) sequentially phosphorylates four serine residues on glycogen synthase (GS), in the sequence SxxxSxxxSxxx-SxxxS(p), by recognising and phosphorylating the first serine in the sequence motif SxxxS(P) (where S(p) represents a phosphoserine). Interaction of GSK-3 with a peptide derived from GSK-3 binding protein prevents GSK-3 interaction with Axin. This interaction thereby inhibits the Axin-dependent phosphorylation of beta-catenin by GSK-3 [[cite:PUB00010493]].

Name: Serine protease-like, trypsin family, histidine active site
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the histidine active site of serine proteases belonging to the MEROPS peptidase family S1 (chymotrypsin family, clan PA(S)). The catalytic activity of the serine proteases from the chymotrypsin family is provided by a charge relay system involving an aspartic acid residue hydrogen-bonded to a histidine, which itself is hydrogen-bonded to a serine. The enzymes are inherently secreted, being synthesised with a signal peptide that targets them to the secretory pathway. Animal enzymes are either secreted directly, packaged into vesicles for regulated secretion, or are retained in leukocyte granules [[cite:PUB00003576]].

Name: Peptidase S1A, chymotrypsin family
ShortDescription:
This group of serine peptidases and non-peptidase homologues belong to the MEROPS peptidase family S1, subfamily S1A (chymotrypsin subfamily, clan PA(S)). These peptidases contain the catalytic triad histidine, aspartate and serine found in all members of subfamily S1A. Testes-specific protein TSP50 is also included in this family which has the serine replaced by threonine, although the serine is conserved in many vertebrates [[cite:PUB00095105]]. The type example being chymotrypsin A from Bos taurus (Bovine).

Members of the chymotrypsin family may occasionally function intracellularly (for example, the intracellular digestion of bacteria in neutrophils), but most function extracellularly, for example in roles such as food digestion, fibrinolysis and complement activation [[cite:PUB00003576]]. The essential catalytic unit of the chymotrypsin family is around 220 amino acids in length, although the protein may be extended at the N terminus with unrelated sequences, often containing modules. They are rarely extended at the C terminus: exceptions include acrosin, complement component C2, and coagulation factor X, which has a 16 residue extension that is removed upon activation [[cite:PUB00003576]].

Name: Ubiquitin fusion degradation protein UFD1, N-terminal subdomain 1
ShortDescription:
This entry corresponds to the first subdomain of UFD1 UT3 which forms a double-psi β-barrel fold.

;

Ufd1 is a 40kDa protein involved in the ubiquitin fusion degradation (UFD) pathway, which recognises post-translational ubiquitin-protein conjugates for degradation, and is essential for vegetative cell viability [[cite:PUB00007707]]. Structurally, Ufd1 comprises an N-terminal conserved region (UT3) and a C-terminal disordered region (UT6). The N-terminal domain contains the ubiquitin-binding site and has a similar structure to p97, consisting of two subdomains [[cite:PUB00155902], [cite:PUB00155903], [cite:PUB00038834]], while the C-terminal region contains binding sites for both Npl4 and Cdc48 [[cite:PUB00155902], [cite:PUB00155903]].

Ufd1 forms a complex with Npl4 that functions as the substrate-recruiting cofactor for Cdc48 segregase. The Cdc48-Ufd1-Npl4 complex is involved in degradation of misfolded ER proteins [[cite:PUB00085171]] and recruits Cdc48 to ubiquitylated CMG (Cdc45-MCM-GINS) helicase at the end of chromosome replication, driving helicase disassembly [[cite:PUB00085175]]. In humans, the Npl4-Ufd1 complex also facilitates proteasomal degradation of RIG-I (a viral RNA sensor), thereby reducing antiviral innate immune responses [[cite:PUB00085176]].

The human UFD1 gene is highly expressed during embryogenesis, particularly in the eyes and inner ear primordia, and is thought to be important in determining ectoderm-derived structures, including neural crest cells [[cite:PUB00007708]]. UFD1 is deleted in CATCH-22 syndrome (cardiac defects, abnormal facies, thymic hypoplasia, cleft palate and hypocalcaemia), which is associated with microdeletions on chromosome 22q11.2. Related developmental defects include DiGeorge syndrome ([omim:188400]) and velo-cardio-facial syndrome ([omim:145410]), both thought to involve defective neural crest cell differentiation [[cite:PUB00007708]].Claude is AI and can make mistakes. Name: Cysteine-rich Golgi apparatus protein 1 repeat, eukaryote
ShortDescription: This entry is found in Golgi apparatus protein 1 (GLG1,[swissprot:Q9Z1E9]) and related proteins in the metazoa. GLG1 is located in Golgi cisterns of various cell types, can bind fibroblast growth factor and E-selectin. Sixteen cysteine-rich GLG1 repeats form the core of the protein and are located in the lumen. The C-terminal part of GLG1 is composed of a transmembrane region and a short cytoplasmic tail. The Cys-rich GLG1 repeat is a ~60 amino acid module that contains 4 Cys residues, which can form intrachain disulphide bridges [[cite:PUB00003683]]. Homologues of the vertebrate GLG1/Golgi sialoglycoprotein MG-160 (Mg160)/E-selectin ligand 1 (ESL1)/cysteine-rich fibroblast growth factor receptor 1 (CFR1)/latent transforming growth factor-beta complex protein 1 (LTCP-1) have been found in insects and the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans [[cite:PUB00043660]].
