Name: JAMM/MPN+ metalloenzymes, peptidase M67A
ShortDescription: The peptidase M67A family, also known as the JAMM/MPN+ metalloenzymes, encompasses proteins with diverse functions related to ubiquitin signaling and protein homeostasis. Members of this family are involved in the cleavage of 'Lys-63'-linked polyubiquitin chains, regulating processes such as DNA damage response, cell cycle progression, and immune signaling. They are components of various multiprotein complexes, including the BRCA1-A complex, which targets DNA damage sites, and the BRISC complex, which is essential for mitotic spindle assembly. The family also includes subunits of the COP9 signalosome, which regulates ubiquitin conjugation pathways, and the 26S proteasome, which degrades ubiquitinated proteins. Additionally, they play roles in translation initiation as part of the eIF-3 complex, targeting specific mRNAs for protein synthesis. This family is characterized by the presence of a JAMM motif, which is crucial for their protease activity, and some members also contain SANT and SWIRM domains for DNA binding and chromatin association.

Name: Cop9 signalosome subunit 5 C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: The COP9 (Constitutive photomorphogenesis 9) signalosome (CSN), a large multiprotein complex that resembles the 19S lid of the 26S proteasome, plays a central role in the regulation of the E3-cullin RING ubiquitin ligases (CRLs) [[cite:PUB00065946]]. The catalytic activity of the CSN complex is carried by subunit 5 (CSN5), also known as c-Jun activation domain-binding protein-1 (Jab1) [[cite:PUB00065946]]. This entry is the C-terminal domain found in CSN5 proteins. CSN5, whose two C-terminal helices form an antiparallel hairpin, inserts its final C-terminal helix (helix II) into the central CSN6 framework at the core of the bundle. Deletion of the C-terminal helices has a pronounced effect on CSN integrity [[cite:PUB00091374]].

Name: Cytokine IL1/FGF
ShortDescription:
This entry includes IL-1 and FGF.

;

The interleukin-1 (IL-1) and fibroblast growth factor (FGF, also known as heparin-binding growth factor) families share low sequence similarity (about 25% [[cite:PUB00004737]]) but have very similar structures. They belong to a superfamily that also contains the Kunitz-type soybean trypsin inhibitors (STIs), all of which have very similar structures. However, IL-1 and FGF share no sequence similarity with the STI family.

The crystal structures of interleukin-1 beta and HGF1 have been solved, showing both families to have the same 12-stranded β-sheet structure [[cite:PUB00003281]]; the β-sheets are arranged in 3 similar lobes around a central axis, 6 strands forming an anti-parallel β-barrel [[cite:PUB00004736], [cite:PUB00005097]]. The β-sheets are generally well preserved and the crystal structures superimpose in these areas. The intervening loops are less well conserved - the loop between β-strands 6 and 7 is slightly longer in interleukin-1 beta.

Name: Fibroblast growth factor family
ShortDescription: Fibroblast growth factors (FGFs) [[cite:PUB00000068], [cite:PUB00005334]] are a family of multifunctional proteins, often referred to as 'promiscuous growth factors' due to their diverse actions on multiple cell types [[cite:PUB00067626], [cite:PUB00067627]]. FGFs are mitogens, which stimulate growth or differentiation of cells of mesodermal or neuroectodermal origin. The function of FGFs in developmental processes include mesoderm induction, anterior-posterior patterning, limb development, and neural induction and development. In mature tissues, they are involved in diverse processes including keratinocyte organisation and wound healing [[cite:PUB00021048], [cite:PUB00067628], [cite:PUB00067629], [cite:PUB00067630], [cite:PUB00067631], [cite:PUB00067632]]. FGF involvement is critical during normal development of both vertebrates and invertebrates, and irregularities in their function leads to a range of developmental defects [[cite:PUB00067633], [cite:PUB00067634], [cite:PUB00067635], [cite:PUB00067636]]. Fibroblast growth factors are heparin-binding proteins and interactions with cell-surface-associated heparan sulfate proteoglycans have been shown to be essential for FGF signal transduction. FGFs have internal pseudo-threefold symmetry (β-trefoil topology) [[cite:PUB00024683]]. There are currently over 20 different FGF family members that have been identified in mammals, all of which are structurally related signaling molecules [[cite:PUB00039267], [cite:PUB00021048]]. They exert their effects through four distinct membrane fibroblast growth factor receptors (FGFRs), FGFR1 to FGFR4 [[cite:PUB00001036]], which belong to the tyrosine kinase superfamily. Upon binding to FGF, the receptors dimerize and their intracellular tyrosine kinase domains become active [[cite:PUB00001036]].

Name: Spp2/MOS2, G-patch domain
ShortDescription:
Spp2 is a yeast G-patch protein and spliceosome component that interacts with the ATP-dependent DExH-box splicing factor Prp2 [[cite:PUB00070186]]. This interaction involves the G-patch sequence in Spp2 and is required for the recruitment of Prp2 to the spliceosome before the first catalytic step of splicing. It has been proposed that Spp2 might be an accessory factor that confers spliceosome specificity on Prp2 [[cite:PUB00067694]].

Proteins containing this G-patch domain also include the plant MOS2 protein, which is required for innate and induced resistance to pathogens, and MOS2 homologues from Metazoa [[cite:PUB00061890]].

Name: G-patch domain and KOW motifs-containing protein, KOW 2
ShortDescription: GPKOW is also known as T54 protein or MOS2 homologue [[cite:PUB00061890]]. It contains one G-patch domain and two KOW motifs. GPKOW is a nuclear protein that is regulated by catalytic (C) subunit of Protein Kinase A (PKA) and binds RNA in vivo [[cite:PUB00092179]]. PKA may be involved in regulating multiple steps in post-transcriptional processing of pre-mRNAs. The KOW domain is known as an RNA-binding motif that is shared so far among some families of ribosomal proteins, the essential bacterial transcriptional elongation factor NusG, the eukaryotic chromatin elongation factor Spt5, the higher eukaryotic KIN17 proteins and Mtr4 [[cite:PUB00005458]].

Name: Pre-mRNA-splicing factor Spp2-like
ShortDescription:
Spp2 is a yeast G-patch protein and spliceosome component that interacts with the ATP-dependent DExH-box splicing factor Prp2 [[cite:PUB00070186]]. This interaction involves the G-patch sequence in Spp2 and is required for the recruitment of Prp2 to the spliceosome before the first catalytic step of splicing. It has been proposed that Spp2 might be an accessory factor that confers spliceosome specificity on Prp2 [[cite:PUB00067694]].

This entry also includes the plant MOS2 protein required for innate and induced resistance to pathogens, and MOS2 homologues from Metazoa [[cite:PUB00061890]].

Name: G-patch domain and KOW motifs-containing protein, KOW 1
ShortDescription: GPKOW is also known as T54 protein or MOS2 homologue [[cite:PUB00061890]]. It contains one G-patch domain and two KOW motifs. GPKOW is a nuclear protein that is regulated by catalytic (C) subunit of Protein Kinase A (PKA) and binds RNA in vivo [[cite:PUB00092179]]. PKA may be involved in regulating multiple steps in post-transcriptional processing of pre-mRNAs. The KOW domain is known as an RNA-binding motif that is shared so far among some families of ribosomal proteins, the essential bacterial transcriptional elongation factor NusG, the eukaryotic chromatin elongation factor Spt5, the higher eukaryotic KIN17 proteins and Mtr4 [[cite:PUB00005458]].

Name: Forkhead box protein J1, forkhead domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the forkhead (FH) domain of FOXJ1 and similar proteins from animals. The FH domain is a winged helix DNA-binding domain.

;

Forkhead box protein J1 (FOXJ1), also called Forkhead-related protein FKHL13 or HFH-4, acts as a transcription factor specifically required for the formation of motile cilia [[cite:PUB00103399], [cite:PUB00103402]]. It acts by activating transcription of genes that mediate assembly of motile cilia, such as CFAP157. FOXJ1 binds the DNA consensus sequences 5'-HWDTGTTTGTTTA-3' or 5'-KTTTGTTGTTKTW-3' (where H is not G, W is A or T, D is not C, and K is G or T). It activates the transcription of a variety of ciliary proteins in the developing brain and lung [[cite:PUB00103403], [cite:PUB00103396], [cite:PUB00103401], [cite:PUB00103400], [cite:PUB00103398], [cite:PUB00103397]]. In humans, FOXJ1 is associated with mucosal inflammation caused by allergen exposure [[cite:PUB00103396]] and a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterised by chronic inflammation and bronchiectasis due to defects in the respiratory cilia [[cite:PUB00103399]].

Name: Fork head domain conserved site 2
ShortDescription: The fork head domain is a conserved domain of about 100 amino-acid residues found in some eukaryotic transcription factors. It is involved in DNA-binding [[cite:PUB00004151]]. This entry represents a conserved heptapeptide located in the central section of the domain.

Name: Fork head domain conserved site1
ShortDescription: The fork head domain is a conserved domain of about 100 amino-acid residues found in some eukaryotic transcription factors. It is involved in DNA-binding [[cite:PUB00004151]]. This entry represents a conserved site found in the N-terminal section of the fork head domain.

Name: Forkhead box protein J1
ShortDescription: Forkhead box protein J1 (FOXJ1), also called Forkhead-related protein FKHL13 or HFH-4, acts as a transcription factor specifically required for the formation of motile cilia [[cite:PUB00103399], [cite:PUB00103402]]. It acts by activating transcription of genes that mediate assembly of motile cilia, such as CFAP157. FOXJ1 binds the DNA consensus sequences 5'-HWDTGTTTGTTTA-3' or 5'-KTTTGTTGTTKTW-3' (where H is not G, W is A or T, D is not C, and K is G or T). It activates the transcription of a variety of ciliary proteins in the developing brain and lung [[cite:PUB00103403], [cite:PUB00103396], [cite:PUB00103401], [cite:PUB00103400], [cite:PUB00103398], [cite:PUB00103397]]. In humans, FOXJ1 is associated with mucosal inflammation caused by allergen exposure [[cite:PUB00103396]] and a form of primary ciliary dyskinesia characterised by chronic inflammation and bronchiectasis due to defects in the respiratory cilia [[cite:PUB00103399]].

Name: Fork head domain
ShortDescription:
The fork head domain is a conserved DNA-binding domain (also known as a "winged helix") of about 100 amino-acid residues.

Drosophila melanogaster fork head protein is a transcription factor that promotes terminal rather than segmental development, contains neither homeodomains nor zinc-fingers characteristic of other transcription factors [[cite:PUB00000827]]. Instead, it contains a distinct type of DNA-binding region, containing around 100 amino acids, which has since been identified in a number of transcription factors (including D. melanogaster FD1-5, mammalian HNF-3, human HTLF, Saccharomyces cerevisiae HCM1, etc.). This is referred to as the fork head domain but is also known as a 'winged helix' [[cite:PUB00000827], [cite:PUB00004151], [cite:PUB00004800]].

The fork head domain binds B-DNA as a monomer [[cite:PUB00004151]], but shows no similarity to previously identified DNA-binding motifs. Although the domain is found in several different transcription factors, a common function is their involvement in early developmental decisions of cell fates during embryogenesis [[cite:PUB00004800]].

Name: IPO4/5-like, TPR repeats domain
ShortDescription: This region of tetratricopeptide (TPR)-like repeats is found towards the N-terminal end of human Importin-4/5 (IPO4/5) and similar eukaryotic proteins. IPO4 serves as receptor for nuclear localisation signals in cargo substrates [[cite:PUB00160731], [cite:PUB00160732]].

Name: Glomulin/ALF4
ShortDescription: In the human adult, FKBP-12, also known as FAP68 or FK506-binding protein, (protein product of the gene glomulin) is expressed at high levels in skeletal muscle, heart, brain and kidney, and at low levels in smaller arteries and veins. The high expression of glomulin in murine vasculature suggests an important role in blood vessel development and/or maintenance, which is supported by the vascular phenotype seen in GVM patients with mutations in this gene [[cite:PUB00044262]]. It is a cytoplasmic protein, specifically bound by the non-phosphorylated form of the hepatocyte growth factor, HGF, receptor and is released upon HGF stimulation and receptor phosphorylation, suggesting a potential role for FKBP12 in linking HGF signaling to the regulation of protein synthesis [[cite:PUB00044263]]. FKBP12 is found to regulate Ca2+release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) by its action on the IP3 receptors (IP3Rs), which crucially regulate diverse cell signalling processes from reproduction to apoptosis, possibly via the kinase rapamycin (mTOR), that potentiates Ca2+ release from the IP3R in smooth muscle [[cite:PUB00044264]].

Name: YAP-binding/ALF4/Glomulin
ShortDescription: This entry contains a number of protein families with apparently unrelated functions. The yeast YAP binding proteins are stress response and redox homeostasis proteins, induced by hydrogen peroxide or induced in response to alkylating agent methyl methanesulphonate (MMS) [[cite:PUB00053725], [cite:PUB00053726]]. Aberrant root formation protein 4 (ALF4) of Arabidopsis thaliana (Mouse-ear cress),is required for the initiation of lateral roots independent from auxin signalling. It may also function in maintaining the pericycle in the mitotically competent state needed for lateral root formation [[cite:PUB00053727]]. Glomulin (FAP68) is essential for normal development of the vasculature and may represent a naturally occurring ligand of the immunophilins FKBP59 and FKBP12 [[cite:PUB00044263], [cite:PUB00053728]].

Name: NADH:ubiquinone oxidoreductase, 30kDa subunit superfamily
ShortDescription:
Respiratory-chain NADH dehydrogenase ([ec:1.6.5.3]) (also known as complex I or NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase) is an oligomeric enzymatic complex located in the inner mitochondrial membrane which also seems to exist in the chloroplast and in cyanobacteria (as a NADH-plastoquinone oxidoreductase). Among the 25 to 30 polypeptide subunits of this bioenergetic enzyme complex there is one with a molecular weight of 30 Kd (in mammals) which has been found to be [[cite:PUB00001392]]:

  • Nuclear encoded, as a precursor form with a transit peptide in mammals, and in Neurospora crassa.
  • Mitochondrial encoded in Paramecium (protein P1), and in the slime mold Dictyostelium discoideum (ORF 209).
  • Chloroplast encoded in various higher plants (ORF 159).

It is also present in bacteria:

  • In the cyanobacteria Synechocystis strain PCC 6803 (gene ndhJ).
  • Subunit C of Escherichia coli NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase (gene nuoC).
  • Subunit Nqo5 of Paracoccus denitrificans NADH-ubiquinone oxidoreductase. Nqo5 composes the hydrogenase-like module together with the Nqo4, Nqo6, and Nqo9 subunits. Homologous proteins of the Nqo5 subunit are also contained in membrane-bound multisubunit hydrogenases, while soluble-type hydrogenases are not. This subunit is essential in complex I assembly [[cite:PUB00097437]].

Name: NADH dehydrogenase, subunit C
ShortDescription: This entry describes the C subunit of the NADH dehydrogenase complex I in bacteria, as well as many instances of the corresponding mitochondrial subunit (NADH dehydrogenase subunit 9) and of the F420H2 dehydrogenase in Methanosarcina. Complex I contains subunits designated A-N. This C subunit often occurs as a fusion protein with the D subunit. This entry excludes the NAD(P)H and plastoquinone-dependent form of chloroplasts and Synechocystis.

This entry represents a conserved region found towards the C terminus of these proteins.

Name: Mff-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents a domain found in mitochondrial fission factor (Mff) and at the C terminus of FATE1. This domain has a predicted transmembrane segment preceded by a coiled-coil region. Despite their similarity in the C terminus, FATE1 lacks a Mff-similar N-terminal domain that is essential for interaction of Mff with the dynamin-related GTPase Drp1, which mediates mitochondrial fission. Instead, FATE1 is involved in the regulation of ER-mitochondria distance and Ca(2+) uptake by mitochondria [[cite:PUB00089016]].

Name: Fetal and adult testis-expressed transcript protein
ShortDescription: FATE1 is a member of the Miff protein family, whose members are involved in the control of mitochondrial and peroxisomal fission. It is localized in mitochondria associated ER membranes (MAM) and is implicated in the regulation of Ca2+ and drug-dependent apoptosis in cancer cells by modulating ER-mitochondria distance [[cite:PUB00089016]]. Homologues are found only in chordates.

Name: Immunoglobulin superfamily V-set and transmembrane domain-containing protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes members that are involved in various cellular processes, including immune response modulation, cell differentiation, and regulation of cell motility. Some proteins in this family function as inhibitors of T-cell proliferation and IL2 production, playing roles in immune regulation. Others are implicated in adipocyte differentiation by promoting the expression of specific transcription factors. Additionally, certain family members are involved in the negative regulation of cell motility, interacting with other proteins to influence cell migration, fusion, and morphology. Some proteins also participate in maintaining neural networks and enhancing calcium channel currents in photoreceptors, indicating a role in neural and visual functions.

Name: IgSF3/IGSF8/FPRP, immunoglobulin-like domain
ShortDescription:
This immunoglobulin-like (Ig-like) domain is found in human Immunoglobulin superfamily member 3 (IgSF3), Immunoglobulin superfamily member 8 (IGSF8), Prostaglandin F2 receptor negative regulator (FPRP) and similar proteins.

IGSF8 links tetraspanin-enriched microdomains to the actin cytoskeleton and plays several important roles in innate and adaptive immunity [[cite:PUB00162085], [cite:PUB00162087]].

FPRP inhibits the binding of prostaglandin F2-alpha (PGF2-alpha) to its specific FP receptor, by decreasing the receptor number rather than the affinity constant [[cite:PUB00162081]].

Variations in IgSF3 have been associated with different human diseases such as osteopetrosis and chronic obstructive pulmonary diseases [[cite:PUB00162079], [cite:PUB00162080]]. Its specific function is unknown.

Name: Molybdenum cofactor sulfurase, middle domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a domain located in the middle of Molybdenum cofactor sulfurases (MOCOS). MOCOS sulfurates the molybdenum cofactor [[cite:PUB00103855]]. Mutations in this protein lead to a disorder characterised by excretion of very large amounts of xanthine in the urine and a tendency to form xanthine stones [[cite:PUB00069600]].

This domain is also found at the N-terminal of Mitochondrial amidoxime-reducing component 1 (mARC1), which catalyses the reduction of N-oxygenated molecules, acting as a counterpart of cytochrome P450 and flavin-containing monooxygenases in metabolic cycles [[cite:PUB00103854], [cite:PUB00103856]], This protein comprises two structural domains which consist of non successive secondary-structure element, with mainly β-strands forming three- and four-stranded antiparallel β-sheets and several α-helices of different lengths [[cite:PUB00103857]].

This domain, also known as the MOSC_N domain, is often found to the N terminus of MOSC domain ([interpro:IPR005302]).

This domain is also found in 6-hydroxylaminopurine reductase YcbX from E.coli, a reductase involved in the detoxification of N-hydroxylated base analogues [[cite:PUB00104737]]. It contributes to the detoxification of 6-N-hydroxylaminopurine (HAP) by catalysing the reduction of HAP to adenine[[cite:PUB00104737], [cite:PUB00163267]].

Name: Molybdenum cofactor sulfurase, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
Molybdenum cofactor (MOCO) sulphurases [[cite:PUB00034759]] catalyse the insertion of a terminal sulphur ligand into the molybdenum cofactor, thereby converting the oxo form of MOCO to a sulphurylated form. Suphurylated MOCO is required by several enzymes, including: aldehyde oxidase ([ec:1.2.3.1]), which function in the last step of abscisic acid biosynthesis in plants [[cite:PUB00035521]]; and xanthine dehydrogenase ([ec:1.17.1.4]), which synthesis uric acid from xanthine during nitrogen metabolism [[cite:PUB00035522]].

This entry represents the β-barrel C-terminal domain of MOCO sulphurase (MOSC domain), which has a β-barrel structure similar to that of the β-barrel domain in pyruvate kinase and contains a highly conserved cysteine residue required for activity. MOSC domains are found in several diverse metal-sulphur cluster biosynthesis proteins from both eukaryotes and prokaryotes. MOSC domains occur as either stand-alone forms, such as the YiiM protein from Escherichia coli, or fused to other domains, such as a NifS-like catalytic domain in MOCO sulphurase. The MOSC domain is predicted to be a sulphur-carrier domain that receives sulphur abstracted from pyridoxal phosphate-dependent NifS-like enzymes, on its conserved cysteine, and delivers it for the formation of diverse sulphur-metal clusters [[cite:PUB00019067]].

The MOSC domain contains several patches of hydrophobic residues and an absolutely conserved cysteine residue situated closer to the C-terminal end of the domain. The absolutely conserved cysteine in the MOSC domain is reminiscent of the analogous conservation of a cysteine in the active site of the thioredoxin and rhodanese superfamilies. Members of both these superfamilies, especially of the latter one, have been implicated in the synthesis of Fe-S clusters, through mobilisation of sulphur with their active cysteine.

Name: Triose Phosphate/Phosphate Translocator
ShortDescription: The TPT transporter family is involved in the transport of various substances across cellular membranes. Members of this family function as nucleotide-sugar transporters, facilitating the import of nucleotide-sugars such as GDP-mannose, UDP-glucose, and UDP-galactose into the Golgi lumen or endoplasmic reticulum. These transport processes are essential for the synthesis of glycoproteins, glycolipids, and oligosaccharides, impacting cell wall composition, glycosylation, and other cellular functions. Some family members also transport sugar phosphates like triose phosphates, phosphoenolpyruvate, and glucose-6-phosphate, playing roles in photosynthesis, carbon fixation, and metabolic pathways. The family includes antiporters specific for GDP-fucose, which are involved in fucosylation processes essential for cell signaling and development. Overall, the TPT transporter family is crucial for various biosynthetic pathways and cellular homeostasis.

Name: Sugar phosphate transporter domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in a number of sugar phosphate transporters, including those with a specificity for triose phosphate [[cite:PUB00020858]].

Name: Solute carrier family 25 member 46
ShortDescription: SLC25A46 is a modified solute transporter that has been recruited to the outer mitochondrial membrane and interacts with the inner membrane remodeling protein mitofilin (Fcj1) [[cite:PUB00089025]]. It plays a role in mitochondrial dynamics and cristae maintenance [[cite:PUB00089027]]. Mutations in the SLC25A46 gene cause optic atrophy spectrum disorder [[cite:PUB00089026]].

Name: Mu2, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of heterotetrameric clathrin-associated adaptor protein complex 2 (AP-2) medium mu2 subunit. Mu2 is ubiquitously expressed in mammals. In higher eukaryotes, AP-2 plays a critical role in clathrin-mediated endocytosis from the plasma membrane in different cells. The membrane-anchored cargo molecules can be linked to the outer lattice of CCVs by AP-2. Those cargo molecules interact with adaptors through short sorting signals in their cytosolic segments. Tyrosine-based endocytotic signals are one of the most important sorting signals. They are of the form Y-X-X-Phi, where Y is tyrosine, X is any amino acid and Phi is a bulky hydrophobic residue that can be Leu, Ile, Met, Phe, or Val. These kinds of sorting signals can be recognized by the C-terminal domain of AP-2 mu2 subunit, also known as Y-X-X-Phi signal-binding domain that contains two hydrophobic pockets, one for the tyrosine-binding and one for the bulky hydrophobic residue-binding. Since the Y-X-X-Phi binding site is buried in the core structure of AP-2, a phosphorylation induced conformational change is required when the cargo molecules binds to AP-2 [[cite:PUB00018527], [cite:PUB00025539]].

Name: Clathrin adaptor, mu subunit
ShortDescription:
Proteins synthesized on the ribosome and processed in the endoplasmic reticulum are transported from the Golgi apparatus to the trans-Golgi network (TGN), and from there via small carrier vesicles to their final destination compartment. These vesicles have specific coat proteins (such as clathrin or coatomer) that are important for cargo selection and direction of transport [[cite:PUB00035769]]. Clathrin coats contain both clathrin (acts as a scaffold) and adaptor complexes that link clathrin to receptors in coated vesicles. Clathrin-associated protein complexes are believed to interact with the cytoplasmic tails of membrane proteins, leading to their selection and concentration. The two major types of clathrin adaptor complexes are the heterotetrameric adaptor protein (AP) complexes, and the monomeric GGA (Golgi-localising, Gamma-adaptin ear domain homology, ARF-binding proteins) adaptors [[cite:PUB00035753], [cite:PUB00035765]].

;

AP (adaptor protein) complexes are found in coated vesicles and clathrin-coated pits. AP complexes connect cargo proteins and lipids to clathrin at vesicle budding sites, as well as binding accessory proteins that regulate coat assembly and disassembly (such as AP180, epsins and auxilin). There are different AP complexes in mammals. AP1 is responsible for the transport of lysosomal hydrolases between the TGN and endosomes [[cite:PUB00035754]]. AP2 associates with the plasma membrane and is responsible for endocytosis [[cite:PUB00035755]]. AP3 is responsible for protein trafficking to lysosomes and other related organelles [[cite:PUB00035756]]. AP4 is less well characterised. AP complexes are heterotetramers composed of two large subunits (adaptins), a medium subunit (mu) and a small subunit (sigma). For example, in AP1 these subunits are gamma-1-adaptin, beta-1-adaptin, mu-1 and sigma-1, while in AP2 they are alpha-adaptin, beta-2-adaptin, mu-2 and sigma-2. Each subunit has a specific function. Adaptins recognise and bind to clathrin through their hinge region (clathrin box), and recruit accessory proteins that modulate AP function through their C-terminal ear (appendage) domains. Mu recognises tyrosine-based sorting signals within the cytoplasmic domains of transmembrane cargo proteins [[cite:PUB00010644]]. One function of clathrin and AP2 complex-mediated endocytosis is to regulate the number of GABA(A) receptors available at the cell surface [[cite:PUB00035757]].

This entry represents the mu subunit of various clathrin adaptors (AP1, AP2 and AP3) [[cite:PUB00025539]]. The mu subunit regulates the coupling of clathrin lattices with particular membrane proteins by self-phosphorylation via a mechanism that is still unclear [[cite:PUB00001404]]. The mu subunit possesses a highly conserved N-terminal domain of around 230 amino acids, which may be the region of interaction with other AP proteins; a linker region of between 10 and 42 amino acids; and a less well-conserved C-terminal domain of around 190 amino acids, which may be the site of specific interaction with the protein being transported in the vesicle [[cite:PUB00001404]].

Name: Mu homology domain
ShortDescription:
The mu homology domain (MHD) is an ~280 residue protein-protein interaction module, which is found in endocytotic proteins involved in clathrin-mediated endocytosis [[cite:PUB00016632], [cite:PUB00018526], [cite:PUB00016661], [cite:PUB00057692]]:

  • Mu subunits of adaptor protein (AP) complexes, AP-1, AP-2, AP-3, and AP-4.
  • Proteins of the stonin family.
  • Proteins of the muniscin family: Syp1, FCHO1/2 and SGIP1.

The MHD domain has an elongated, banana-shaped, all β-sheet structure. It can be considered as two β-sandwich subdomains (A and B), with subdomain B inserted between strands 6 and 15 of subdomain A, and joined edge to edge such that the convex surface is a continuous nine-stranded mixed β-sheet that runs the whole length of the molecule. The tyrosine based signal binds to a site on the surface of two parallel β-sheet strands (β1 and β16) in subdomain A [[cite:PUB00057692], [cite:PUB00018527]].

Name: AP-2 complex subunit mu, N-terminal
ShortDescription: This entry represents the N-terminal domain of heterotetrameric clathrin-associated adaptor protein complex 2 (AP-2) medium mu2 subunit. Mu2 is ubiquitously expressed in mammals. In higher eukaryotes, AP-2 plays a critical role in clathrin-mediated endocytosis from the plasma membrane in different cells. The membrane-anchored cargo molecules can be linked to the outer lattice of CCVs by AP-2. Those cargo molecules interact with adaptors through short sorting signals in their cytosolic segments. Tyrosine-based endocytotic signals are one of the most important sorting signals. These kinds of sorting signals can be recognized by the C-terminal domain of AP-2 mu2 subunit, also known as Y-X-X-Phi signal-binding domain that contains two hydrophobic pockets, one for the tyrosine-binding and one for the bulky hydrophobic residue-binding. Since the Y-X-X-Phi binding site is buried in the core structure of AP-2, a phosphorylation induced conformational change is required when the cargo molecules binds to AP-2 [[cite:PUB00018527], [cite:PUB00025539]].

Name: Clathrin adaptor, mu subunit, conserved site
ShortDescription: This entry represents the mu subunit of various clathrin adaptors (AP1, AP2 and AP3) [[cite:PUB00025539]]. Name: AP-2 complex subunit mu, C-terminal superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily describes the C-terminal domain of the Mu subunit (Mu2-adaptin, AP50) of adaptor protein (AP) complexes AP-1, AP-2, AP-3, and AP-4. It has an elongated, banana-shaped, all β-sheet structure. It can be considered as two β-sandwich subdomains (A and B), with subdomain B inserted between strands 6 and 15 of subdomain A, and joined edge to edge such that the convex surface is a continuous nine-stranded mixed β-sheet that runs the whole length of the molecule. The tyrosine based signal binds to a site on the surface of two parallel β-sheet strands (β1 and β16) in subdomain A [[cite:PUB00057692], [cite:PUB00018527]].

Name: Adaptor complexes medium subunit
ShortDescription: The adaptor complexes medium subunit family is involved in the selection and concentration of membrane proteins into vesicles for intracellular trafficking. Members of this family are components of various adaptor protein (AP) complexes, such as AP-1, AP-2, AP-3, and AP-4, which are not always clathrin-associated. These complexes play roles in sorting proteins at the trans-Golgi network, endosomes, and plasma membrane, contributing to processes like endocytosis, vesicle formation, and cargo selection. Some family members are directly involved in recognizing tyrosine-based sorting signals on cargo proteins. The family also includes proteins like Stonin-1 and Stonin-2, which are implicated in the endocytic recycling of synaptic vesicles and may facilitate clathrin-coated vesicle uncoating.

Name: RTP801-like
ShortDescription: RTP801, also known as REDD1, is the protein product of a hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1)- responsive gene and is thought to be involved in various cellular processes [[cite:PUB00016594]]. Both RTP801 and RTP801-like (REDD2) work downstream of AKT and upstream of TSC2 to inhibit mTOR, a serine/threonine kinase that plays an essential role in cell growth control [[cite:PUB00057842]]. Two members of this family expressed by Drosophila melanogaster, Scylla ([swissprot:Q9NHN4]) and Charybde ([swissprot:Q9NHN5]), are designated as Hox targets [[cite:PUB00016594], [cite:PUB00057843]].

Name: RTP801-like, C-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents the C-terminal domain of RTP801 (also known as REDD1), the protein product of a hypoxia-inducible factor 1 (HIF-1)- responsive gene [[cite:PUB00016594]]. It is thought to be involved in various cellular processes [[cite:PUB00016594]]. Both RTP801 and RTP801-like (REDD2) work downstream of AKT and upstream of TSC2 to inhibit mTOR, a serine/threonine kinase that plays an essential role in cell growth control [[cite:PUB00057842]]. Overexpression of RTP801 causes the apoptosis- resistant phenotype in cycling cells, and apoptosis sensitivity in growth arrested cells [[cite:PUB00016594]]. Two members of this superfamily expressed by Drosophila melanogaster, Scylla ([swissprot:Q9NHN4]) and Charybde ([swissprot:Q9NHN5]), are designated as Hox targets [[cite:PUB00016594], [cite:PUB00057843]].

Name: Golgi apparatus membrane protein TVP23-like
ShortDescription: Tvp23 is a Golgi membrane protein involved in vesicular trafficking [[cite:PUB00086476]].

Name: DCN1-like, PONY binding domain
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents a domain is found in DCN1-like proteins. Proteins of the DCN family may contribute to neddylation of cullin components of SCF-type E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes, which are multi-protein complexes required for polyubiquitination and subsequent degradation of target proteins by the 26S proteasome [[cite:PUB00021043], [cite:PUB00057468]].

The structure of this domain is composed entirely of α helices [[cite:PUB00047735], [cite:PUB00050725]]. It has been referred to as potentiating neddylation domain (PONY) and can be found in association with an N-terminal UBA domain. The PONY domain contains a cullin-binding surface within its C-terminal region and is sufficient to promote neddylation [[cite:PUB00050725], [cite:PUB00064019]].

Name: Potentiating neddylation domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found in the eukaryotic family defective in cullin neddylation, which includes DCN1 and DCN1-like proteins. Proteins of the DCN family may contribute to neddylation of cullin components of SCF-type E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes, which are multi-protein complexes required for polyubiquitination and subsequent degradation of target proteins by the 26S proteasome [[cite:PUB00021043], [cite:PUB00057468]].

The structure of this domain is composed entirely of α helices [[cite:PUB00047735], [cite:PUB00050725]]. It has been referred to as potentiating neddylation domain (PONY) and can be found in association with an N-terminal UBA domain. The PONY domain contains a cullin-binding surface within its C-terminal region and is sufficient to promote neddylation [[cite:PUB00050725], [cite:PUB00064019]].

Name: Defective-in-cullin neddylation protein
ShortDescription:
The eukaryotic defective in cullin neddylation (DCN) protein family, contributes to neddylation of cullin components of SCF-type E3 ubiquitin ligase complexes. These multi-protein complexes are required for polyubiquitination and subsequent degradation of target proteins by the 26S proteasome [[cite:PUB00021043], [cite:PUB00064019], [cite:PUB00097937]]. Proteins in the DCN family include:

  • Yeast DCN1.
  • Vertebrate DCN1-like protein 1-5.
  • Plant Defective in cullin neddylation protein AAR3 [[cite:PUB00097939]].

DCN family proteins all contain a Potentiating neddylation (PONY) domain ([interpro:IPR005176]), contains a cullin-binding surface within its C-terminal region and is sufficient to promote neddylation [[cite:PUB00050725], [cite:PUB00064019]]. The N-terminal region of the protein often contains a UBA-like domain.

Name: Protein N-terminal glutamine amidohydrolase, alpha beta roll
ShortDescription: This entry represents a structural domain found in the N-terminal glutamine amidohydrolase (NtQ-amidase) family of proteins. These proteins contain a region of approximately 200 residues carrying several distinctive motifs including a WDYHV motif and one of three cysteines. Protein N-terminal glutamine amidohydrolase is responsible for degradation of N-terminal glutamine [[cite:PUB00054026]].

Name: Protein N-terminal glutamine amidohydrolase
ShortDescription: The N-end rule pathway is an ubiquitin (Ub)-dependent proteolytic system that mediates and regulates the degradation of intracellular proteins through the recognition of their N-terminal residues. NTAQ1 (also known as Nta1 in fungi) is an N-terminal amidohydrolase, which converts N-terminal Asn and Gln to the N-terminal residues Asp and Glu, the first step of the hierarchically organized N-end rule pathway [[cite:PUB00054026]]. The structure of Nta1 has been determined [[cite:PUB00090033]].

Name: Protein N-terminal glutamine amidohydrolase, alpha beta roll superfamily
ShortDescription: This entry represents a structural domain superfamily found in the N-terminal glutamine amidohydrolase (NtQ-amidase) family of proteins. These proteins contain a region of approximately 200 residues carrying several distinctive motifs including a WDYHV motif and one of three cysteines. Protein N-terminal glutamine amidohydrolase is responsible for degradation of N-terminal glutamine [[cite:PUB00054026]].

Name: MORF4 family-associated protein 1
ShortDescription: MRFAP1 (MORF4 family-associated protein 1) and its interaction partner MORF4L1 (or MRG15) are target proteins of the NEDD8-cullin pathway, which plays an important role in the degradation of cell cycle regulators and transcriptional control networks. It has been suggest that MRFAP1 competes with MRGBP for binding to MORF4L1, thereby regulating MORF4L1 function in chromatin modification [[cite:PUB00069946]].

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex, subunit 3
ShortDescription: This entry includes Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 3 (COG3, also known as Sec34), a component of the peripheral membrane COG complex that is involved in intra-Golgi protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00009854]]. COG is a member of the complexes associated with tethering containing helical rods (CATCHR) family which also includes the exocyst, GARP and DSL1 complexes, which are evolutionarily related and share structural features consisting of α-helical bundles towards the C-terminal and an N-terminal coiled-coil region [[cite:PUB00100048], [cite:PUB00100047]].

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 3, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the α-helical bundles of COG3.

;

This entry includes the Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 3 (COG3, also known as Sec34) which is a component of the peripheral membrane COG complex, involved in intra-Golgi protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00009854], [cite:PUB00100048], [cite:PUB00100047]]. COG is a member of the complexes associated with tethering containing helical rods (CATCHR) family which also includes the exocyst, GARP and Dsl1 complexes, which are evolutionarily related and share structural features consisting of α-helical bundles towards the C-terminal and an N-terminal coiled-coil region [[cite:PUB00100048], [cite:PUB00100047]].

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 3, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal domain of COG3.

;

This entry includes the Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 3 (COG3, also known as Sec34) which is a component of the peripheral membrane COG complex, involved in intra-Golgi protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00009854], [cite:PUB00100048], [cite:PUB00100047]]. COG is a member of the complexes associated with tethering containing helical rods (CATCHR) family which also includes the exocyst, GARP and Dsl1 complexes, which are evolutionarily related and share structural features consisting of α-helical bundles towards the C-terminal and an N-terminal coiled-coil region [[cite:PUB00100048], [cite:PUB00100047]].

Name: Spatacsin
ShortDescription: Defects in the spatacsin gene are the cause of spastic paraplegia 11, a neurodegenerative disorder characterised by a slow, gradual, progressive weakness and spasticity of the lower limbs [[cite:PUB00067524]]. Human and rat spacticin protein has been shown to be expressed in the central nervous system, particularly in cortical and spinal motor neurons as well as in retina [[cite:PUB00067525]].

Name: Spatacsin, C-terminal domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the C-terminal domain of spatacsin. Defects in the spatacsin gene are the cause of spastic paraplegia 11 [[cite:PUB00067524]].

Name: Sperm microtubule inner protein 9
ShortDescription: This entry represents homologs of Sperm microtubule inner protein 9 (SPMIP9 also known as TEX37, TSC21) [[cite:PUB00070026]]. SPMIP9 is a microtubule-associated protein (MIP) that is found only in mammalian sperm. The EM structure of sperm DMTs shows that SPMIP9 is part of the tektin bundle making contacts with TECT3-1 and DUSP21 [[cite:PUB00151496]].

Name: BMERB domain-containing protein 1
ShortDescription: This entry includes human C16orf45 and related proteins. Their function is not clear.

Name: bMERB domain
ShortDescription:
A variety of different effector proteins interact specifically with GTP-bound Rab proteins and mediate their versatile roles in membrane trafficking, including budding of vesicles from a donor membrane, directed transport through the cell and finally tethering and fusion with a target membrane. The "bivalent Mical/EHBP Rab binding" (bMERB) domain is a Rab effector domain that is present in proteins of the Mical and EHBP families, both known to act in endosomal trafficking. The bMERB domain displays a preference for Rab8 family proteins (Rab8, 10, 13 and 15) and at least some of the bMERB domains contain two separate binding sites for Rab-proteins, allowing Micals and EHBPs to bind two Rabs simultaneously. The strong similarity between the two binding sites within one bMRB domain strongly suggests an evolutionarily development via duplication of a common ancestor supersecondary structure element [[cite:PUB00088663]].

The bMERB domain has a completely α-helical fold consisting of a central helix and N- and C-terminal helices folding back on this central helix [[cite:PUB00088663]].

Name: Krueppel C2H2-type Zinc Finger
ShortDescription: The Krueppel C2H2-type zinc-finger protein family is characterized by its involvement in transcriptional regulation. Members of this family typically contain C2H2-type zinc-finger domains, which are known for their role in DNA binding and gene expression modulation. Some proteins within the family may function as transcriptional repressors, potentially suppressing transcriptional activities mediated by specific signaling pathways, such as the MAPK pathway. Others may act as transcriptional activators, directly influencing the expression of genes like NPPA. Certain members are implicated in cellular processes like apoptosis, and may interact with proteins such as p53/TP53, BAX, and TRAF2 to mediate cell death pathways in response to DNA damage. Domains like the KRAB and SCAN domains contribute to the transcriptional repressor activity and enable dimerization, respectively, which further diversifies the regulatory roles of the family in gene expression.

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8
ShortDescription: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8 acts as component of the peripheral membrane COG complex that is involved in intra-Golgi protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00009854]].

Name: Conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8, Metazoal and Viridiplantae
ShortDescription: This entry represents conserved oligomeric Golgi complex subunit 8 from metazoans and viridiplantae. It is a component of the peripheral membrane COG complex that is involved in intra-Golgi protein trafficking [[cite:PUB00009854]].

Name: ENTH domain
ShortDescription:
The ENTH (Epsin N-terminal homology) domain is approximately 150 amino acids in length and is always found located at the N-termini of proteins. The domain forms a compact globular structure, composed of 9 α-helices connected by loops of varying length. The general topology is determined by three helical hairpins that are stacked consecutively with a right hand twist [[cite:PUB00007107]]. An N-terminal helix folds back, forming a deep basic groove that forms the binding pocket for the Ins(1,4,5)P3 ligand [[cite:PUB00007108]]. The ligand is coordinated by residues from surrounding α-helices and all three phosphates are multiply coordinated. The coordination of Ins(1,4,5)P3 suggests that ENTH is specific for particular head groups.

Proteins containing this domain have been found to bind PtdIns(4,5)P2 and PtdIns(1,4,5)P3 suggesting that the domain may be a membrane interacting module. The main function of proteins containing this domain appears to be to act as accessory clathrin adaptors in endocytosis, Epsin is able to recruit and promote clathrin polymerisation on a lipid monolayer, but may have additional roles in signalling and actin regulation [[cite:PUB00005059]]. Epsin causes a strong degree of membrane curvature and tubulation, even fragmentation of membranes with a high PtdIns(4,5)P2 content. Epsin binding to membranes facilitates their deformation by insertion of the N-terminal helix into the outer leaflet of the bilayer, pushing the head groups apart. This would reduce the energy needed to curve the membrane into a vesicle, making it easier for the clathrin cage to fix and stabilise the curved membrane. This points to a pioneering role for epsin in vesicle budding as it provides both a driving force and a link between membrane invagination and clathrin polymerisation.

Name: AP-4 complex accessory subunit Tepsin
ShortDescription: Tepsin associates with the adapter-like complex (AP-4) complex, which forms a non-clathrin coat around cytoplasmic vesicles in plants and animals [[cite:PUB00089389]]. Mutagenesis studies have identified two phylogenetically conserved peptide motifs within the C-terminal of tepsin that interact with the C-terminal ear (or appendage) domains of the beta4 and epsilon subunits of AP-4 [[cite:PUB00086230]]. The homologue from Arabidopsis thaliana is known as MTV1 (At3g16270), which mediates clathrin-dependent trafficking of vacuolar cargo from the trans-Golgi network [[cite:PUB00089789]].

Name: Tepsin, ENTH/VHS domain
ShortDescription:
Tepsin (also known as the product of the ENTHD2 or AP4AT gene) is an AP-4 accessory protein. It binds to the beta4-ear domain of AP-4, and is recruited to the trans-Golgi network (TGN) in manner dependent on this interaction [[cite:PUB00086230]]. This is the ENTH/VHS domain in tepsin and in A. thaliana protein At3g16270 [[cite:PUB00046754]].

Unlike the other members of the ENTH/ANTH/VHS superfamily, the tepsin ENTH domain lacks helix0, helix8, and a lipid binding pocket. Loss of helix0 precludes formation of a lipid binding pocket and explains why tepsin ENTH domain cannot interact directly with phosphoinositide head groups [[cite:PUB00086426]].

Name: AP-4 complex accessory subunit Tepsin, VHS/ENTH-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry describes the VHS/ENTH-like domain found in human AP-4 complex accessory subunit Tepsin and similar animal proteins. The Epsin N-Terminal Homology (ENTH) domain is an evolutionarily conserved protein module found primarily in proteins that participate in clathrin-mediated endocytosis. ENTH is structurally similar to the VHS domain and is composed of a superhelix of eight α-helices. ENTH domains bind both, inositol phospholipids and proteins. They contribute to the nucleation and formation of clathrin coats on membranes [[cite:PUB00086426]]. Tepsin associates with the Adapter-like complex 4 (AP-4) and may therefore play a role in vesicular trafficking of proteins at the trans-Golgi network [[cite:PUB00086230]].

Name: Matrin/U1-C-like, C2H2-type zinc finger
ShortDescription:
This entry represents U1-type zinc finger domains, a family of C2H2-type zinc fingers present in matrin, U1 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein C and other RNA-binding proteins [[cite:PUB00031914], [cite:PUB00035823]].

;

C2H2-type (classical) zinc fingers (Znf) were the first class to be characterised. They contain a short β-hairpin and an α-helix (β/β/α structure), where a single zinc atom is held in place by Cys(2)His(2) (C2H2) residues in a tetrahedral array. C2H2 Znf's can be divided into three groups based on the number and pattern of fingers: triple-C2H2 (binds single ligand), multiple-adjacent-C2H2 (binds multiple ligands), and separated paired-C2H2 [[cite:PUB00035808]]. C2H2 Znf's are the most common DNA-binding motifs found in eukaryotic transcription factors, and have also been identified in prokaryotes [[cite:PUB00035809]]. Transcription factors usually contain several Znf's (each with a conserved β/β/α structure) capable of making multiple contacts along the DNA, where the C2H2 Znf motifs recognise DNA sequences by binding to the major groove of DNA via a short α-helix in the Znf, the Znf spanning 3-4 bases of the DNA [[cite:PUB00035811]]. C2H2 zinc fingers can also bind to RNA and protein targets [[cite:PUB00043274]].

;

Zinc finger (Znf) domains are relatively small protein motifs which contain multiple finger-like protrusions that make tandem contacts with their target molecule. Some of these domains bind zinc, but many do not; instead, they bind other metals, such as iron, or no metal at all. For example, some family members form salt bridges to stabilise the finger-like folds. They were first identified as a DNA-binding motif in transcription factor TFIIIA from Xenopus laevis (African clawed frog); however, they are now recognised to bind DNA, RNA, protein and/or lipid substrates [[cite:PUB00035807], [cite:PUB00035805], [cite:PUB00035806], [cite:PUB00035804], [cite:PUB00014077]]. Their binding properties depend on the amino acid sequence of the finger domains and of the linker between fingers, as well as on the higher-order structures and the number of fingers. Znf domains are often found in clusters, where fingers can have different binding specificities. There are many superfamilies of Znf motifs, varying in both sequence and structure. They display considerable versatility in binding modes, even between members of the same class (e.g., some bind DNA, others protein), suggesting that Znf motifs are stable scaffolds that have evolved specialised functions. For example, Znf-containing proteins function in gene transcription, translation, mRNA trafficking, cytoskeleton organisation, epithelial development, cell adhesion, protein folding, chromatin remodelling and zinc sensing, to name but a few [[cite:PUB00035812]]. Zinc-binding motifs are stable structures, and they rarely undergo conformational changes upon binding their target.

Name: Zinc finger, double-stranded RNA binding
ShortDescription: This zinc finger is mainly found in eukaryotic sequences, and is approximately 30 amino acids in length. The mammalian members of this group occur multiple times along the protein, joined by flexible linkers, and are referred to as JAZ - dsRNA-binding ZF protein - zinc-fingers. The JAZ proteins are expressed in all tissues tested and localise in the nucleus, particularly the nucleolus [[cite:PUB00053807]]. JAZ preferentially binds to double-stranded (ds) RNA or RNA/DNA hybrids rather than DNA. In addition to binding double-stranded RNA, these zinc-fingers are required for nucleolar localisation.

Name: U4/U6.U5 small nuclear ribonucleoprotein component Snu23
ShortDescription: Pre-mRNA splicing is an important step in eukaryotic gene expression. Yeasts and humans share a common set of core spliceosomal proteins that are evolutionarily conserved such as B complex proteins Snu23 (known as ZMAT2 in humans), Prp38 and MFAP1 [[cite:PUB00062925], [cite:PUB00090272]]. This entry represents Snu23. Its structure has been revealed [[cite:PUB00090272], [cite:PUB00090527]].

Name: Nectin-3/4, second Ig domain
ShortDescription:
Nectins are single-pass type I membrane glycoproteins belonging to the immunoglobulin superfamily. They are characterised by three Ig-like domains (a distal IgV domain and two IgC domains) in the ectodomain, followed by a transmembrane region and a cytoplasmic tail [[cite:PUB00078406]]. Unlike cadherins, nectins are Ca2+-independent cell adhesion molecules that mediate not only homotypic but also heterotypic cell-cell adhesion [[cite:PUB00078408]]. The cytoplasmic tail of nectins possesses a conserved afadin-binding motif, except for nectin-4 which binds the PDZ domain of afadin at its carboxyl terminus. Afadin connects nectins to F-actin and the actin cytoskeleton [[cite:PUB00078406], [cite:PUB00078416], [cite:PUB00078417]].

;

This entry represents the second Ig domain of nectin-3 and 4. Nectin-3 [[cite:PUB00078422]] plays a role in cell-cell adhesion through heterophilic transinteractions with other nectins. Nectin-2 and nectin-3 are expressed in Sertoli cells and spermatids, respectively, and their transinteraction regulates the organization of the Sertoli cell-spermatid junctions that plays a critical role in spermatid development [[cite:PUB00078419], [cite:PUB00078423]]. Nectin-3 and nectin-1 interactions play a critical role in selective axo-dendritic adhesion [[cite:PUB00078425]]. Nectin-4 seems to be involved in cell adhesion through trans-homophilic and -heterophilic interactions [[cite:PUB00078429]]. It acts as a receptor for measles virus [[cite:PUB00078427], [cite:PUB00067246], [cite:PUB00078428]]. Nectin 4 plays a significant role in cancer cell growth and invasion [[cite:PUB00078430], [cite:PUB00078432]].

Name: Nectin and Nectin-like
ShortDescription: The Nectin family is involved in various cell-cell adhesion processes. Members of this family mediate adhesion through homophilic and heterophilic interactions, which can include specific interactions between different nectins. These interactions are crucial for the formation of cell-cell junctions, including adherens junctions and synapses. Some family members act as receptors for viruses, facilitating entry into cells, while others are involved in neurite outgrowth by interacting with growth factor receptors. Additionally, the family plays roles in synaptic inhibition in the brain, regulating presynaptic differentiation through interactions with other synaptic proteins. The family's involvement in cell adhesion and signaling underpins its importance in tissue morphogenesis, immune response, and neural network formation.

Name: Flagellum-associated coiled-coil domain-containing protein 1
ShortDescription: Juvenile amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) is a form of chronic motor neuron disease characterised by combined upper and lower motor neuron symptoms. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis 2 (ALS2) is an autosomal recessive form of juvenile ALS and has been mapped to human chromosome 2q33 [[cite:PUB00061628]]. Amyotrophic lateral sclerosis 2 chromosomal region candidate gene 12 protein (ALS2CR12), also known as FLACC1, is a putative GTPase regulator and its mutation is linked to the familial amyotrophic lateral sclerosis 2 [[cite:PUB00061628]].

Name: TRPM, tetramerisation domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents a short anti-parallel coiled-coil tetramerisation domain of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member proteins 1/3/6/7. It is held together by extensive core packing and interstrand polar interactions. Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels comprise a large family of tetrameric cation-selective ion channels that respond to diverse forms of sensory input. The presence of cytoplasmic domains that direct channel assembly appears to be a feature of many voltage-gated ion channel superfamily members [[cite:PUB00051613]].

Name: Calcium channel YVC1-like, C-terminal transmembrane domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in members of the transient receptor potential Ca2+/cation channel (TRP-CC) family. It is found in Calcium channel YVC1 from Saccharomyces cerevisiae, for example, which is a transient receptor potential (TRP) channel required for release of calcium ions from the vacuole in response to hyperosmotic shock. This domain adopts an all-α configuration [[cite:PUB00155926], [cite:PUB00155706]]. It is often found associated with [interpro:IPR056337].

Name: Transient receptor potential cation channel M
ShortDescription: The TRPM family comprises ion channels with diverse regulatory mechanisms and functions, including cellular divalent cation homeostasis, sensory perception, and response to environmental changes. Members are involved in mediating calcium and magnesium influx, contributing to membrane depolarization, and are activated by various stimuli such as temperature changes, ligand binding, and intracellular Ca(2+) levels. Some members possess kinase activity, playing roles in phosphorylation processes. The family is implicated in physiological processes like taste transduction, insulin secretion, cell migration, and response to oxidative stress. TRPM channels are also essential in neuronal cell death regulation and immune responses.

Name: Alpha-type protein kinase, alpha-kinase domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a protein kinase catalytic domain with no detectable similarity to conventional kinases that is found in eukaryotic alpha-kinases [[cite:PUB00033799]]. This domain is shared by EF-2 kinase and the myosin heavy chain kinase A (MHCK A) [[cite:PUB00007404], [cite:PUB00007403]].

As in classical kinase, this domain consists of two lobes that bind nucleotide at the interface between them. The N-terminal lobe is very similar in structure to that of classical protein kinases, whereas its C-terminal lobe resembles that of ATP-grasp proteins more closely. A conserved C-terminal glycine rich motif which locates in the region that corresponds to the activation loop of classical kinases is essential for the enzymatic activity [[cite:PUB00007405]].

Name: Transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 7, alpha-kinase domain
ShortDescription:
The TRPM subfamily of mammalian TRP channels includes TRPM7, which is a bifunctional molecule consisting of a TRP ion channel fused to a serine/threonine-protein kinase domain. It conducts Zn(2+), Mg(2+), and Ca(2+) as well as monovalent cations [[cite:PUB00070766]]. The kinase domain is proteolytically cleaved from the channel domain in a cell-type-specific manner, with the cleaved kinase fragments translocating to the nucleus and binding multiple components of chromatin-remodeling complexes [[cite:PUB00070766]]. TRPM7 plays a prominent role in cellular and systemic magnesium homeostasis, and is a key player in embryonic development, global ischemia, cardiovascular disease, and cancer [[cite:PUB00070534]].

;

This entry represents the alpha-kinase domain of TRMP7.

Name: TRPM-like domain
ShortDescription:
This domain is found in human transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member 1-8 (TRPM 1-8) and similar proteins. This domain is found associated with [[interpro:IPR005821]] and adopts an all-α configuration. This entry also includes protein ced-11 of Caenorhabditis elegans, which plays a major role in programmed cell death [[cite:PUB00160452]].

;

Transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M (TRPM) is a group of cation-permeable channels within the larger TRP superfamily. The TRPM subfamily consists of eight members: TRPM1-TRPM8. TRPMs have been involved in several physiological and pathological processes, including cellular proliferation, temperature sensing, vascular development, cancer progression, neurological diseases, endothelial dysfunction, inflammation, type II diabetes, and many other processes. TRPM channels possess a large cytosolic domain consisting of 732 and 1611 aa for each subunit, making them the largest members of the TRP superfamily [[cite:PUB00160453]].

Name: TRPM, SLOG domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the SLOG-like domain found in several eukaryotic channels including diverse ciliate channels and the TRPM class of animal ion channels. The SLOG (SMF/DprA-LOG) domain adopts a three-layered α/β sandwich Rossmannoid fold. It is positioned near the N terminus of all TRPM channels and is predicted to play a regulatory role for the channel in potentially recognizing a universal nucleotide or nucleotide-derived ligand [[cite:PUB00091021]].

Name: TRPM, tetramerisation domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This entry represents a short anti-parallel coiled-coil tetramerisation domain superfamily of the transient receptor potential cation channel subfamily M member proteins 1/3/6/7. It is held together by extensive core packing and interstrand polar interactions. Transient receptor potential (TRP) channels comprise a large family of tetrameric cation-selective ion channels that respond to diverse forms of sensory input. The presence of cytoplasmic domains that direct channel assembly appears to be a feature of many voltage-gated ion channel superfamily members [[cite:PUB00051613]].

Name: Sorting nexin 9 family
ShortDescription: Proteins in the sorting nexin 9 subfamily includes SNX9, SNX18 and SNX33 [[cite:PUB00068942]]. They are characterised by the presence of an N-terminal SH3 domain ([interpro:IPR001452]), a PX domain that is a phosphoinositide-binding module ([interpro:IPR001683]), and a Bin/Amphiphysin/Rvs (BAR) domain at the C terminus, which allows membrane binding and bending. They are required for progression and completion of mitosis [[cite:PUB00068943]].

Name: SNX18, PX domain
ShortDescription:
Sorting nexin-18 (SNX18) is localized to peripheral endosomal structures, and acts in a trafficking pathway that is clathrin-independent but relies on AP-1 and PACS1 [[cite:PUB00068944]]. It binds FIP5 and is required for apical lumen formation [[cite:PUB00085579]]. It may also play a role in axonal elongation [[cite:PUB00085581]]. SNXs are Phox homology (PX) domain containing proteins that are involved in regulating membrane traffic and protein sorting in the endosomal system [[cite:PUB00068944], [cite:PUB00068948]]. SNX18 also contains BAR and SH3 domains.

;

The PX domain is a phosphoinositide (PI) binding module present in many proteins with diverse functions. Sorting nexins (SNXs) make up the largest group among PX domain containing proteins. They are involved in regulating membrane traffic and protein sorting in the endosomal system. The PX domain of SNXs binds PIs and targets the protein to PI-enriched membranes [[cite:PUB00084390]].

Name: Sorting nexin protein, WASP-binding domain
ShortDescription: The C-terminal region of the Sorting nexin group of proteins appears to carry a BAR-like (Bin/amphiphysin/Rvs) domain. This domain is very diverse and the similarities with other BAR domains are few. In the Sorting nexins it is associated with [interpro:IPR001683], and in combination with PX appears to be necessary to bind WASP along with p85 to form a multimeric signalling complex [[cite:PUB00014978]].

Name: Sorting nexin-18, SH3 domain
ShortDescription:
Sorting nexin-18 (SNX18) is localized to peripheral endosomal structures, and acts in a trafficking pathway that is clathrin-independent but relies on AP-1 and PACS1 [[cite:PUB00068944]]. It binds FIP5 and is required for apical lumen formation [[cite:PUB00085579]]. It may also play a role in axonal elongation [[cite:PUB00085581]]. SNXs are Phox homology (PX) domain containing proteins that are involved in regulating membrane traffic and protein sorting in the endosomal system [[cite:PUB00068944], [cite:PUB00068948]]. SNX18 also contains BAR and SH3 domains.

;

This entry represent the SH3 domain of SNX18.

Name: CDK5 regulatory subunit-associated protein 2
ShortDescription: CDK5 regulatory subunit-associated protein 2 (CDK5RAP2) is a centrosomal protein that regulates centrosomal maturation by recruitment of a gamma-tubulin ring complex (gamma-TuRC) onto centrosomes [[cite:PUB00093344]]. It interacts directly with EB1, a prototypic member of microtubule plus-end tracking proteins. The CDK5RAP2-EB1 complex regulates microtubule dynamics and stability [[cite:PUB00093345]]. CDK5RAP2 also interacts with Cep169, a microtubule plus-end-tracking centrosomal protein; this interaction regulates stability of microtubules [[cite:PUB00093343]]. Mutations in the CDK5RAP2 gene cause microcephaly 3, primary, autosomal recessive (MCPH3) [[cite:PUB00093346], [cite:PUB00093347]].

Name: CDK5 regulatory subunit-associated protein 2/Myomegalin, coiled coil
ShortDescription:
This domain is found in human CDK5 regulatory subunit-associated protein 2 (CDK5RAP2), myomegalin (MYOME, also known as PDE4DIP) and related sequences mainly from vertebrates.

CDK5RAP2 is a potential regulator of CDK5 activity that plays a role in the spindle checkpoint activation and regulates centrosomal maturation [[cite:PUB00093343]]. It plays a role in the spindle checkpoint activation by acting as a transcriptional regulator of both BUBR1 and MAD2 promoter. Together with EB1/MAPRE1, it may promote microtubule polymerization, bundle formation, growth and dynamics at the plus [[cite:PUB00093343]]. It forms a complex with MYOME isoform 13/MMG8/SMYLE, MAPRE1 and AKAP9, to contribute to microtubules nucleation and extension from the centrosome to the cell periphery [[cite:PUB00091368]]. MYOME participates in microtubule dynamics, promoting microtubule assembly. Depending upon the cell context, may act at the level of the Golgi apparatus or that of the centrosome [[cite:PUB00156007], [cite:PUB00156008], [cite:PUB00156009], [cite:PUB00091368]]. It forms a complex with AKAP9, and recruits CAMSAP2 to the Golgi apparatus and tethers non-centrosomal minus-end microtubules to the Golgi, an important step for polarised cell movement [[cite:PUB00156008], [cite:PUB00156009]].

This entry represents a centrally located region that forms an α-helical coiled-coil (CC) in these proteins.

Name: Myomegalin-like, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
This domain is found towards the C-terminal end of human Myomegalin (PDE4DIP) and CDK5RAP2, and similar animal sequences. This domain is predicted to adopt an all-α configuration.

;

PDE4DIP functions as an anchor sequestering component of the cAMP-dependent pathway to Golgi and/or centrosomes [[cite:PUB00075362]]. It may participate in microtubule dynamics, promoting microtubule assembly, in an isoform-specific manner [[cite:PUB00156007], [cite:PUB00156008], [cite:PUB00156009]].

;

CDK5RAP2 is a potential regulator of CDK5 activity via its interaction with CDK5R1 [[cite:PUB00162526]]. It plays a role in the spindle checkpoint activation by acting as a transcriptional regulator of both BUBR1 and MAD2 promoter [[cite:PUB00162219]]. It regulates centrosomal maturation by recruitment of the gamma-tubulin ring complex (gTuRC) onto centrosomes [[cite:PUB00075363]].

Name: Centrosomin, N-terminal motif 1
ShortDescription: This domain (Cnn_1N) is a short conserved motif found in the N-terminal of a group of centrosome or spindle pole body (SPB) associated proteins, including Mto1 and Pcp1 from S. pombe [[cite:PUB00016981], [cite:PUB00045027]], centrosomin from flies [[cite:PUB00075361], [cite:PUB00075364]] and myomegalin/CDK5RAP2 from mammals [[cite:PUB00075363], [cite:PUB00075362]].

Name: Spen paralogue and orthologue SPOC, C-terminal
ShortDescription:
Spen (split end) proteins regulate the expression of key transcriptional effectors in diverse signalling pathways. They are large proteins characterised by N-terminal RNA-binding motifs and a highly conserved C-terminal SPOC (Spen paralog and ortholog C-terminal) domain. The function of the SPOC domain is unknown, but the SPOC domain of the SHARP Spen protein has been implicated in the interaction of SHARP with the SMRT/NcoR corepressor, where SHARP plays an essential role in the repressor complex [[cite:PUB00013949]].

The SPOC domain is folded into a single compact domain consisting of a β-barrel with seven strands framed by six α helices. A number of deep grooves and clefts in the surface, plus two nonpolar loops, render the SPOC domain well suited to protein-protein interactions; most of the conserved residues occur on the protein surface rather than in the core. Other proteins containing a SPOC domain include Drosophila Split ends, which promotes sclerite development in the head and restricts it in the thorax, and mouse MINT (homologue of SHARP), which is involved in skeletal and neuronal development via its repression of Msx2.

Name: RBM15, RNA recognition motif 2
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the RNA recognition motif 2 (RRM2) of RBM15.

;

RNA-binding motif protein 15 (RBM15), also termed one-twenty two protein 1 (OTT1), is a novel mRNA export factor and component of the NXF1 pathway. It binds to NXF1 and serves as receptor for the RNA export element RTE [[cite:PUB00083591]]. It also possesses mRNA export activity and can facilitate the access of DEAD-box protein DBP5 to mRNA at the nuclear pore complex (NPC) [[cite:PUB00083592]].

Name: SPOC-like, C-terminal domain superfamily
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents the Spen Paralogue and Orthologue C-terminal (SPOC) domain and its structural homologues. This domain has a closed β-barrel fold of complex topology. Proteins that carry a SPOC-like domain include:

  • Spen proteins, such as SHARP (SMRT/HDAC1-associated repressor protein), which carry a SPOC domain at the C-terminal and an RNA-binding motif in the N-terminal; Spen proteins regulate the expression of key transcriptional effectors in diverse signalling pathways, the SHARP protein being a component of transcriptional repression complexes in both nuclear receptor and Notch/RBP-Jkappa signalling pathways [[cite:PUB00013949]].
  • The middle domains of Ku70 and Ku80 (which includes the C-terminal α-helical arm and the DNA encircling insertion); the Ku heterodimer, which is composed of Ku70 and Ku80 subunits, contributes to genomic integrity through its ability to bind DNA double-strand breaks and facilitate repair by the non-homologous end-joining pathway [[cite:PUB00007947]].

Name: Protein Phosphatase 1 Regulatory Subunit
ShortDescription: The protein family is involved in the regulation of protein phosphatase 1 (PP1) activity, which is central to various cellular processes. Members of this family mediate the binding to myosin and regulate myosin phosphatase activity, influencing muscle contraction and cell motility. Some members are involved in the dephosphorylation of key proteins such as PLK1, affecting cell cycle progression, and HIF1A, impacting cellular responses to hypoxia. Others contribute to endothelial cell barrier function, angiogenesis, and the PI3K/AKT signaling pathway. Additionally, the family includes proteins that modulate Notch and Wnt signaling pathways, playing roles in development and cell fate determination. Overall, the family members act as key regulators of various signaling cascades and cellular mechanisms through their interactions with and modulation of PP1 activity.

Name: Protein phosphatase 1, regulatory subunit 16A/B
ShortDescription:
Protein phosphatase 1(PP-1) is a major protein serine/threonine phosphatase that regulates a vast array of cellular processes. PP-1 action is controlled through regulatory subunits that not only dictate substrate specificity and subcellular localisation, but often regulate PP-1 activity [[cite:PUB00073640]]. The myosin phosphatase targeting protein (MYPT) family consists of regulatory subunits MYPT1, MYPT2, MBS85, MYPT3 and TIMAP. MYPT family members share several conserved domains, including an RVxF motif for PP1c binding, and several ankyrin repeats that mediate protein-protein interactions [[cite:PUB00073641]].

This entry consists of protein phosphatase 1 regulatory subunits 16A (MYPT3) and 16B (TIMAP). MYPT3 and TIMAP contain a C-terminal CaaX box (a prenylation motif where 'a' indicates an aliphatic amino acid: CLLM in MYPT3 and CRIS in TIMAP), similar to that identified in the Rho family of small GTPases, which targets the proteins to the cell membrane [[cite:PUB00073642]]. MYPT3 binding to PP1c inhibits its catalytic activity towards LC20, contrary to other MYPT family members [[cite:PUB00073643]]. TIMAP (TGF-beta-inhibited membrane-associated protein) is primarily localised to the plasma membrane of endothelial cells [[cite:PUB00073642], [cite:PUB00073645]]. TIMAP-PP1c substrates identified include the non-integrin laminin receptor 1 (LAMR1), which is involved in regulation of cell motility and angiogenesis [[cite:PUB00073644]], and ERM (ezrin-radixin-moesin) proteins, which crosslink actin filaments with plasma membranes [[cite:PUB00073646]].

Name: Translocation protein Sec62
ShortDescription: Members of the NSCC2 family have been sequenced from various yeast, fungal and animals species including Saccharomyces cerevisiae, Drosophila melanogaster and Homo sapiens. These proteins are the Sec62 proteins, believed to be associated with the Sec61 and Sec63 constituents of the general protein secretary systems of yeast microsomes. They are also the non-selective cation (NS) channels of the mammalian cytoplasmic membrane. The yeast Sec62 protein has been shown to be essential for cell growth. The mammalian NS channel proteins have been implicated in platelet derived growth factor(PGDF) dependent single channel current in fibroblasts. These channels are essentially closed in serum deprived tissue-culture cells and are specifically opened by exposure to PDGF. These channels are reported to exhibit equal selectivity for Na+, K+ and Cs+ with low permeability to Ca2+, and no permeability to anions.

Name: Prefoldin alpha-like
ShortDescription:
This entry represents prefoldin subunit alpha-like proteins. Prefoldin (PFD) is a chaperone that interacts exclusively with type II chaperonins, hetero-oligomers lacking an obligate co-chaperonin that are found only in eukaryotes (chaperonin-containing T-complex polypeptide-1 (CCT)) and archaea. Eukaryotic PFD is a multi-subunit complex containing six polypeptides in the molecular mass range of 14-23kDa. In archaea, on the other hand, PFD is composed of two types of subunits, two alpha and four beta. The six subunits associate to form two back-to-back up-and-down eight-stranded barrels, from which hang six coiled coils. Each subunit contributes one (beta subunits) or two (alpha subunits) β hairpin turns to the barrels. The coiled coils are formed by the N and C termini of an individual subunit. Overall, this unique arrangement resembles a jellyfish. The eukaryotic PFD hexamer is composed of six different subunits; however, these can be grouped into two alpha-like (PFD3 and -5) and four beta-like (PFD1, -2, -4, and -6) subunits based on amino acid sequence similarity with their archaeal counterparts. Eukaryotic PFD has a six-legged structure similar to that seen in the archaeal homologue [[cite:PUB00013306], [cite:PUB00013187]]. This family contains the archaeal alpha subunit, eukaryotic prefoldin subunits 3 and 5 and the UXT (ubiquitously expressed transcript) family.

Eukaryotic PFD has been shown to bind both actin and tubulin co-translationally. The chaperone then delivers the target protein to CCT, interacting with the chaperonin through the tips of the coiled coils. No authentic target proteins of any archaeal PFD have been identified, to date.
