Name: CD209-like, C-type lectin-like domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the C-type lectin-like domain (CTLD) of the type found in human dendritic cell (DC)-specific intercellular adhesion molecule 3-grabbing non-integrin (DC-SIGN), also known as CD209 antigen, and the related receptor, DC-SIGN receptor (DC-SIGNR), also known as CD209 antigen-like protein 1 or C-type lectin domain family 4 member M. This group also contains proteins similar to hepatic asialoglycoprotein receptor (ASGP-R) and langerin (also known as CD207 or C-type lectin domain family 4 member K) in human. These proteins are type II membrane proteins with a CTLD ectodomain. CTLD refers to a domain homologous to the carbohydrate-recognition domains (CRDs) of the C-type lectins [[cite:PUB00081335]].

DC-SIGN is thought to mediate the initial contact between dendritic cells and resting T cells, and may also mediate the rolling of DCs on epithelium [[cite:PUB00081979]]. DC-SIGN and DC-SIGNR bind to oligosaccharides present on human tissues, as well as on pathogens including parasites, bacteria, and viruses. DC-SIGN and DC-SIGNR bind to HIV, enhancing viral infection of T cells [[cite:PUB00031102]]. DC-SIGN and DC-SIGNR are homotetrameric, and contain four CTLDs stabilized by a coiled coil of α helices [[cite:PUB00032369]]. The hepatic ASGP-R is an endocytic recycling receptor which binds and internalizes desialylated glycoproteins having a terminal galactose or N-acetylgalactosamine residues on their N-linked carbohydrate chains, via the clathrin-coated pit mediated endocytic pathway, and delivers them to lysosomes for degradation. It has been proposed that glycoproteins bearing terminals 'Sia (sialic acid) alpha2, 6GalNAc' and 'Sia alpha2, 6Gal' are endogenous ligands for ASGP-R, and that ASGP-R participates in regulating the relative concentration of serum glycoproteins bearing alpha 2,6-linked Sia [[cite:PUB00081982]]. The human ASGP-R is a hetero-oligomer composed of two subunits, both of which are found within this group [[cite:PUB00081981]]. Langerin is expressed in a subset of dendritic leukocytes, the Langerhans cells (LC). Langerin induces the formation of Birbeck Granules (BGs) and associates with these BGs following internalization [[cite:PUB00081976]]. Langerin binds, in a calcium-dependent manner, to glyco-conjugates containing mannose and related sugars mediating their uptake and degradation. Langerin molecules oligomerize as trimers with three CTLDs held together by a coiled-coil of α helices [[cite:PUB00081980]].

Name: C-type Lectin Receptor Immune Modulators
ShortDescription: The protein family is composed of C-type lectin domain-containing receptors with diverse roles in the immune system. Members are involved in pathogen recognition, mediating immune cell interactions, and antigen presentation. They recognize various molecular patterns, including those from bacteria, fungi, and damaged cells, and are implicated in the activation and modulation of immune responses. Some family members function as costimulatory molecules, enhancing T-cell proliferation, or as endocytic receptors, facilitating antigen uptake and presentation. Others contain ITIM motifs, which modulate cellular responses by binding phosphatases upon phosphorylation. Collectively, the family contributes to innate and adaptive immunity by detecting pathogens, presenting antigens, and regulating immune cell signaling.

Name: Syntaxin-8, SNARE domain
ShortDescription: Syntaxin 8 forms a complex with syntaxin 7 (Qa), Vti1b (Qb) and either VAMP7 or VAMP8 (R-SNARE) and is involved in the transport from early endosomes to the lysosome [[cite:PUB00092015], [cite:PUB00092016]]. Syntaxin 8 is a member of the Qc subgroup of SNARE (soluble N-ethylmaleimide-sensitive factor attachment protein receptor) proteins, which consist of coiled-coil helices (called SNARE motifs) that mediate the interactions between SNARE proteins, and a transmembrane domain [[cite:PUB00036793]].

Name: RH2 domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the entire RH2 domain.

The RH2 (RILP homology 2) Rab-binding domain is found in the following animal proteins [[cite:PUB00084277], [cite:PUB00037685], [cite:PUB00084278]]:

  • Rab interacting lysosomal proteins (RILP), which interacts with Rab7, Rab34, and Rab36.
  • RILP-like 1 (RILP-L1), which interacts with Rab12, Rab34, and Rab36.
  • RILP-like 2 (RILP-L2), which interacts with Rab34 and Rab36.
  • JNK-interacting protein 3 (JIP3), which interacts with Rab36 alone.
  • JNK-interacting protein 4 (JIP4), which interacts with Rab36 alone.

The RH2 domain is folded into a long helix alpha1 and a short helix alpha2 connected by a very tight loop. The RH2 domain forms a tightly associated four helices homodimer in which both helices alpha1 and alpha2 are involved in dimerisation. Such a homodimer binds to two separate Rab-GTP molecules on opposite sides, with both helices involved in the interaction with Rab. In the complex interface, although each Rab-GTP interacts with both helices of the RH2 domain, these two helices are contributed by two different molecules, with helix alpha1 coming from one protomer and helix alpha2 from the other protomer [[cite:PUB00037685]].

Name: JNK-interacting protein, leucine zipper II
ShortDescription: This is the second leucine zipper domain (LZII) of several JNK-interacting proteins (JIP). It interacts with the small GTP-binding protein ARF6 [[cite:PUB00052729]].

Name: RH1 domain
ShortDescription:
This is the RILP homology 1 (RH1) protein-protein interaction domain found at the N-terminal of Rab36-binding proteins including Rab interacting lysosomal proteins (RILP), RILP1/2 NK-interacting protein 3 (JIP3) and NK-interacting protein 4 (JIP4). This domain binds to the myosin Va globular tail domain (MyoVa-GTD) [[cite:PUB00084276]].

;

The RH1 (RILP homology 1) protein-protein interaction domain is found in the following animal Rab36-binding proteins:

  • Rab interacting lysosomal proteins (RILP),
  • RILP-like 1 (RILP-L1),
  • RILP-like 2 (RILP-L2),
  • JNK-interacting protein 3 (JIP3),
  • JNK-interacting protein 4 (JIP4).

It binds to the myosin Va globular tail domain (MyoVa-GTD) in mainly hydrophobic interactions.

The RH1 domain adopts an all-helical structure and forms a homodimer with a four-helix bundle conformation to interact with MyoVa-GTD. The RH1 homodimer is structurally separated into two parts, the N-terminal four-helix bundle formed by alpha2 and alpha3N and the C-terminal coiled-coil formed by alpha3C. The four-helix bundle in the RH1 dimer is mainly stabilised by forming a hydrophobic core. The N-terminal small helix (alpha1) and its following loop pack on alpha2 from the same molecule and alpha3 from the neighbouring molecule and thus contribute to the bundle stability. The RH1 homodimer is further strengthened by a coiled coil formed by the C-terminal half of the alpha3-helix [[cite:PUB00084276]].

Name: JNK-interacting protein 3/4
ShortDescription:
C-Jun-amino-terminal kinase (JNK)-interacting protein 3 (JIP3) and 4 (JIP4) are two highly related scaffolding proteins for MAP kinases. They are binding partners for molecular motors kinesin-1 and dynactin, as well as for the small G protein ARF6, which they bind through their leucine zipper II (LZII) region [[cite:PUB00090295], [cite:PUB00090296], [cite:PUB00090294]]. ARF6, together with JIP3 and JIP4, regulates membrane-tethered membrane type 1-matrix metalloproteinase exocytosis in cancer invasion [[cite:PUB00090297]].

The function of JIP4 has been shown to be different from that of other JIP proteins. Although JIP4 binds JNK, it does not activate JNK signaling [[cite:PUB00090301]].

Name: Ubiquitin-associated domain
ShortDescription: UBA domains are a commonly occurring sequence motif of approximately 45 amino acid residues that are found in diverse proteins involved in the ubiquitin/proteasome pathway, DNA excision-repair, and cell signalling via protein kinases [[cite:PUB00005450]]. The human homologue of yeast Rad23A is one example of a nucleotide excision-repair protein that contains both an internal and a C-terminal UBA domain. The solution structure of human Rad23A UBA(2) showed that the domain forms a compact three-helix bundle [[cite:PUB00003958]]. Comparison of the structures of UBA(1) and UBA(2) reveals that both form very similar folds and have a conserved large hydrophobic surface patch which may be a common protein-interacting surface present in diverse UBA domains. Evidence that ubiquitin binds to UBA domains leads to the prediction that the hydrophobic surface patch of UBA domains interacts with the hydrophobic surface on the five-stranded β-sheet of ubiquitin [[cite:PUB00007089]]. This domain is similar in sequence to the N-terminal domain of translation elongation factor EF1B (or EF-Ts) from bacteria, mitochondria and chloroplasts [[cite:PUB00006344]].

Name: Ubiquitin-specific peptidase 24, ubiquitin-like domain
ShortDescription:
Ubiquitin-specific peptidase 24 (USP24, MEROPS identifier C19.047) is a de-ubiquitinating enzyme that is associated with late-onset Parkinson's Disease [[cite:PUB00078668]]. The enzyme is known to remove ubiquitin from damage-specific DNA-binding protein 2 (DDB2), increasing its stability. DDB2 is involved in DNA damage recognition in the nucleotide excision repair pathway, and is a component of an E3 ligase that targets XPC, histones and DDB2 itself [[cite:PUB00078669]]. USP24 also de-ubiquitinates p53, and cells are resistant to apoptosis following UV irradiation if USP24 is depleted because p53 is stabilized [[cite:PUB00078670]]. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms of the USP24 gene have been identified in lung cancer malignancy and could be diagnostic markers for the disease [[cite:PUB00078671]]. The USP24 gene is up-regulated when the USP9X gene is down-regulated by shRNA, leading to increased survival of B-cell myeloma cells [[cite:PUB00078672]]. USP24 positively regulates ferritinophagy, a process in which ferritin is degraded in lysosomes and releases free iron [[cite:PUB00095288]].

;

This entry represents the ubiquitin-like (Ubl) domain of UBP24.

Name: UBP24/USP9X/USP9Y, ubiquitin-like domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents a Ubiquitin-like domain found in a ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolases, such as UBP24, USP9X and USP9Y from human and its orthologue from Drosophila, the probable ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolase FAF. UCHs are thiol proteases that recognise and hydrolyse the peptide bond at the C-terminal glycine of ubiquitin [[cite:PUB00069571]].

UBP24 regulates cell survival in various contexts through modulating the protein stability of some of its substrates including DDB2, MCL1 or TP53 [[cite:PUB00078669]]. It plays a positive role on ferritinophagy where ferritin is degraded in lysosomes and releases free iron [[cite:PUB00095288]]. USP9X and USP9Y are involved in deubiquitination of target proteins [[cite:PUB00154898]]. USP9X is also involved in the processing of ubiquitin precursors [[cite:PUB00132877], [cite:PUB00045907], [cite:PUB00154899], [cite:PUB00154900], [cite:PUB00154901]] and therefore, it may play an important regulatory role at the level of protein turnover by preventing degradation of proteins.

Name: UBP34/UBP24/USP9X/USP9Y-like, ARM repeat region
ShortDescription: This entry represents an ARM-repeats domain found in ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolases (UCHs), such as human UBP24, UBP34, USP9X and USP9Y and the orthologues from Drosophila. UCHs are thiol proteases that recognise and hydrolyse the peptide bond at the C-terminal glycine of ubiquitin [[cite:PUB00069571]]. UBP24 regulates cell survival in various contexts through modulating the protein stability of some of its substrates including DDB2, MCL1 or TP53 [[cite:PUB00078669]]. USP9X and USP9Y are involved in deubiquitination of target proteins [[cite:PUB00154898]].

Name: Ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolases
ShortDescription: The peptidase C19 family, also known as ubiquitin carboxyl-terminal hydrolases, encompasses deubiquitinating enzymes that play crucial roles in various cellular processes by removing ubiquitin from specific proteins and polyubiquitin chains. These enzymes are involved in the regulation of protein turnover, DNA damage repair, cell cycle progression, apoptosis, immune response, and signal transduction pathways such as Wnt and TGF-beta/BMP. They function by processing ubiquitin precursors, recycling ubiquitin molecules, editing polyubiquitin chains, and preventing proteasomal degradation of substrates. Some family members are also implicated in the regulation of mitophagy, endosomal protein recycling, and maintenance of circadian rhythm. The family includes enzymes that act as tumor suppressors, regulators of cell growth and differentiation, and modulators of inflammatory and antiviral responses.

Name: Ubiquitin-specific peptidase 24, UBA domain
ShortDescription:
Ubiquitin-specific peptidase 24 (USP24, MEROPS identifier C19.047) is a de-ubiquitinating enzyme that is associated with late-onset Parkinson's Disease [[cite:PUB00078668]]. The enzyme is known to remove ubiquitin from damage-specific DNA-binding protein 2 (DDB2), increasing its stability. DDB2 is involved in DNA damage recognition in the nucleotide excision repair pathway, and is a component of an E3 ligase that targets XPC, histones and DDB2 itself [[cite:PUB00078669]]. USP24 also de-ubiquitinates p53, and cells are resistant to apoptosis following UV irradiation if USP24 is depleted because p53 is stabilized [[cite:PUB00078670]]. Single-nucleotide polymorphisms of the USP24 gene have been identified in lung cancer malignancy and could be diagnostic markers for the disease [[cite:PUB00078671]]. The USP24 gene is up-regulated when the USP9X gene is down-regulated by shRNA, leading to increased survival of B-cell myeloma cells [[cite:PUB00078672]]. USP24 positively regulates ferritinophagy, a process in which ferritin is degraded in lysosomes and releases free iron [[cite:PUB00095288]].

;

This entry represents the N-terminal ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain of UBP24.

Name: ATP-dependent Zinc Metalloprotease
ShortDescription: The ATP-dependent zinc metalloprotease family, characterized by the presence of peptidase M41 and AAA ATPase domains, is involved in the quality control, assembly, and regulation of mitochondrial and membrane proteins. Members of this family exhibit processive, ATP-dependent metallopeptidase activity, targeting both cytoplasmic and membrane proteins for degradation. They play crucial roles in the maintenance of mitochondrial function, including the formation and regulation of the mitochondrial permeability transition pore, the turnover of misfolded or mistranslated polypeptides, and the assembly of mitochondrial respiratory chain complexes. Some family members are essential for neuron development, mediating the degradation of specific mitochondrial proteins to promote efficient assembly of protein complexes. This family also contributes to the proteolytic maturation of other mitochondrial proteases and is involved in the regulation of mitochondrial dynamics through the processing of key proteins like OPA1.

Name: Class I myosin tail homology domain
ShortDescription:
Class I myosins (Myo1s) are widely expressed in eukaryotic cells. Myo1s exist as monomers and can sense cellular mechanical forces and function as tension- sensitive anchors or transporters. Each Myo1 contains from N terminus to C terminus, a motor domain, a neck region consisting of several calmodulin (CaM)-binding IQ motifs and a tail region. All Myo1s contain a tail homology (TH1) domain featuring an embedded pleckstrin-homology (PH) domain capable of binding to lipid membranes. In addition, Myo1s with long tails also contain a TH2 (or GPA) domain and a C-terminal TH3 (or SH3) domain, the latter of which may be responsible for binding to cargos. All Myo1s are capable of bridging actin cytoskeletons with lipid membranes by using their motor heads and tail TH1 domains.

The TH1 domain is an extended PH domain capable of binding to lipids [[cite:PUB00077755], [cite:PUB00077756]].

Name: Class I myosin, motor domain
ShortDescription:
Class I myosins are present in a wide range of species from yeast to man, and have been implicated in actin cytoskeleton organization, cell motility, and endocytosis [[cite:PUB00085523], [cite:PUB00086497]]. They are actin-dependent molecular motors that play important roles in muscle contraction, cell motility, and organelle transport. S. cerevisiae has two class I myosins, Myo3 and Myo5, whereas S. pombe has only Myo1 [[cite:PUB00086498]]. Vertebrates have eight class I myosin genes, six of which encode short-tailed forms (Myo1a, b, c, d, g, and h) and two of which encode long-tailed forms (Myo1e, f) [[cite:PUB00085523]]. Myosin I, an unconventional myosin, does not form dimers [[cite:PUB00086448]].

Myosin I consist of a N-terminal motor domain, a C-terminal tail homology domain (TH1), and in some cases additional C-terminal structures that can mediate protein-protein interactions. The class 1 myosin motor domain contains motifs that are conserved across the myosin superfamily, including an actin binding cleft and a nucleotide binding pocket. When ATP is present, the motor has a low affinity for actin. Attachment to actin is accompanied by a force generating conformational change, referred to as a 'working stroke' [[cite:PUB00086499]].

Name: Centrosomal and Immune Signaling Modulators
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes various members with roles in cellular structure and signaling. Some proteins in this family are involved in the organization of microtubules and are essential for the assembly of centriole subdistal appendages, indicating a role in cell division and cytoskeletal organization. Other members function as adapter proteins that are crucial for both innate and adaptive immune responses. They mediate T-cell receptor-stimulated activation, regulate thymocyte development, and contribute to regulatory T-cell stability and function. These proteins also modulate signaling pathways by facilitating the recruitment of specific kinases to the Golgi apparatus and lysosomes, and by regulating the translocation of receptors to lipid rafts in response to external stimuli such as viral infection or inflammation. Additionally, some proteins may play a role in myoblast fusion during muscle development and in acrosome formation in spermatogenesis.

Name: Tumor Necrosis Factor Ligand Superfamily
ShortDescription: The protein family is part of the tumor necrosis factor superfamily, which includes cytokines involved in a wide range of biological processes such as cell proliferation, differentiation, apoptosis, lipid metabolism, and coagulation. Members of this family are key players in the immune system and inflammatory response. They function as ligands that activate various receptors, including EDAR, EDA2R, TNFRSF13B/TACI, and TNFRSF17/BCMA, influencing cell signaling pathways like NF-kappa-B activation. They are involved in epithelial-mesenchymal signaling during the morphogenesis of ectodermal organs, regulation of tumor cell growth, angiogenesis, endothelial cell proliferation, and the regulation of humoral immunity. Some isoforms may also play roles in cell adhesion and have tumor suppressor activity. The family's involvement extends to the innate immune response and the melanization immune response, as well as the development of thermal allodynia following tissue damage.

Name: Protein SSUH2 homolog
ShortDescription: SSUH2 protein is implicated in the biological process of odontogenesis, which is the complex development of teeth. Members of this family are homologous proteins that share a conserved function across different species, including zebrafish, mice, and humans. The role of the SSUH2 in odontogenesis suggests their involvement in the tooth development [[cite:PUB00155260]].

Name: Sorting nexin PX domain-containing protein
ShortDescription: This family of proteins is involved in intracellular trafficking, indicating a role in the transport and sorting of molecules within the cell. Members of this family are characterized by the presence of a PX domain, which is known to bind specifically to phosphatidylinositol 3-phosphate (PtdIns(P3)) enriched membranes. This lipid-binding ability suggests that these proteins may associate with endosomal membranes or other intracellular compartments where PtdIns(P3) is present, thereby influencing the localization and function of these proteins in cellular trafficking pathways.

Name: Ribosome maturation protein SDO1/SBDS, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the N-terminal domain of proteins that are highly conserved in species ranging from archaea to vertebrates and plants [[cite:PUB00020303]], including several Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome (SBDS, OMIM 260400) proteins from both mouse and humans. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder with clinical features that include pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, haematological dysfunction and skeletal abnormalities. It is characterised by bone marrow failure and leukemia predisposition.

Members of this entry play a role in RNA metabolism [[cite:PUB00020305], [cite:PUB00020304]]. In yeast, SBDS orthologue SDO1 is involved in the biogenesis of the 60S ribosomal subunit and translational activation of ribosomes. Together with the EF-2-like GTPase RIA1 (EfI1), it triggers the GTP-dependent release of TIF6 from 60S pre-ribosomes in the cytoplasm, thereby activating ribosomes for translation competence by allowing 80S ribosome assembly and facilitating TIF6 recycling to the nucleus, where it is required for 60S rRNA processing and nuclear export. This data links defective late 60S subunit maturation to an inherited bone marrow failure syndrome associated with leukemia predisposition [[cite:PUB00045126]].

The SBDS protein is composed of three domains. The N-terminal domain (FYSH, represented in this entry) is the most frequent target for disease mutations and contains a novel mixed α/β-fold, the central domain ([interpro:IPR018978]) consists of a three-helical bundle and the C-terminal domain ([interpro:IPR046928]) has a ferredoxin-like fold [[cite:PUB00020305], [cite:PUB00076340]].

Name: Ribosome maturation protein SBDS, conserved site
ShortDescription: Proteins identified by this conserved site are involved in the biogenesis of the 60S ribosomal subunit and translational activation of ribosomes in eukaryotes. Together with the EF-2-like GTPase RIA1, they may trigger the GTP-dependent release of TIF6 from 60S pre-ribosomes in the cytoplasm, thereby activating ribosomes for translation competence by allowing 80S ribosome assembly and facilitating TIF6 recycling to the nucleus, where it is required for 60S rRNA processing and nuclear export.

Name: Ribosome maturation protein Sdo1/SBDS
ShortDescription:
The proteins in this entry are highly conserved in species ranging from archaea to vertebrates and plants [[cite:PUB00020303]]. The family contains several Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome (SBDS, OMIM 260400) proteins from both mouse and humans. Shwachman-Diamond syndrome is an autosomal recessive disorder with clinical features that include pancreatic exocrine insufficiency, haematological dysfunction and skeletal abnormalities. It is characterised by bone marrow failure and leukemia predisposition [[cite:PUB00045126]]. SBDS is required for the assembly of mature ribosomes and ribosome biogenesis [[cite:PUB00076340]].

Homologue of SBDS from budding yeast is known as Sdo1, which is a guanine nucleotide exchange factor (GEF) involved in ribosome maturation. Together with the EF-2-like GTPase RIA1 (EfI1), it triggers the GTP-dependent release of TIF6 from 60S pre-ribosomes in the cytoplasm, allowing the assembly of mature ribosomes [[cite:PUB00076339]].

Name: Ribosome maturation protein Sdo1/SBDS-like
ShortDescription: Shwachman-Bodian-Diamond syndrome (SDS) is an autosomal disorder with pancreatic, skeletal and bone marrow deficiencies and a predisposition to hematological dysfunction. The syndrome is associated with mutations in the SBDS gene, which encodes a protein that is required for biogenesis of the 60S ribosomal subunit and activation of the ribosome [[cite:PUB00088931]]. Maturation of the ribosomal 60S subunit requires SBDS and the GTPase EFL1, which release the anti-association factor eIF6 from the surface of the ribosomal subunit 60S [[cite:PUB00088932]]. In yeast, SBDS is known as Sdo1, which with the EF-2-like GTPase Ria1, may trigger the GTP-dependent release of Tif6 from 60S pre-ribosomes in the cytoplasm, thereby activating them [[cite:PUB00045126]].

Name: Myosin 5a, cargo-binding domain
ShortDescription: Class V myosins are well studied unconventional myosins, represented by three paralogs (Myo5a,b,c) in vertebrates. Their C-terminal cargo binding domains (CBDs) are important for the binding of a diverse set of cargos, including membrane vesicles, organelles, proteins and mRNA. They interact with several adaptor proteins, in case of Myo5a-CBD, melanophilin (MLPH), Rab interacting lysosomal protein-like 2 (RILPL2), and granuphilin [[cite:PUB00084276]]. Mutations in human Myo5a (many of which map to the cargo binding domain) lead to Griscelli syndrome, a severe neurological disease [[cite:PUB00088006]].

Name: Unconventional myosin-Va/b domain
ShortDescription: This domain is found in mouse Unconventional myosin-Va/b (Myo5a/b) and similar sequences mainly found in animals. Myo5a is a processive actin-based motor that can move in large steps approximating the 36-nm pseudo-repeat of the actin filament. This protein is involved in melanosome transport and mediates the transport of vesicles to the plasma membrane [[cite:PUB00161363]]. Myo5b may be involved in vesicular trafficking via its association with the CART complex, which is necessary for efficient transferrin receptor recycling but not for EGFR degradation [[cite:PUB00161636]]. This domain shows an α helical configuration.

Name: E3 ubiquitin-protein ligase ARIH1-like, UBA-like domain
ShortDescription: This entry represents the UBA-like (UBL) domain from the Human Homologue of Ariadne (HHARI) and its homologues, which are Ariadne subfamily E3 ubiquitin ligase proteins [[cite:PUB00099066], [cite:PUB00152080], [cite:PUB00151735], [cite:PUB00151736]]. This domain binds to Ubiquitin and NEDD8 [[cite:PUB00151735], [cite:PUB00151736]].

Name: Transportin-3/Importin-13, second TPR domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the second TPR domain found in Transportin-3 (TNPO3) from animals, as well as orthologues MTR10 and uncharacterised protein YNR7 from yeast and MOS14 from plant. This entry also includes Importin-13 (IPO3) from animals. This domain is involved in the binding to the globular Ran protein in TNOP3 [[cite:PUB00155880]]. In IPO13, this domain is involved in the protein interaction with Ubc9 for nuclear import [[cite:PUB00155881]] and with eIF1A for nuclear import [[cite:PUB00067136]].

;

These proteins are involved in transport of target proteins into the nucleus. TNPO3 mediates the nuclear import of splicing factor serine/arginine (SR) proteins, such as RBM4, SFRS1 and SFRS2, by recognising phosphorylated SR domains [[cite:PUB00130144], [cite:PUB00155879]].

Name: Transportin-3/Importin-13, fourth TPR domain
ShortDescription:
This entry represents the third TPR domain found in Transportin-3 (TNPO3) from animals, as well as orthologues MTR10 and uncharacterised protein YNR7 from yeast and MOS14 from plants. This entry also includes Importin-13 (IPO3) from animals. This domain interacts with the RS region of the ASF protein for nuclear transport [[cite:PUB00155879]].

Name: Importin beta-like nuclear transport receptors
ShortDescription: The importin beta family is involved in the nuclear-cytoplasmic transport of proteins. Members of this family function as nuclear transport receptors, mediating the import of proteins into the nucleus by recognizing nuclear localization signals (NLS) in cargo substrates. They are also involved in the nuclear export of certain proteins. The transport process is typically energy-dependent, requiring the GTPase Ran, which helps dissociate the cargo-importin complex within the nucleus. The family plays a crucial role in various cellular processes, including mRNA transport, protein import for transcription, splicing, and ribonucleotide reductase function. Some members are also implicated in plant immunity and viral infection processes, such as HIV-1 integration.

Name: Nucleoside phosphatase GDA1/CD39
ShortDescription: A number of nucleoside diphosphate and triphosphate hydrolases as well as some yet uncharacterised proteins have been found to belong to the same family [[cite:PUB00000253], [cite:PUB00002967]]. The uncharacterised proteins all seem to be membrane-bound.

Name: Origin recognition complex, subunit 6, metazoa/plant
ShortDescription:
The Origin Recognition Complex (ORC) is a six-subunit ATP-dependent DNA-binding complex encoded by ORC1-6 [[cite:PUB00052559]]. ORC is a central component for eukaryotic DNA replication, and binds chromatin at replication origins throughout the cell cycle [[cite:PUB00052560]]. ORC directs DNA replication throughout the genome and is required for its initiation [[cite:PUB00052561], [cite:PUB00052562], [cite:PUB00052563]]. ORC bound at replication origins serves as the foundation for assembly of the pre-replicative complex (pre-RC), which includes Cdc6, Tah11 (aka Cdt1), and the Mcm2-7 complex [[cite:PUB00052564], [cite:PUB00052565], [cite:PUB00052566], [cite:PUB00102275]]. Pre-RC assembly during G1 is required for replication licensing of chromosomes prior to DNA synthesis during S phase [[cite:PUB00052567], [cite:PUB00052568], [cite:PUB00052569]]. Cell cycle-regulated phosphorylation of ORC2, ORC6, Cdc6, and MCM by the cyclin-dependent protein kinase Cdc28 regulates initiation of DNA replication, including blocking reinitiation in G2/M phase [[cite:PUB00052560], [cite:PUB00052570], [cite:PUB00052571], [cite:PUB00052572]].

In yeast, ORC also plays a role in the establishment of silencing at the mating-type loci Hidden MAT Left (HML) and Hidden MAT Right (HMR) [[cite:PUB00052561], [cite:PUB00052562], [cite:PUB00052563]]. ORC participates in the assembly of transcriptionally silent chromatin at HML and HMR by recruiting the Sir1 silencing protein to the HML and HMR silencers [[cite:PUB00052563], [cite:PUB00052573], [cite:PUB00052574]].

Name: ORC6, second cyclin-like domain
ShortDescription:
The metazoan and plant origin recognition complex subunit 6 (ORC6) contains two homologous domains that are arranged in tandem and both adopting a cyclin-like topology [[cite:PUB00154135]]. This entry represents the second cyclin-like domain of ORC6, a protein that directs DNA replication by binding to replication origins and is also involved in transcriptional silencing; interacts with Spp1 and with trimethylated histone H3; phosphorylated by Cdc28 [[cite:PUB00011408], [cite:PUB00052582]].

Name: Transcription factor Tfc4/TFIIIC-102/Sfc4
ShortDescription:
TFIIIC-102, also known as general transcription factor 3C polypeptide 3 (GTF3C3), is required for RNA polymerase III-mediated transcription and is a component of the DNA-binding TFIIIC2 subcomplex that directly binds tRNA and virus-associated RNA promoters [[cite:PUB00089467]]. GTF3C3 contains several tetratricopeptide repeats.

In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, this protein is known as transcription factor tau 131kDa subunit (Tfc4). It is the TFIIIB-assembling subunit of RNA polymerase III transcription initiation factor complex (TFIIIC) [[cite:PUB00089468]]. In Schizosaccharomyces pombe, this subunit is known as Sfc4 [[cite:PUB00089469]].

Name: G-protein Coupled Orphan Receptors
ShortDescription: This family of proteins includes G-protein coupled receptors (GPCRs) that are predominantly categorized as orphan receptors, which means their endogenous ligands are unknown. Members of this family are characterized by a significant level of constitutive activity, which is the ability to activate intracellular signaling pathways in the absence of a ligand. The signaling is primarily mediated through the G(s)-alpha protein, stimulating adenylate cyclase to increase intracellular cAMP levels. One member is identified as a high-affinity receptor for lysophosphatidic acid (LPA), indicating a role in mediating cellular responses to this lipid mediator. The family members are implicated in various functions, including potential roles in brain function and cellular signaling.

Name: Kaptin
ShortDescription: This entry represents kaptin (KPTN), an actin-associated protein and component of the KICSTOR complex found in vertebrates. Kaptin may be involved in actin organisation in platelets and neurons [[cite:PUB00071393], [cite:PUB00071391], [cite:PUB00071392]], and localises to lamellipodia and stereocilia. KPTN functions as part of the four-protein KICSTOR complex (KPTN, ITFG2, KICS2, SZT2), which is found at the lysosome and recruits the GATOR1 complex to the lysosomal membrane surface. KICSTOR acts as a negative regulator of mTORC1 signalling during amino acid or glucose starvation, and in the absence of amino acids negatively regulates mTORC1 activity, while loss of KICSTOR function results in constitutive mTORC1 activation [[cite:PUB00085648]]. Mutations in the human KPTN gene cause intellectual developmental disorder with macrocephaly, also known as mental retardation autosomal recessive 41 (MRT41) [[cite:PUB00071392]].

Name: Integrin alpha, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
This superfamily represents a region containing the β-propeller folds found at the N terminus of integrin alpha.

Integrins are the major metazoan receptors for cell adhesion to extracellular matrix proteins and, in vertebrates, also play important roles in certain cell-cell adhesions, make transmembrane connections to the cytoskeleton and activate many intracellular signalling pathways [[cite:PUB00009789], [cite:PUB00035000]]. The integrin receptors are composed of alpha and beta subunit heterodimers. Each subunit crosses the membrane once, with most of the polypeptide residing in the extracellular space, and has two short cytoplasmic domains. Within the N-terminal domain of alpha subunits, seven sequence repeats, each of approximately 60 amino acids, have been found [[cite:PUB00006166], [cite:PUB00005772]].

Name: ZHX, C2H2 finger domain
ShortDescription: This is a C2H2 zinc-finger domain found in ZHX proteins such as ZHX1. ZHXs are multidomain proteins comprising two C2H2 zinc finger motifs and five homeodomains. Both homeodomains and zinc fingers are short protein modules involved in protein-DNA and/or protein-protein interactions; they are frequently associated with roles in transcriptional regulation. All members of the ZHX family are reported to be able to form both homo- and heterodimers via the region containing homeodomain 1 [[cite:PUB00091418]]. ZHX1 is a transcriptional repressor which is ubiquitously expressed. It interacts with nuclear factor Y subunit A (NFYA) and DNA methyl transferase 3B (DNMT3B) for its repression activity. Changes in expression profiles of rat ZHX1 ortholog have been associated with glomerular disease. In addition to the five homeodomains, ZHX1, which also contains of two N-terminal C2H2 zincfingers forms homodimers via homeodomain and can also form heterodimers with ZHX3 [[cite:PUB00091419]].

Name: Major vault protein repeat domain 2
ShortDescription: This short domain is found repeated numerous times in the Major vault protein.

Name: Major vault protein, N-terminal
ShortDescription:
Vaults are the largest ribonucleoprotein particles known, having a mass of approximately 13 MDa. They are multi-subunit structures that may act as scaffolds for proteins involved in signal transduction and may also play a role in nucleo-cytoplasmic transport. Vaults are present in most normal tissues, but are more highly expressed in epithelial cells with secretory and excretory functions, as well as in cells chronically exposed to xenobiotics, such as bronchial cells and cells lining the intestine [[cite:PUB00035318]]. Overexpression of these proteins is linked with multidrug-resistance in cancer cells.

The mammalian vault structure is highly regular and consists of approximately 96 molecules of the 100kDa major vault protein (MVP), 2 molecules of the 240kDa minor vault protein TEP1, 8 molecules of the 193kDa minor vault protein VPARP and at least 6 copies of a small untranslated RNA of 88-141 bases. The MVP molecules form the core of the complex, which is a barrel-like structure with an invaginated waist and two protruding caps. The complex can unfold into two symmetrical flower-like structures with 8 petals each supposedly consisting of 6 MVP molecules [[cite:PUB00005308]].

Name: Major vault protein repeat domain
ShortDescription: The vault is a ubiquitous and highly conserved ribonucleoprotein particle of approximately 13 mDa of unknown function [[cite:PUB00005308]]. This entry corresponds to a repeated domain found in the amino terminal half of the major vault protein.

Name: Major vault protein
ShortDescription: The major vault protein is the major polypeptide component of a large cellular ribonuclear protein complex found in the cytoplasm of eukaryotic cells (known as vaults). Several roles for vaults have been proposed. Vault proteins have been associated with development of multi-drug resistance [[cite:PUB00080565]]. They have also being implicated in the regulation of several cellular processes including transport mechanisms, signal transmission and immune responses [[cite:PUB00080571], [cite:PUB00080566]].

Name: Major vault protein repeat domain superfamily
ShortDescription: This superfamily represents a repeated domain found in the amino terminal half of the Major Vault Protein (MVP). Vaults are one of the largest cytoplasmic ribonucleoprotein particles, found in numerous eukaryotic species. The cellular function carried out by these ribonucleoproteins remains unclear, although roles in multidrug resistance and innate immunity have been suggested [[cite:PUB00050447]]. The primary sequence of MVP consists of seven short sequence repeats of ~55 amino acid residues followed by a central region and a coiled-coil protein association domain, which mediates the interactions between MVP molecules [[cite:PUB00035319]].

Name: Major vault protein repeat domain 2 superfamily
ShortDescription:
The vault complex is the largest ribonucleoprotein particle found in eukaryotes [[cite:PUB00057759]]. Although several functions have been proposed for vaults since their discovery in 1986, including roles in multidrug resistance, cell signaling, and innate immunity, their cellular function remains unclear [[cite:PUB00050447]]. In mammals, vaults contain three proteins: the 100kDa major vault protein (MVP), the 193kDa vault poly(ADP-ribosyl)ating polymerase VPARP and the 240kDa telomerase-associated protein TEP1. Approximately 75% of the vault particle mass is due to MVP [[cite:PUB00057759]]. The MVP monomer folds to form structural repeat domains at the N terminus, a shoulder domain, a cap-helix and cap-ring domains.
